INTU.sells: TurboTax for people doing taxes, QuickBooks and Mailchimp for small businesses, and Credit Karma tips.
INTU.moat: Businesses keep years of books and payroll in QuickBooks, and accountants know it, so moving is a hassle.
INTU.grows: More small businesses running payroll, payments and loans through QuickBooks, plus AI helpers.
INTU.risk: Free government tax filing or cheap AI tools that do taxes and bookkeeping could pull customers away.

ADBE.sells: Photoshop, Premiere, Illustrator and Acrobat subscriptions paid for by creators, students and companies.
ADBE.moat: Designers learn Photoshop in school and clients expect its files, so teams stick with Adobe tools.
ADBE.grows: Pricier plans with Firefly AI features, plus marketing software sold to big brands.
ADBE.risk: Cheap AI image and video makers and simple apps like Canva could make Adobe's tools feel unneeded.

CRM.sells: Software big companies pay for to track customers and run sales and service teams, plus Slack chat.
CRM.moat: A company's whole customer history and daily work live inside Salesforce, so ripping it out hurts.
CRM.grows: Selling extra tools like Slack, data tools and Agentforce AI agents to companies already using it.
CRM.risk: AI agents from rivals, or ones companies build themselves, could make Salesforce less needed.

PAYX.sells: Payroll, HR, retirement plans and insurance services that small and medium businesses pay for monthly.
PAYX.moat: Getting paychecks and taxes right is scary, so once payroll runs smoothly, owners rarely switch.
PAYX.grows: Clients hiring more workers, plus adding HR, benefits and insurance services to each customer.
PAYX.risk: Cheaper app-based rivals like Gusto, or a slowdown that closes small businesses and cuts jobs.

F.sells: Ford pickups, Bronco and Explorer SUVs, Transit work vans and Lincolns for families and fleets, plus loans.
F.moat: Truck buyers are very loyal to Ford, and businesses rely on its huge dealer and repair network for vans.
F.grows: Ford Pro selling software and service to work fleets, plus hybrid trucks that customers want.
F.risk: Car making is costly and cutthroat; recalls, cheap Chinese EVs and money-losing electric cars hurt it.

KO.sells: Coca-Cola, Sprite, Fanta, Dasani, Minute Maid and BODYARMOR drinks sold to shoppers, restaurants and stores.
KO.moat: People everywhere know and trust the Coke name, and bottling partners put it in nearly every store and fridge.
KO.grows: Selling more drinks in growing countries, adding zero-sugar versions, and buying new brands like fairlife.
KO.risk: People cutting back on sugary soda for health reasons, plus sugar taxes and store-brand drinks.

MCD.sells: Burgers, fries, chicken, breakfast and coffee to families, plus rent and fees paid by franchise owners.
MCD.moat: Its huge number of restaurants buys food cheaply, owns prime land, and makes the Golden Arches easy to find.
MCD.grows: Opening new restaurants abroad, app orders and drive-thru, and limited-time menu items that bring people back.
MCD.risk: Shoppers short on money eating at home or switching to cheaper or healthier fast-food rivals.

A.sells: Lab machines that separate and measure chemicals, plus parts and service, paid for by drug and food labs.
A.moat: Labs build their tested methods around Agilent machines and software, so switching means redoing approvals.
A.grows: Drug makers, disease testers and safety labs keep needing more tests, columns, supplies and repair plans.
A.risk: Drug and research labs cutting spending, or rivals like Thermo Fisher and Waters winning new instruments.

AAL.L.sells: Copper and iron ore dug from mines, sold to steel mills, wire makers and factories around the world.
AAL.L.moat: Its metals are the same as everyone's, so it mostly depends on owning big, rich mines that run cheaply.
AAL.L.grows: More copper is needed for electric cars, power lines and data centers, plus higher metal prices.
AAL.L.risk: Falling metal prices, China building less, or trouble at mines and with governments where it digs.

AAPL.sells: iPhones, Macs, iPads, Watches and AirPods, plus App Store, Music and iCloud, paid for by people and firms.
AAPL.moat: People love the brand, and their photos, apps and devices all work together, so leaving feels like a hassle.
AAPL.grows: Selling more services like iCloud, Apple Music and App Store fees to the many people already using iPhones.
AAPL.risk: Courts and regulators forcing App Store changes, or a slowdown in people upgrading their iPhones.

ABBV.sells: Medicines like Skyrizi and Rinvoq for immune diseases, plus Botox, paid by patients, insurers and clinics.
ABBV.moat: Patents block copycats for years, and doctors trust its proven drugs and the famous Botox name.
ABBV.grows: Skyrizi and Rinvoq being used for more diseases, plus new cancer, brain and beauty treatments.
ABBV.risk: Patents running out so cheaper copies arrive, or government rules that push drug prices down.

ABF.L.sells: Cheap clothes at Primark and Penneys stores, plus Twinings tea, sugar, bread and yeast for shops and bakers.
ABF.L.moat: Primark keeps prices very low by skipping ads and online sales and ordering huge amounts of clothing.
ABF.L.grows: Opening new Primark stores in America and Europe, and selling more food brands like Twinings and Ovaltine.
ABF.L.risk: Shoppers moving to online sellers like Shein, or higher costs that squeeze its very low prices.

ABT.sells: Heart devices, FreeStyle Libre sugar sensors, lab tests and Similac formula, paid by hospitals and families.
ABT.moat: Hospitals rely on its tested machines and devices, and its sensor and heart tech is hard to copy fast.
ABT.grows: More people with diabetes wearing Libre sensors, plus new heart devices and tests used around the world.
ABT.risk: Rivals like Dexcom winning sensor users, or recalls like its past baby formula problem.

ACAD.sells: Nuplazid for Parkinson's hallucinations and Daybue for Rett syndrome, paid for by insurers and patients.
ACAD.moat: Patents protect its two approved drugs, and few other medicines are approved for these same illnesses.
ACAD.grows: More Rett patients starting Daybue, selling it in more countries, and new brain drugs now in testing.
ACAD.risk: Cheap copies once patents end, or new drugs failing in testing so nothing replaces the current ones.

ACB.sells: Medical and fun-use cannabis like dried flower, oils, vapes and edibles, sold to patients and stores.
ACB.moat: Cannabis is easy to grow and many rivals sell similar products, so it is hard to keep customers loyal.
ACB.grows: Selling more medical cannabis in places like Germany, Australia and Poland where it is newly allowed.
ACB.risk: Too many growers pushing prices down, and changing laws in each country it sells in.

ACGL.sells: Business insurance, backup insurance for other insurers, and mortgage insurance paid for by home lenders.
ACGL.moat: Mortgage insurers must be approved by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, and few companies clear that bar.
ACGL.grows: Charging higher prices after disasters and writing more policies as brokers bring in new business.
ACGL.risk: A huge hurricane or a housing crash could bring far more claims than the prices it charged covered.

ACHR.sells: Electric air taxis that take off straight up, meant for city rides and for military customers.
ACHR.moat: It is still early, and rivals like Joby are racing to build very similar air taxis.
ACHR.grows: Sales would grow only if regulators approve its aircraft and airlines and cities start flying them.
ACHR.risk: Delays in safety approval, or running out of cash before air taxis earn real money.

ACN.sells: Consulting and tech help like cloud moves, cybersecurity and AI projects for big companies and governments.
ACN.moat: Clients trust it with deep, long projects, and swapping consultants midway is costly and messy.
ACN.grows: Companies keep paying for help adopting AI, moving to the cloud and running their back offices.
ACN.risk: AI tools could let clients do the work themselves and need fewer paid consultants.

ADI.sells: Chips that turn real signals like sound, motion and power into data, for carmakers, factories and phones.
ADI.moat: Its chips get designed into products that stay in use for years, and analog design skill is hard to learn.
ADI.grows: More electronics in cars, factory robots, health devices and cell towers need more of its chips.
ADI.risk: A slump in factory and car demand, or cheaper Chinese rivals catching up on analog chips.

ADP.sells: Payroll and HR software like RUN and Workforce Now, paid for by businesses to pay and manage workers.
ADP.moat: Moving payroll is risky and painful, so businesses rarely leave once their workers are paid through ADP.
ADP.grows: Clients hiring more people, higher prices, and more benefits and HR services through TotalSource.
ADP.risk: Newer, easier payroll apps like Gusto and Rippling winning over small and mid-sized businesses.

AEE.sells: Electricity and natural gas for homes and businesses in Missouri and Illinois, paid through monthly bills.
AEE.moat: It is the approved local utility, so customers in its area cannot simply pick another power company.
AEE.grows: Regulators let it earn more as it builds power lines, plants and grid upgrades, including for data centers.
AEE.risk: Regulators refusing rate increases, or storms and costly plant projects eating into earnings.

AERO.sells: Plane tickets and cargo flights across Mexico and to the US, Latin America, Europe and Asia.
AERO.moat: Its Mexico City hub and Delta partnership help, but airlines compete hard on price.
AERO.grows: More travel between Mexico and the US, more business trips, and its loyalty program.
AERO.risk: High fuel costs, price wars with rivals, or a downturn that keeps people from flying.

AES.sells: Power from solar, wind, gas and coal plants, sold to utilities, tech firms and homes in many countries.
AES.moat: Long power contracts and its own utilities keep customers, but many rivals build solar and wind too.
AES.grows: Tech companies signing deals for clean power to run data centers, plus energy storage projects.
AES.risk: Heavy debt could squeeze it if building new power projects gets pricier or slower.

AFL.sells: Extra cancer, accident and hospital insurance that pays cash, sold to workers in Japan and America.
AFL.moat: The famous duck and deep ties with Japan Post and employers make Aflac a trusted name for cancer cover.
AFL.grows: New policies sold at workplaces, plus money earned by investing the premiums customers pay each month.
AFL.risk: Japan's shrinking, aging population and a weak yen could shrink its biggest market.

AFRM.sells: Pay-later loans at checkout on Amazon and Shopify; stores pay fees and some shoppers pay interest.
AFRM.moat: Big store deals help, but Klarna, PayPal and Apple offer similar pay-later plans, so the edge is not clear.
AFRM.grows: More stores adding it at checkout and more shoppers using the Affirm Card for everyday spending.
AFRM.risk: If shoppers stop repaying in a downturn or lenders stop funding loans, losses could jump fast.

AIG.sells: Insurance for big companies against fires, storms, lawsuits and accidents, plus travel and home cover.
AIG.moat: Few insurers can cover a giant company's factories in many countries at once like AIG can.
AIG.grows: Raising prices when disasters make insurance scarce and winning more global business customers.
AIG.risk: A string of huge hurricanes, wildfires or lawsuits could cost far more than it collected.

AIT.sells: Bearings, belts, pumps, hoses and robot parts sold to factories and food plants to keep machines running.
AIT.moat: Its many local service centers can rush the right part to a broken machine fast, which small rivals can't.
AIT.grows: Factories adding automation and robots, and Applied acquiring smaller parts distributors.
AIT.risk: A slowdown in factory output means fewer repairs and fewer parts sold.

AJG.sells: Helps businesses, schools and churches shop for insurance and handle claims; insurers pay it commissions.
AJG.moat: Clients stay with a broker who knows their risks, since switching means starting over with someone new.
AJG.grows: Acquiring smaller brokers and rising insurance prices, which lift the commissions it earns.
AJG.risk: If insurance prices fall or acquisitions stop adding value, growth could slow sharply.

AKAM.sells: Speeds up and protects websites, video streams and game downloads for banks, stores and media companies.
AKAM.moat: Its servers sit inside networks worldwide, a huge web that took decades to build and is hard to copy.
AKAM.grows: Selling more security tools that block hackers and bots, plus renting out cloud computing power.
AKAM.risk: Cloudflare, Amazon and Microsoft offer cheaper delivery and security, squeezing Akamai's prices.

ALB.sells: Lithium for electric-car and phone batteries, plus bromine fire-safety chemicals and refinery catalysts.
ALB.moat: It owns some of the cheapest lithium sources, but lithium is a commodity and prices swing wildly.
ALB.grows: More electric cars and power-grid batteries needing lithium as the world shifts to cleaner energy.
ALB.risk: New lithium supply, especially from China, could keep prices low and squeeze its profits.

ALC.sells: Cataract lens implants, eye-surgery machines and contact lenses, paid for by surgeons, hospitals and shoppers.
ALC.moat: Surgeons train on its Unity and LenSx machines, then keep ordering the matching packs and lenses.
ALC.grows: More older people need cataract surgery, and premium lenses that fix reading vision cost more.
ALC.risk: Hospitals squeezing prices or a rival's better surgery machine could pull surgeons away.

ALGN.sells: Invisalign clear braces and iTero mouth scanners, paid for by dentists, orthodontists and their patients.
ALGN.moat: Invisalign is the name patients ask for, and dentists who own iTero scanners send cases its way.
ALGN.grows: More teens and kids moving from metal braces to clear aligners, plus scanners in more dental offices.
ALGN.risk: Cheaper aligner rivals and families cutting back on pricey dental work when money is tight.

ALL.sells: Car and home insurance sold through agents and online, paid for by drivers and homeowners.
ALL.moat: Its agents and well-known name help, but drivers can easily switch to a cheaper insurer.
ALL.grows: Raising insurance prices and adding protection plans for phones, cars and identity theft.
ALL.risk: Big storms, wildfires and costly car repairs can pay out more in claims than it collects.

ALLE.sells: Schlage locks, Von Duprin exit bars and keycard systems for schools, hospitals, offices and homes.
ALLE.moat: Builders and safety inspectors trust its names, and buildings stick with one key system for years.
ALLE.grows: Old buildings swapping metal keys for electronic and phone-based door locks and software.
ALLE.risk: A slowdown in new building and tech firms selling cheaper smart locks.

ALLY.sells: Car loans and leases through dealers plus online savings accounts, paid for by drivers and dealers.
ALLY.moat: Deep ties with car dealers help, but many banks offer car loans and savings accounts too.
ALLY.grows: Pulling in more online savers and making more car and dealer loans.
ALLY.risk: Drivers falling behind on car loans in a weak economy could cause big losses.

ALNY.sells: RNA medicines like AMVUTTRA for rare heart and nerve diseases, paid for by insurers and health systems.
ALNY.moat: It pioneered RNA-silencing drugs and holds patents and lab know-how rivals lack.
ALNY.grows: AMVUTTRA reaching more heart patients and new drugs for blood pressure and brain diseases.
ALNY.risk: Drug trials failing, rival heart medicines, or patents running out could shrink sales.

AMAT.sells: Machines that etch and layer materials on chips, paid for by chipmakers like TSMC, Samsung and Intel.
AMAT.moat: Its tools are built into chip factories, and long materials know-how is hard to copy.
AMAT.grows: AI and phone chips need new factories and more manufacturing steps per chip.
AMAT.risk: Chipmakers cutting factory spending in a slump or trade limits on selling tools to China.

AMCR.sells: Plastic films, pouches, bottles and medicine packs, paid for by food, drink, drug and beauty brands.
AMCR.moat: Its size lets it make packaging cheaply and serve giant brands in many countries at once.
AMCR.grows: Steady demand for packaged food and medicine plus newer recyclable packaging.
AMCR.risk: Rules against plastic, swings in plastic costs, and big brands pushing hard on price.

AMD.sells: Ryzen chips for PCs, Radeon graphics for gamers, and EPYC and Instinct chips that tech giants buy for data centers.
AMD.moat: Designing top chips takes years of skill and patents, and only a few companies in the world can do it well.
AMD.grows: Cloud companies buying more server and AI chips to run apps and train AI models.
AMD.risk: Nvidia leads in AI chips, and Intel or custom chips from cloud giants could take away customers.

AME.sells: Precision instruments, sensors, and motors that factories, airlines, hospitals, and labs build into their gear.
AME.moat: Its parts are designed into planes and machines, so swapping them means costly retesting and approvals.
AME.grows: Buying smaller niche instrument makers and selling more to aerospace, medical, and power customers.
AME.risk: A slowdown in factory spending, or paying too much for companies it buys.

AMGN.sells: Medicines like Enbrel, Prolia, and Repatha that doctors, hospitals, and pharmacies buy for patients.
AMGN.moat: Patents block copies for years, and making complex biologic medicines is very hard to do well.
AMGN.grows: New drugs from its labs and from companies it buys, like treatments for rare diseases and cancer.
AMGN.risk: Patents running out lets cheaper copycat versions in, and new drugs can fail in testing.

AMP.sells: Financial advisors who help families plan and invest, plus Columbia Threadneedle funds and insurance.
AMP.moat: People trust their advisor and rarely move their savings once a long-term plan is set up.
AMP.grows: More savers needing retirement help and earning fees as clients' investments grow over time.
AMP.risk: Cheap online investing apps and low-fee index funds could pull clients and squeeze fees.

AMR.sells: Metallurgical coal from mines in Virginia and West Virginia that steelmakers buy to make steel.
AMR.moat: Coal is a commodity, so buyers mostly pick the cheapest supplier and prices swing with demand.
AMR.grows: Steelmakers around the world needing coal when they build more buildings, cars, and bridges.
AMR.risk: Steel prices falling, or steelmakers switching to cleaner methods that need no coal.

AMT.sells: Space on cell towers and in data centers that phone companies like Verizon and AT&T rent.
AMT.moat: Towns limit new towers, and phone companies rarely move gear once it's up, so long leases stick.
AMT.grows: People using more phone data, which pushes carriers to add equipment to more towers.
AMT.risk: Phone companies merging or cutting spending, and higher interest rates making its debt costlier.

AMZN.sells: Online shopping and Prime for shoppers, ads for sellers, and AWS cloud computing for businesses.
AMZN.moat: Its huge warehouse network and cloud data centers deliver faster and cheaper than most rivals.
AMZN.grows: Businesses moving to the AWS cloud and AI, plus more ads and more shoppers joining Prime.
AMZN.risk: Government antitrust cases, and cloud rivals like Microsoft and Google winning AI customers.

ANET.sells: Network switches and EOS software that cloud giants like Microsoft and Meta use to link servers.
ANET.moat: Its EOS software is known for being reliable and flexible, and big customers build their networks on it.
ANET.grows: Tech companies building giant AI data centers that need fast networks to connect their chips.
ANET.risk: Relying on a few huge customers, and rivals like Nvidia and Cisco pushing their own networking.

ANGX.sells: Family-friendly movies and shows like Sound of Freedom, paid for by Guild members, moviegoers and viewers.
ANGX.moat: A loyal faith-and-family fan club votes on and funds its shows, but big studios can make similar films.
ANGX.grows: More Guild members paying monthly, plus new movies in theaters and on its streaming app.
ANGX.risk: A few flops in a row could shrink the fan club, and hit movies are hard to make again and again.

AON.sells: Help for big companies buying insurance, worker health plans and retirement plans, paid for by fees.
AON.moat: Few firms are big enough to place huge risks worldwide, and clients rarely switch advisers they trust.
AON.grows: Rising insurance and health costs mean bigger fees, plus companies needing more help with new risks.
AON.risk: Losing top brokers to rivals, or software making insurance shopping simpler and cheaper for clients.

APA.sells: Oil and natural gas pumped from Texas, Egypt and the North Sea, sold to refiners and gas buyers.
APA.moat: Oil and gas are the same no matter who drills them, so customers pick on price, not on the company.
APA.grows: Finding new oil fields, like the offshore projects near Suriname, and pumping more from existing wells.
APA.risk: Oil and gas prices falling, which it cannot control, or problems in the countries where it drills.

APD.sells: Oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen and helium piped or trucked to factories, refineries, hospitals and chip makers.
APD.moat: Its gas plants sit right next to big customers on long contracts, so switching suppliers is costly.
APD.grows: New factories and chip plants needing gases, plus long contracts that raise prices over time.
APD.risk: Spending heavily on giant clean hydrogen plants that may not find enough paying customers.

APG.sells: Installing and inspecting fire sprinklers, alarms, security systems and elevators for buildings and factories.
APG.moat: Laws require regular fire and safety inspections, so building owners keep calling the same trusted crew.
APG.grows: Steady repeat inspection work, new data centers and warehouses, and buying smaller local safety firms.
APG.risk: A slowdown in new construction, or mistakes when blending in the many companies it keeps buying.

APH.sells: Connectors, cables and sensors that link parts inside cars, planes, phones, servers and military gear.
APH.moat: Its parts are designed into products early, and makers rarely swap a tested part once a product ships.
APH.grows: AI data centers needing fast connections, more electronics in cars, and buying smaller part makers.
APH.risk: A slowdown in data center spending or factory orders, since its sales rise and fall with customers' builds.

APP.sells: AI tools that place ads inside mobile games and apps, paid for by advertisers who want new customers.
APP.moat: More apps using its ad auction means more data, which makes its ads work better and pulls in more apps.
APP.grows: Bringing its ad engine beyond games to online shops and other businesses, plus ads on smart TVs.
APP.risk: Apple or Google changing privacy rules, or regulators questioning how it collects and uses data.

APPN.sells: Software that lets banks, insurers and government offices build apps to automate paperwork and approvals.
APPN.moat: Once a company runs key processes like claims on its platform, rebuilding them elsewhere is painful.
APPN.grows: Existing customers adding more processes, new AI features, and more government and insurance deals.
APPN.risk: Bigger rivals like Microsoft and ServiceNow offering similar tools bundled with what clients already use.

ARBK.sells: It runs big rooms of computers that mine bitcoin and sells the coins it earns to get cash.
ARBK.moat: Any miner with cheap power and machines can do the same work, so there is little to stop rivals.
ARBK.grows: Sales rise when bitcoin's value goes up and when it adds faster, more efficient mining machines.
ARBK.risk: A drop in bitcoin's value or a jump in power costs could make mining lose money.

ARCB.sells: It moves freight for businesses in shared trucks and arranges shipping by truck, sea and air for shippers.
ARCB.moat: Its network of freight terminals and trucks across the country is slow and costly for a newcomer to build.
ARCB.grows: More factory and store shipments, plus selling extra services like brokerage, warehousing and moving.
ARCB.risk: A slow economy means fewer shipments, and bigger rivals with cheaper networks can win customers on price.

ARE.sells: It owns and rents lab and office campuses to drug makers and science companies in cities like Boston.
ARE.moat: Its campuses sit in top science hubs near universities, and lab buildings are hard to build and move out of.
ARE.grows: New science companies needing lab space, rent increases on renewals, and building new campuses.
ARE.risk: If biotech companies run short of money or too many new labs get built, buildings could sit empty.

ARES.sells: It manages money for pension funds and insurers, lending to mid-size firms and investing in companies and property.
ARES.moat: Its huge size and long track record let it make big loans that smaller lenders cannot, so clients keep returning.
ARES.grows: Banks pulling back from lending to mid-size firms, and big investors handing more money to private funds.
ARES.risk: A bad economy could make many of its borrowers fail to repay, hurting results and scaring off clients.

ARQQ.sells: It sells encryption software that makes secret keys to protect data, aimed at governments and businesses.
ARQQ.moat: It is still early and small, and big tech and security firms are building their own quantum-safe tools.
ARQQ.grows: Worries that future quantum computers could crack today's codes may push customers to try new security tools.
ARQQ.risk: Few paying customers so far, and larger rivals or free open standards could make its product unneeded.

ARRY.sells: It makes motorized racks that tilt solar panels to follow the sun, sold to builders of big solar farms.
ARRY.moat: Its trackers have a good reliability record, but strong rivals sell similar products and fight on price.
ARRY.grows: More big solar farms being built as power companies add clean, cheap electricity to the grid.
ARRY.risk: Changes to clean-energy tax rules, high interest rates or steel costs could slow solar farm orders.

ASAN.sells: It sells online software that helps teams plan projects and track tasks, paid for by companies and governments.
ASAN.moat: Once a company puts all its projects and workflows in Asana, moving everything to another tool is painful.
ASAN.grows: Getting more workers inside each customer to use it and selling add-ons like its AI teammates.
ASAN.risk: Rivals like Microsoft, Monday.com and Notion offer similar tools, and AI could make them easy to replace.

ASML.sells: It builds giant machines that print tiny circuits onto chips, sold to chipmakers like TSMC, Samsung and Intel.
ASML.moat: It is the only maker of the most advanced chip-printing machines, which took decades of science to build.
ASML.grows: Demand for faster chips for AI, phones and cars pushes chipmakers to order newer, pricier machines.
ASML.risk: Export limits on selling to China and chipmakers pausing new factories could cut orders for its machines.

ASTS.sells: Space-based cell service that lets ordinary smartphones connect, paid for by phone carriers and governments.
ASTS.moat: Its big BlueBird satellites and carrier deals are hard to copy, but the service is still early and unproven.
ASTS.grows: Launching more satellites and signing more phone carriers that want coverage where towers don't reach.
ASTS.risk: Launch delays, high costs, or rivals like SpaceX Starlink reaching phones first could break the plan.

ATO.sells: Natural gas piped to homes, shops, schools and factories, plus gas pipelines and storage in Texas.
ATO.moat: It holds government-approved local service areas, and nobody builds a second set of gas pipes to your house.
ATO.grows: Regulators letting it earn a return on replacing and expanding pipes as towns like Dallas keep growing.
ATO.risk: Regulators cutting allowed returns, or cities and builders moving away from gas toward electric heat.

ATRC.sells: Heart surgery tools like AtriClip and Isolator clamps plus nerve-freezing pain probes, bought by hospitals.
ATRC.moat: Surgeons train on its devices, and patents plus safety approvals make it slow for rivals to copy them.
ATRC.grows: More surgeons closing the heart's appendage during surgery and using its cryoSPHERE probes for pain relief.
ATRC.risk: Newer catheter treatments or big rivals like Medtronic could make its surgical tools less needed.

AVB.sells: Apartments to rent in big cities like Boston, New York, Seattle and California, paid for by renters.
AVB.moat: It owns buildings in crowded, pricey areas where new land is scarce and building permits are hard to get.
AVB.grows: Raising rents over time and building new apartment communities in growing cities like Charlotte and Austin.
AVB.risk: Too many new apartments, rent limits from cities, or a weak job market could push rents down.

AVGO.sells: Chips for AI data centers, phones and networks, plus VMware software, bought by tech giants and businesses.
AVGO.moat: Custom AI chips and VMware are built into customers' systems, so switching away is costly and slow.
AVGO.grows: Big companies like Google building custom AI chips and faster networks for their data centers.
AVGO.risk: A few giant customers making their own chips, or angry VMware users moving to other software.

AVY.sells: Sticky label materials, clothing tags and RFID tracking tags, bought by brands, retailers and packagers.
AVY.moat: Its huge size and long ties with brands let it make labels cheaply and supply them reliably worldwide.
AVY.grows: Stores like Walmart putting tiny RFID chips on more items to track stock and stop theft.
AVY.risk: Labels are partly a commodity, so cheaper rivals or slow shopping could squeeze its sales.

AWK.sells: Clean drinking water and sewer service to homes, businesses, towns and military bases.
AWK.moat: It holds government-approved local water systems, and no town builds a second set of water pipes.
AWK.grows: Buying small town water systems and getting regulators to approve rates for fixing old pipes.
AWK.risk: Regulators refusing rate increases, or costly new rules on water safety it must pay to meet.

AXNX.sells: Interior design and fit-out work in Hong Kong, with a newer push into AI and robotics services.
AXNX.moat: It is a small firm that recently renamed itself around AI, with nothing clear that rivals can't copy.
AXNX.grows: Winning more office and shop fit-out jobs and finding paying customers for its new AI and robot work.
AXNX.risk: Tiny size, a brand-new unproven AI business, and a slow Hong Kong building market.

AXON.sells: TASER devices, body cameras and Axon Evidence cloud software, paid for by police departments and governments.
AXON.moat: Police keep years of video in Axon Evidence and train on its gear, so moving to a rival is slow and costly.
AXON.grows: Departments add software like Draft One, Axon Records and drones on top of the cameras they already use.
AXON.risk: Government budget cuts, public backlash over policing tools, or a cheaper rival winning big city contracts.

AXP.sells: Credit and charge cards like Platinum and Gold, paid by cardholder fees and by stores that accept them.
AXP.moat: Its premium name and travel perks attract big spenders, and stores accept the card to reach those shoppers.
AXP.grows: Younger members joining premium cards, more spending per card, and more shops worldwide taking Amex.
AXP.risk: A recession that makes cardholders stop paying their debts, or rivals copying its perks for less.

AZN.L.sells: Prescription medicines like Tagrisso, Farxiga and Enhertu, paid for by health systems, insurers and patients.
AZN.L.moat: Patents block copies of its drugs for years, and its labs know how to invent new cancer and heart medicines.
AZN.L.grows: New cancer, rare-disease and heart drugs coming from its labs and partners to replace older ones.
AZN.L.risk: Patents ending lets cheap copies in, and governments pushing hard to lower what they pay for medicines.

B.sells: Gold and copper dug from its mines, sold to refiners, banks, jewelers and factories around the world.
B.moat: Gold is the same no matter who mines it, though owning big long-life mines helps keep its costs lower.
B.grows: Higher gold and copper prices and new copper projects, since it cannot set the price itself.
B.risk: Falling gold prices, mine accidents, or governments in mining countries taking a bigger share.

BA.sells: Jetliners like the Max and Dreamliner, plus military planes and repair services, paid by airlines and armies.
BA.moat: Only Boeing and Airbus build big jetliners; it takes giant factories, safety approvals and deep skill.
BA.grows: Airlines need more planes as travel grows, and spare parts and repairs keep paying for many years.
BA.risk: Safety and quality failures that slow production, anger regulators and push airlines toward Airbus.

BABA.sells: Shopping sites Taobao, Tmall and AliExpress plus cloud computing, paid by merchants through ads and fees.
BABA.moat: Millions of shoppers draw sellers and sellers draw shoppers, so a new marketplace struggles to catch up.
BABA.grows: Its cloud and AI services for businesses, quick delivery in cities, and its shopping sites abroad.
BABA.risk: Fierce price wars with rivals like PDD and JD, plus Chinese government rules and US-China tensions.

BAC.sells: Checking accounts, loans, credit cards, Merrill investing and Wall Street services for people and companies.
BAC.moat: Its huge branch and app network gathers cheap deposits, and people rarely bother switching their main bank.
BAC.grows: More customers using its app, more savings in Merrill accounts, and more lending as the economy grows.
BAC.risk: A recession that leaves borrowers unable to repay loans, or interest rate swings that squeeze its profit.

BARC.L.sells: Bank accounts, mortgages, Barclaycard credit cards and investment banking for UK families and big companies.
BARC.L.moat: A long-trusted UK bank whose millions of customers rarely switch, though rivals offer very similar services.
BARC.L.grows: UK lending and credit cards, US card partnerships with brands, and wealth management for richer clients.
BARC.L.risk: A weak UK economy causing loan losses, or trading losses and fines in its investment bank.

BATS.L.sells: Cigarettes like Lucky Strike, Pall Mall and Newport plus Vuse vapes and Velo pouches, bought by adult smokers.
BATS.L.moat: Smokers stick with the brand they know, and strict tobacco laws make it very hard for new rivals to start.
BATS.L.grows: Selling more Vuse vapes, glo heated sticks and Velo nicotine pouches, and raising prices on cigarettes.
BATS.L.risk: Fewer people smoking each year, plus new laws or taxes that ban flavors or limit nicotine products.

BAX.sells: IV bags, infusion pumps, hospital beds and injectable drugs, bought by hospitals, clinics and dialysis centers.
BAX.moat: Hospitals rely on huge steady supplies of approved IV fluids and pumps, which few makers can produce safely.
BAX.grows: Hospitals always need IV fluids and drugs, and older patients mean more surgeries and care at home.
BAX.risk: Factory shutdowns, product recalls and heavy debt could push hospitals toward rival suppliers.

BBAI.sells: AI software that helps the military, spy agencies and airports spot threats, track supplies and check identities.
BBAI.moat: It holds some security clearances and government ties, but many bigger tech firms offer similar AI tools.
BBAI.grows: Winning new defense and border contracts and selling its Ask Sage AI platform to government agencies.
BBAI.risk: Losing a few big government contracts or being outcompeted by larger AI companies with deeper pockets.

BBWI.sells: Scented candles, hand soaps, body lotions and fragrance mists, bought by shoppers in malls and online.
BBWI.moat: Fans love its signature scents and seasonal launches, and the store experience is a habit for many shoppers.
BBWI.grows: New scents each season, holiday gift shopping, online sales and partner-run stores in other countries.
BBWI.risk: Shoppers getting bored of the scents or switching to cheaper copycat candles and soaps at big stores.

BDX.sells: Syringes, needles, IV catheters, blood tubes and lab test machines, bought by hospitals, labs and drug makers.
BDX.moat: Nurses and labs are trained on its tools and systems, and few rivals can make so many approved supplies.
BDX.grows: Steady hospital demand for basic supplies plus new devices, lab automation and prefilled drug syringes.
BDX.risk: Product recalls, safety problems or hospitals cutting costs by switching to cheaper supply makers.

BEAM.sells: Gene-editing medicines still being tested for sickle cell and rare liver diseases, with drug partners like Pfizer.
BEAM.moat: It owns patents on base editing know-how, but it is early-stage and has no approved medicines selling yet.
BEAM.grows: Getting a treatment approved and earning payments from partners like Pfizer for jointly built programs.
BEAM.risk: Trials could fail or show safety problems, and it may run short of cash before any medicine is approved.

BEN.sells: Mutual funds and investment plans for families, pension plans and institutions, who pay fees to have money managed.
BEN.moat: Its long trusted name and advisor ties keep savers around, though switching funds is fairly easy to do.
BEN.grows: Bringing in new savings, adding private and alternative funds, and markets lifting the money it manages.
BEN.risk: Savers moving to cheap index funds and ETFs, which squeezes the fees it can charge for managing money.

BG.sells: Soybean oil, animal feed meal, flour and grain shipping, bought by food makers, farms and fuel companies.
BG.moat: Its huge network of silos, crushing plants, ports and ships is very costly and slow for a rival to build.
BG.grows: Rising demand for cooking oil, animal feed and plant-based fuels like renewable diesel around the world.
BG.risk: Crop prices and trade fights swing wildly, which can shrink the thin profit it makes on each ton of grain.

BIDU.sells: Baidu runs China's big search app, ERNIE Bot, iQIYI videos and Apollo Go robotaxis, paid mostly by advertisers.
BIDU.moat: Years of Chinese search data and a huge user base make its ads and AI hard for a newcomer to match.
BIDU.grows: Selling AI cloud services and ERNIE to businesses, plus expanding Apollo Go self-driving rides.
BIDU.risk: Users shifting to apps like Douyin and rival chatbots, plus strict Chinese government rules.

BIIB.sells: Biogen makes medicines for MS, spinal muscular atrophy and Alzheimer's, paid by insurers and health systems.
BIIB.moat: Patents and deep brain-disease science protect its drugs, and new rivals need years of costly trials.
BIIB.grows: Newer drugs like LEQEMBI, SKYCLARYS and ZURZUVAE, plus partner deals for future medicines.
BIIB.risk: Patents ending on older MS drugs lets cheaper copies take sales before new drugs fill the gap.

BILI.sells: Bilibili is a Chinese video site for young people that earns from games, ads, memberships and live streams.
BILI.moat: Creators go where fans gather and fans stay for creators and the inside-joke community, which is hard to copy.
BILI.grows: More ads, mobile game hits, and fans paying creators and buying premium memberships.
BILI.risk: Douyin and Kuaishou pulling young viewers away, plus China's tight rules on games and content.

BILL.sells: BILL sells software that helps small businesses pay bills, get paid and track spending, used by accountants too.
BILL.moat: Once a firm's suppliers, approvals and bank links live in BILL, moving to another tool is a big headache.
BILL.grows: Signing more small firms through accountants and banks, and earning more on each payment they send.
BILL.risk: Bigger players like Intuit, banks and cheaper rivals bundling similar tools for free or less.

BKNG.sells: Booking runs Booking.com, Priceline, Agoda, KAYAK and OpenTable, earning fees from hotels and travel sellers.
BKNG.moat: Travelers go where the most hotels are listed and hotels list where the most travelers search.
BKNG.grows: More people traveling, more vacation rentals and flights on the app, and more direct app bookings.
BKNG.risk: Google or AI assistants sending travelers straight to hotels, skipping Booking's sites.

BLDR.sells: Builders FirstSource sells lumber, trusses, wall panels, windows and doors to professional home builders.
BLDR.moat: Its many yards and factories let it buy cheaper and deliver ready-made parts faster than small dealers.
BLDR.grows: More new homes being built and builders using more factory-made framing to save time and labor.
BLDR.risk: A slump in home building, since fewer new houses means far fewer orders for its products.

BLK.sells: BlackRock manages money for pensions, insurers and savers through iShares funds, charging small fees.
BLK.moat: Its huge size lets it charge tiny fees and its Aladdin software is woven into how big investors work.
BLK.grows: Savers moving money into low-cost ETFs, plus new private market funds and Aladdin software clients.
BLK.risk: A long market slump shrinks the money it manages, and fee wars with Vanguard squeeze what it earns.

BLNK.sells: Blink sells EV chargers and charging network service to businesses, cities and drivers who pay to charge.
BLNK.moat: Chargers are easy for rivals to install, and drivers simply use whichever station is closest.
BLNK.grows: More electric cars on the road and more hotels, stores and cities adding charging spots.
BLNK.risk: Tesla, ChargePoint and carmakers' own networks crowding it out while it still struggles to profit.

BMY.sells: Medicines like Eliquis for blood clots and Opdivo for cancer, paid for by insurers and hospitals.
BMY.moat: Patents block copies for years, and each drug needed long, costly trials that rivals must repeat.
BMY.grows: New drugs like Camzyos, Cobenfy and Breyanzi replacing older hits as their patents run out.
BMY.risk: Big sellers like Eliquis and Revlimid losing patents, letting cheap generic copies take sales.

BN.sells: Invests money for pensions and savers in office towers, power plants, ports and private firms.
BN.moat: Few firms can buy and run giant assets like pipelines and wind farms, so big investors keep coming back.
BN.grows: Pensions and insurers handing it more money to invest in infrastructure, clean power and private loans.
BN.risk: High interest rates or a property slump could lower asset values and make new money harder to raise.

BNTX.sells: Covid vaccines sold with Pfizer to governments and pharmacies, while it tests new cancer drugs.
BNTX.moat: Its mRNA know-how is real, but covid vaccine demand has shrunk and its cancer drugs are still unproven.
BNTX.grows: Hopes that experimental cancer drugs and new mRNA vaccines pass trials and get approved.
BNTX.risk: Cancer drug trials failing while covid vaccine sales keep fading.

BOKF.sells: Loans, checking and wealth advice for families and businesses in Oklahoma, Texas and nearby states.
BOKF.moat: Businesses that run payroll and payments through the bank find it a hassle to move all their accounts.
BOKF.grows: Lending to growing Texas and Southwest businesses, plus fees from wealth management and trading.
BOKF.risk: Bad loans if oil prices or local property values drop, since many borrowers work in energy.

BP.L.sells: Oil, gas, jet fuel, BP gasoline and Castrol motor oil, bought by drivers, airlines and businesses.
BP.L.moat: Oil and gas are commodities, so prices are set by the world market, not by the BP name.
BP.L.grows: Pumping more oil and gas from new fields, plus selling more at its stations and EV chargers.
BP.L.risk: Falling oil prices or a costly spill could squeeze its profits quickly.

BR.sells: Sends shareholder voting papers and runs trading back-office software for banks and brokers.
BR.moat: Its systems are wired deep into brokers' daily work, so switching is risky, costly and slow.
BR.grows: More people owning funds and shares, plus banks handing more back-office tech work to it.
BR.risk: Rule changes in how shareholder votes and fund papers are sent could shrink its main business.

BRK-B.sells: GEICO car insurance, BNSF freight trains, electricity, See's Candies, Dairy Queen and much more.
BRK-B.moat: Its railroad, power networks and huge insurance cash pile are nearly impossible for anyone to rebuild.
BRK-B.grows: Investing insurance cash into new businesses and stocks while its many companies grow over time.
BRK-B.risk: A huge disaster hitting its insurers at once, or new leaders making poorer investment choices.

BRO.sells: Helps businesses, dentists and families buy insurance, earning commissions paid by insurers.
BRO.moat: Clients stick with a broker who knows their business, and changing means redoing all their coverage.
BRO.grows: Buying smaller insurance agencies, plus rising insurance prices that lift its commissions.
BRO.risk: Insurance prices falling or deals for new agencies drying up, which would slow its growth.

BSX.sells: Heart, stomach and bladder devices like WATCHMAN, pacemakers and scopes, bought by hospitals and doctors.
BSX.moat: Doctors train on its devices and new rivals need patents, safety trials and regulator approval to compete.
BSX.grows: More older patients need heart and gut procedures, and new devices like WATCHMAN replace pills or surgery.
BSX.risk: A device recall or a better product from a big rival could push doctors to switch.

BTBT.sells: It holds and stakes ether coins and rents data center space and computers to AI companies.
BTBT.moat: Holding crypto and renting servers are things many companies can copy, so there is no clear lasting edge.
BTBT.grows: Sales grow if ether rises in value and more AI companies rent its computer power.
BTBT.risk: A big drop in crypto prices or cheaper rival data centers could hurt it fast.

BURL.sells: Brand-name clothes, shoes, toys and home goods at off-price discounts to bargain-hunting families.
BURL.moat: It buys leftover brand-name stock cheaply in bulk, so shoppers find deals that full-price stores lack.
BURL.grows: Opening more stores and winning shoppers who want brand names for less when money feels tight.
BURL.risk: Bigger off-price rivals like TJ Maxx and Ross or online deal sites could steal its shoppers.

BWA.sells: Turbochargers, transmission parts, electric motors and battery packs, bought by carmakers worldwide.
BWA.moat: Carmakers design its parts into models years ahead, so swapping suppliers mid-model is costly and slow.
BWA.grows: Selling more parts for hybrids and electric cars as carmakers shift away from gas engines.
BWA.risk: If gas engine sales fade faster than its electric parts grow, or carmakers build parts themselves.

BWXT.sells: Nuclear reactors and fuel for US Navy submarines and carriers, plus parts for power plants and hospitals.
BWXT.moat: Very few firms hold the government licenses and secret know-how to build naval nuclear reactors.
BWXT.grows: Navy shipbuilding plans, new small nuclear power plants and medical isotopes for cancer scans.
BWXT.risk: Depending heavily on one main customer, the US government, means budget cuts could hurt.

BXP.sells: It rents fancy office towers in cities like Boston and New York to big companies and law firms.
BXP.moat: Its top buildings sit in prime city spots where there is little room left to build new rivals.
BXP.grows: Companies that want workers back in the office pick the nicest buildings, raising demand for its space.
BXP.risk: If more people keep working from home, companies need less office space and rents could fall.

BYND.sells: Plant-based burgers, sausages and chicken sold in grocery stores, restaurants and schools.
BYND.moat: Many food giants and store brands make similar plant meats, so shoppers can easily switch.
BYND.grows: Sales grow only if more people choose plant-based meat and new restaurant partners sign on.
BYND.risk: Shoppers losing interest in fake meat and the company running short of cash could break it.

C.sells: Bank accounts, credit cards, loans, trading and cash-moving services for people, firms and governments.
C.moat: Its banking network in many countries helps global companies move money in ways few rivals can match.
C.grows: Big companies trading across borders need its cash and payment services, and card spending keeps rising.
C.risk: Bad loans in a recession or costly fines from regulators could weaken its profits.

CACI.sells: CACI sells spy-tech, cyber defense, radio-jamming gear and IT systems to the US military and spy agencies.
CACI.moat: Its work needs top-secret security clearances and trusted track records that new rivals take a long time to earn.
CACI.grows: Governments keep spending more on cyber defense, space protection and electronic warfare tools.
CACI.risk: Government budget cuts or losing a big contract when it comes up for rebidding could hurt sales.

CAG.sells: Conagra sells Birds Eye veggies, Slim Jim, Healthy Choice and Marie Callender's meals to grocery shoppers.
CAG.moat: Shoppers know and trust these familiar names, so stores keep giving them shelf space.
CAG.grows: Raising prices, new snack flavors and frozen meals for busy families keep sales moving.
CAG.risk: Cheaper store brands and shoppers eating fresher food could pull buyers away from its brands.

CAH.sells: Cardinal Health delivers medicines to pharmacies and hospitals and sells gloves, syringes and gowns to doctors.
CAH.moat: Few companies have its giant warehouses and delivery network that move medicine everywhere quickly.
CAH.grows: More people need medicines as they age, and costly specialty drugs need careful handling.
CAH.risk: Thin profit margins, big customers pushing on prices, or drugmakers shipping direct could squeeze it.

CARR.sells: Carrier sells air conditioners, furnaces, heat pumps and truck fridges to homeowners and building owners.
CARR.moat: Contractors trust Carrier and Bryant names and its dealer network, and buildings stick with it for repairs.
CARR.grows: Hotter summers, energy-saving heat pumps and data centers needing cooling keep demand rising.
CARR.risk: A slowdown in home building or cheaper rival brands could cut how many new units it sells.

CASY.sells: Casey's sells gas, pizza, donuts, snacks and drinks to drivers in small Midwest towns.
CASY.moat: Its stores sit in small towns where rivals rarely build, and its homemade pizza draws loyal fans.
CASY.grows: Opening and buying more stores and selling more pizza and prepared food keeps sales growing.
CASY.risk: Electric cars needing less gas, or big chains moving into its towns, could weaken its edge.

CAT.sells: Caterpillar sells bulldozers, excavators, mining trucks, engines and generators to builders and miners.
CAT.moat: Its famous yellow machines and worldwide dealers that fix them fast keep customers coming back.
CAT.grows: Road building, mining and power generators for data centers keep orders and parts sales coming.
CAT.risk: Slowdowns in construction and mining make customers delay buying expensive machines.

CATY.sells: Cathay Bank offers checking accounts, mortgages and business loans to families and small companies.
CATY.moat: It has loyal customers in Chinese-American communities, but banking services are easy for rivals to offer.
CATY.grows: Making more loans as its community customers grow their homes and businesses keeps it growing.
CATY.risk: Bad real estate loans or tougher competition for deposits could hurt the bank.

CB.sells: Chubb sells insurance for businesses, homes, cars, farms and travel to companies and wealthy families.
CB.moat: It is very skilled at pricing tricky risks, and big clients trust it to pay claims on complex losses.
CB.grows: More valuable stuff to protect, new risks like cyber attacks and expansion in Asia keep it growing.
CB.risk: A huge disaster year, like big hurricanes or wildfires, could bring more claims than expected.

CBOE.sells: Places to trade options, stocks, futures and currencies, paid by traders, brokers and big funds per trade.
CBOE.moat: It holds exclusive rights to list popular index options and VIX products, so traders must come to its markets.
CBOE.grows: More people trading index options and VIX products, plus selling market data to firms that need it.
CBOE.risk: Regulators changing trading rules, or rivals winning the rights to list similar index products.

CBRS.sells: Giant single-wafer AI chips in data-center racks, bought by AI labs, cloud giants and governments.
CBRS.moat: Its whole-wafer chip is very hard to build, but it is young and buyers can still pick Nvidia instead.
CBRS.grows: Companies wanting faster answers from AI models and countries building their own AI supercomputers.
CBRS.risk: Nvidia and other chipmakers out-building it, or a few big customers making up most of its sales.

CCC.sells: Cloud software that car insurers and body shops pay for to estimate damage and handle crash claims.
CCC.moat: Insurers, repair shops, parts sellers and automakers all work inside the same system, so leaving is hard.
CCC.grows: Selling more add-on tools like AI photo estimates, injury claims and payments to the same customers.
CCC.risk: A big insurer building its own tools or a rival platform luring shops and insurers away together.

CCI.sells: Space on cell towers rented to phone carriers like Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile under long leases.
CCI.moat: Towns rarely allow new towers, so the ones already standing are very hard for rivals to replace.
CCI.grows: Phone carriers adding more antennas and gear to towers as people use more mobile data.
CCI.risk: Carriers merging or cutting spending, which means fewer tenants and lower rent on the towers.

CCL.sells: Cruise vacations on Carnival, Princess, Holland America and other ships, paid for by travelers.
CCL.moat: It runs the most ships and owns private islands, so it can spread costs and fill ships cheaper than rivals.
CCL.grows: More families choosing cruises as good-value vacations and spending extra on drinks and trips ashore.
CCL.risk: Recessions, outbreaks or high fuel costs that empty ships, plus lots of debt to pay back.

CDNS.sells: Software and chip building blocks that chipmakers like Nvidia and Apple use to design and test chips.
CDNS.moat: Engineers train for years on its tools and chip projects depend on them, so switching is risky and slow.
CDNS.grows: Chips getting more complex for AI, phones and cars, so designers need more and better tools.
CDNS.risk: Export limits on selling to China or a big chip customer moving more work to rival Synopsys.

CDW.sells: Laptops, servers, software and IT help sold to businesses, schools, hospitals and governments.
CDW.moat: Its huge buying power and sales team let it offer many brands and quick service small resellers can't match.
CDW.grows: Customers replacing old computers, moving to the cloud and buying more security tools.
CDW.risk: Tech makers selling direct to customers, or schools and businesses cutting tech budgets.

CE.sells: Plastics and chemicals like acetic acid used by makers of car parts, paints, glue and packaging.
CE.moat: Its own process for making acetyl chemicals is known for being cheaper to run than most rivals' plants.
CE.grows: Car makers, electronics firms and builders needing more tough plastics and coating ingredients.
CE.risk: These are mostly commodity chemicals, so weak demand or cheap rivals can crush prices, and debt is high.

CEG.sells: Electricity from nuclear plants plus wind, solar, gas and water power, sold to utilities, businesses and homes.
CEG.moat: Big nuclear plants are nearly impossible to build today, so its steady carbon-free power is hard to copy.
CEG.grows: Tech companies want clean round-the-clock power for data centers and sign long deals to buy it.
CEG.risk: A nuclear accident, long plant outages, or falling power prices could hurt what its plants earn.

CELH.sells: Celsius, Alani Nu and Rockstar energy drinks and hydration powders sold in stores, gyms and online.
CELH.moat: Fans pick Celsius as a fitness-style energy drink, and PepsiCo's delivery trucks put it on many shelves.
CELH.grows: New flavors, the Alani Nu brand and more shelf space in more countries bring in new drinkers.
CELH.risk: Red Bull, Monster and new brands fight for the same fridge space, and drinkers can switch flavors fast.

CFG.sells: Bank accounts, mortgages, credit cards and business loans for families and companies, mostly in the Northeast.
CFG.moat: Moving paychecks, bills and business accounts to a new bank is a hassle, so many customers stay put.
CFG.grows: Lending more to businesses, adding wealthy clients and earning fees from deal advice and money services.
CFG.risk: Bad loans in a downturn, especially on office buildings, or customers moving cash to higher-paying rivals.

CGC.sells: Cannabis flower, gummies, drinks and vapes under Tweed and other brands, plus Storz & Bickel vaporizers.
CGC.moat: Many growers sell similar cannabis, so buyers switch easily; only its vaporizer brand really stands out.
CGC.grows: Selling more in Germany and other countries opening up medical cannabis, plus more vaporizer sales.
CGC.risk: Too many sellers pushing prices down, ongoing losses, and slow or uncertain changes to cannabis laws.

CHPT.sells: Electric car chargers and the software to run them, sold to businesses, fleets, apartments and homes.
CHPT.moat: Many chargers run on its network and app, but rivals like Tesla also sell chargers drivers can use.
CHPT.grows: More people and delivery fleets switching to electric cars need more places to plug in.
CHPT.risk: Slower electric car sales, cash running low, and strong rivals like Tesla's charging network.

CHRW.sells: It books trucks, trains, ships and planes to move goods for shippers and earns a fee for arranging it.
CHRW.moat: Its huge web of shippers and truck owners, plus its software, helps it match loads cheaply and fast.
CHRW.grows: Using smarter software and automation to handle more shipments with fewer people.
CHRW.risk: Weak freight demand and digital rivals that match trucks to loads for lower fees.

CHTR.sells: Spectrum home internet, mobile phone plans and cable TV that families and businesses pay for monthly.
CHTR.moat: Its cables already run to homes across its towns, and wiring every street again costs rivals a fortune.
CHTR.grows: Bundling Spectrum Mobile with internet and wiring rural areas that never had fast service.
CHTR.risk: Fiber companies and phone carriers selling wireless home internet could pull its customers away.

CI.sells: Health plans for employers and families, plus Express Scripts drug benefits and mail-order pharmacy.
CI.moat: Its huge size lets Express Scripts bargain hard on drug prices, and employers rarely switch plans quickly.
CI.grows: More specialty drug sales, like costly medicines for rare and long-term illnesses, through its pharmacies.
CI.risk: New laws or rules cutting what drug benefit managers can earn from their deals with drug makers.

CIFR.sells: Builds big data centers that rent space and power to tech giants for AI, and mines bitcoin.
CIFR.moat: Its edge is locked-in power and land, but rivals with power can build similar data centers.
CIFR.grows: Signing more long leases with cloud giants that need room and electricity for AI computers.
CIFR.risk: Bitcoin prices can crash, and tech tenants could pick other builders or need less AI space.

CINF.sells: Sells home, car, business and life insurance through local independent agents to families and firms.
CINF.moat: Loyal ties with local agents help, but many insurers sell similar policies at similar prices.
CINF.grows: Raising insurance prices, adding agents in new states, and earning on the bonds and stocks it holds.
CINF.risk: Huge storms, fires or lawsuits can cost more than the insurance payments it collected.

CL.sells: Sells Colgate toothpaste, Palmolive soap, Irish Spring and Hill's pet food to shoppers through stores.
CL.moat: Dentists and vets recommend Colgate and Hill's, so families trust the names and keep picking them.
CL.grows: Selling more toothpaste in growing countries and more Hill's science-based pet food to pet owners.
CL.risk: Cheaper store brands and rising costs could push shoppers away from paying extra for the names.

CLH.sells: Collects and safely destroys dangerous waste for factories, labs, oil firms and auto repair shops.
CLH.moat: Permits for hazardous waste burners and landfills are very hard to get, so few rivals can compete.
CLH.grows: Stricter pollution rules, steady factory work, and Safety-Kleen turning used oil into new motor oil.
CLH.risk: Weaker factory and oil activity, or looser pollution rules, would mean less waste to handle.

CLSK.sells: Runs big computer farms that mine bitcoin, earning new coins paid out by the bitcoin network.
CLSK.moat: Anyone with cheap power and machines can mine, so its main help is low power costs and size.
CLSK.grows: Adding more mining machines and power sites, and possibly renting space for AI computing.
CLSK.risk: A bitcoin price drop or the network's built-in reward cuts can wipe out mining profits fast.

CLX.sells: Sells Clorox bleach, Glad bags, Brita filters, Kingsford charcoal and Burt's Bees to store shoppers.
CLX.moat: Shoppers trust names like Clorox and Glad, and stores give these well-known brands the best shelf spots.
CLX.grows: New scents and products, higher prices, and selling cleaning supplies to hospitals and offices.
CLX.risk: Store brands that cost less and higher costs for plastic and chemicals could squeeze it.

CMCSA.sells: Sells Xfinity internet, TV and phone to homes and businesses, plus NBC, Peacock and Universal parks.
CMCSA.moat: Its cables already reach homes across the country, which is very costly for rivals to rebuild.
CMCSA.grows: Adding phone plans, business internet, new Universal theme parks and more Peacock subscribers.
CMCSA.risk: Fiber and wireless home internet from phone companies are taking customers, and cord-cutting hurts TV.

CME.sells: Runs the markets where traders and banks trade futures on oil, corn, gold, stocks and interest rates.
CME.moat: Traders go where the most other traders already are, so its busy markets keep pulling in more.
CME.grows: More trading when markets are bumpy, new products like sports futures, and selling market data.
CME.risk: Calm markets mean less trading, and rival exchanges or new rules could take some business.

CMG.sells: Burritos, bowls, tacos and salads that hungry customers order in its restaurants, on its app or by delivery.
CMG.moat: Fans know and trust the Chipotle name and fast build-your-own meals, so many pick it over other quick spots.
CMG.grows: Opening more restaurants, adding drive-up pickup lanes and getting more people to order on the app.
CMG.risk: A food safety scare or prices that feel too high could push customers to cheaper or nearby rivals.

CMI.sells: Diesel and gas engines, generators and parts that truck makers, builders and data centers pay for.
CMI.moat: Its huge repair and parts network and long trusted engines make truck makers slow to switch suppliers.
CMI.grows: Selling replacement parts and service, plus backup generators for data centers and hospitals.
CMI.risk: If trucks and machines move to electric power faster than Cummins can keep up, engine sales could fade.

CMS.sells: Electricity and natural gas that homes and businesses in Michigan pay for every month.
CMS.moat: The state lets it be the main power and gas company in its area, so rivals cannot easily build competing lines.
CMS.grows: Regulators allowing higher rates as it builds new wind, solar and grid upgrades for more customers.
CMS.risk: Regulators could refuse rate increases or storms could cause costly damage and angry customers.

CNC.sells: Health insurance plans paid for mostly by government programs like Medicaid and Medicare for families.
CNC.moat: Its large size and long ties with state governments help it win contracts that smaller insurers struggle to get.
CNC.grows: Winning more state Medicaid contracts and signing up more people for marketplace and Medicare plans.
CNC.risk: Government rule changes or patients' medical bills rising faster than payments could squeeze its profits.

CNP.sells: Electricity delivery and natural gas that homes and businesses in Texas, Indiana, Ohio and Minnesota pay for.
CNP.moat: Governments let it be the main wires and gas pipe company in its areas, so customers have no other choice.
CNP.grows: Building more grid and pipes as the Houston area adds people, factories and data centers.
CNP.risk: Regulators could limit rate increases, especially after hurricanes knock out power and anger customers.

CNXC.sells: Call center workers and AI chat tools that big companies pay for to answer their own customers' questions.
CNXC.moat: Clients do sign long contracts, but many rivals offer similar help and switching between them is doable.
CNXC.grows: Selling AI helpers and data tools to clients that want cheaper, faster customer support.
CNXC.risk: AI chatbots could let companies replace the human call center work that brings in most of its sales.

COF.sells: Credit cards, bank accounts and car loans that everyday people and businesses pay interest and fees on.
COF.moat: Its huge pile of customer data and well-known brand help it judge who will repay loans better than small banks.
COF.grows: Adding card customers and running its own card payment network after buying Discover.
COF.risk: If many borrowers stop paying their card and car loans in a weak economy, losses could pile up.

COIN.sells: An app where people and big firms buy, sell and hold crypto like Bitcoin, paying trading fees.
COIN.moat: Many people see it as the trusted, rule-following place to hold crypto in America.
COIN.grows: More people and funds using crypto, plus fees from its Base network, staking and stablecoins.
COIN.risk: Crypto prices crashing or cheaper rival apps could cut trading, and trading fees are most of its money.

COLD.sells: Freezer and fridge warehouse space plus trucking, paid for by food makers, distributors and grocery chains.
COLD.moat: Giant cold warehouses near farms, ports and cities are costly and slow to build, and food firms hate moving stock.
COLD.grows: More frozen and fresh food shipped worldwide, plus higher rent and service fees from existing customers.
COLD.risk: Rivals building too many new cold warehouses, pushing prices down while power and debt costs stay high.

CORZ.sells: Data center space, power and cooling rented to AI companies, plus mining bitcoin for itself and others.
CORZ.moat: Its big power hookups are useful, but bitcoin mining is a commodity and the AI hosting business is still young.
CORZ.grows: Turning old mining sites into AI data centers rented on long contracts to cloud and AI customers.
CORZ.risk: Relying on a few big AI tenants and on bitcoin's price, while power costs and debt stay heavy.

COST.sells: Bulk groceries, gas, TVs, tires and Kirkland Signature goods to shoppers who pay a yearly membership fee.
COST.moat: Huge buying power keeps prices very low, and members who paid the fee keep coming back to get their money's worth.
COST.grows: Opening new warehouses around the world, more members renewing, and more online and delivery orders.
COST.risk: Rivals like Walmart's Sam's Club or Amazon matching its low prices so members stop renewing.

CPAY.sells: Fuel cards, toll payments, business bill pay, cross-border payments and hotel booking for work crews, paid by companies.
CPAY.moat: Fleets and finance teams build their spending rules and reports around its cards, so swapping systems is painful.
CPAY.grows: Signing more businesses to pay bills digitally, more cross-border payments, and buying smaller payment firms.
CPAY.risk: Electric trucks needing fewer fuel cards, plus fintech rivals and banks offering cheaper business payment tools.

CPB.sells: Campbell's soup, Goldfish crackers, Prego and Rao's sauces, Cape Cod chips and Pepperidge Farm cookies sold to grocery shoppers.
CPB.moat: Families trust names they grew up with, and stores give those famous brands the best shelf space.
CPB.grows: Raising prices, pushing popular brands like Rao's and Goldfish, and adding new snack flavors.
CPB.risk: Shoppers switching to cheaper store brands, eating fewer snacks or eating healthier, shrinking demand for its foods.

CPG.L.sells: Cafeteria meals, cleaning and building services for offices, hospitals, schools, stadiums and remote work camps.
CPG.L.moat: Being the biggest food service firm lets it buy food cheaper and run kitchens more smoothly than smaller rivals.
CPG.L.grows: Winning contracts from schools, hospitals and companies that still run their own kitchens, and keeping old clients.
CPG.L.risk: Losing big contracts to rivals like Sodexo or Aramark, or rising wages and food costs squeezing thin profits.

CPNG.sells: Online shopping with super fast Rocket Delivery in South Korea, plus food delivery, video streaming and Farfetch fashion.
CPNG.moat: Its own warehouses and delivery drivers across Korea make next-day delivery hard for others to copy cheaply.
CPNG.grows: More members joining its paid Wow plan, more grocery and food delivery orders, and expanding into Taiwan.
CPNG.risk: Chinese shopping apps undercutting prices in Korea, or shoppers losing trust after customer data leaks.

CPRT.sells: Online auctions for wrecked and used cars, paid by insurers, banks and rental firms selling to dealers worldwide.
CPRT.moat: Most buyers shop where the cars are and insurers sell where buyers bid, and its huge storage yards are hard to copy.
CPRT.grows: More cars being called a total loss as repairs get pricier, plus more buyers from overseas bidding online.
CPRT.risk: Fewer crashes from safer, self-driving cars, or insurers moving business to its rival IAA.

CRL.sells: Lab mice and rats, safety tests and drug lab work, paid for by drug and biotech companies before human trials.
CRL.moat: Drug makers trust its huge network of breeding sites and labs that regulators already know and accept.
CRL.grows: More new drugs, cell therapies and antibodies being invented means more early testing to hand off to it.
CRL.risk: Biotech funding drying up, or new non-animal test methods replacing much of its animal testing work.

CRON.sells: Cannabis flower, pre-rolls, vapes, oils and edibles under Spinach and Lord Jones, sold to adult shoppers.
CRON.moat: Cannabis is easy to grow and sell, so many rivals offer similar products and shoppers switch on price.
CRON.grows: More countries and provinces allowing legal cannabis, plus new products like edibles and vapes.
CRON.risk: Price wars and too much supply in Canada keep squeezing what every cannabis seller can earn.

CROX.sells: Crocs foam clogs, sandals and Jibbitz charms plus HEYDUDE shoes, sold to kids and adults in stores and online.
CROX.moat: The Crocs look is instantly known, and fans keep collecting charms and limited editions with famous partners.
CROX.grows: New styles, celebrity and cartoon collabs, more charms, and selling to shoppers in new countries.
CROX.risk: Fashion fads fade, and if Crocs or HEYDUDE stop feeling cool, shoppers can drift to other shoes.

CRS.sells: Special metal alloys and powders that jet engine, defense and medical device makers pay for.
CRS.moat: Plane parts need metals tested and approved over many years, so makers rarely switch to a new supplier.
CRS.grows: Airlines ordering more planes and engines, plus defense and medical needs for tough, heat-proof metals.
CRS.risk: A slump in airplane building or delays at big jet makers would cut demand for its special metals.

CRSP.sells: Gene-editing medicines like CASGEVY for sickle cell disease, paid for by hospitals and insurers via Vertex.
CRSP.moat: Editing DNA safely takes rare science skill and patents, and it was among the first to get a cure approved.
CRSP.grows: More patients treated with CASGEVY and new programs for cancer, heart disease and diabetes working out.
CRSP.risk: Most of its programs are still experiments, and failed trials or rival gene editors could hurt it.

CRWD.sells: Falcon cloud security software that companies and governments pay for yearly to stop hackers.
CRWD.moat: Once Falcon guards every laptop and server, ripping it out is risky, and its threat data improves with use.
CRWD.grows: Customers adding more modules like cloud, identity and AI security on top of the Falcon platform.
CRWD.risk: A big outage like the global crash it caused once, or Microsoft and Palo Alto bundling cheaper security.

CRWV.sells: Rented Nvidia AI computer power in its data centers, paid for by AI labs and big tech firms.
CRWV.moat: It moved fast to get scarce AI chips, but big clouds like Amazon and Microsoft rent the same kind of power.
CRWV.grows: AI companies needing ever more computing power to train and run their models.
CRWV.risk: Heavy borrowing to build data centers, few huge customers, and AI demand cooling or chips getting cheaper.

CSCO.sells: Network switches, routers, Wi-Fi, security and Webex video tools that businesses and governments pay for.
CSCO.moat: IT teams are trained on Cisco gear and its systems run whole networks, so replacing it is costly and risky.
CSCO.grows: AI data centers needing faster networks, plus more security and software subscriptions sold to customers.
CSCO.risk: Cloud giants building their own cheap network gear and rivals like Arista winning the fastest AI networks.

CSGP.sells: CoStar property data and sites like LoopNet and Homes.com, paid for by brokers, lenders, owners and agents.
CSGP.moat: Its researchers spent decades building a huge property database that a rival would struggle to rebuild.
CSGP.grows: More subscribers for its data tools and more agents paying to advertise homes on Homes.com.
CSGP.risk: Heavy spending to battle Zillow with Homes.com might never pay off and could drag on the whole company.

CSL.sells: Roofing sheets, insulation and waterproofing like Carlisle SynTec and Versico, paid for by roofing contractors.
CSL.moat: Contractors trust its trained-installer network and long roof warranties, so they stick with its products.
CSL.grows: Old flat roofs on stores and warehouses need replacing, plus stricter energy rules call for more insulation.
CSL.risk: A slowdown in building and reroofing, or cheaper rival membranes, could squeeze its sales and profits.

CSX.sells: Train hauling of coal, chemicals, cars, grain and shipping containers, paid for by factories and shippers.
CSX.moat: Nobody can lay a brand-new railroad across the crowded eastern states, so few rivals can ever compete.
CSX.grows: Moving more containers off highways onto trains and serving new factories built along its tracks.
CSX.risk: Trucks taking freight, falling coal shipments, or a big rival railroad merger could weaken its position.

CTAS.sells: Rented work uniforms, mats, first aid kits and fire extinguisher checks, paid for by businesses of all sizes.
CTAS.moat: Its dense delivery routes let one truck serve many nearby customers, so it can beat small rivals on cost.
CTAS.grows: Selling more services like first aid and fire safety to businesses already on its weekly delivery routes.
CTAS.risk: A recession that cuts jobs means fewer workers needing uniforms, and that would shrink its business.

CTRI.sells: Crews that fix and replace gas pipes and power lines, paid for by gas and electric utility companies.
CTRI.moat: It has long utility relationships and skilled crews, but many contractors bid for the same jobs.
CTRI.grows: Utilities replacing old gas pipes and expanding power grids to feed data centers and growing towns.
CTRI.risk: Losing big utility contracts or utilities cutting repair budgets could quickly shrink its work.

CTVA.sells: Pioneer seeds and weed and bug killers, paid for by farmers growing corn, soybeans, fruit and vegetables.
CTVA.moat: Its patented seed genetics and crop chemicals take many years of research for rivals to match.
CTVA.grows: Farmers paying for better seeds and new nature-based crop protection to grow more food per field.
CTVA.risk: Patents expiring, cheap copycat chemicals, or poor farm incomes could cut what farmers will pay.

CUBE.sells: CubeSmart rents self-storage units to families and small businesses needing extra space for their stuff.
CUBE.moat: Customers rarely move their stuff once stored, but rivals can open new storage buildings nearby.
CUBE.grows: People moving homes, downsizing or running small businesses keep needing places to store things.
CUBE.risk: Too many new storage buildings nearby could force price cuts and leave its units sitting empty.

CURLF.sells: Cannabis products sold in its own stores and to other sellers, paid for by medical and adult users.
CURLF.moat: States hand out only a limited number of cannabis licenses, which keeps many rivals out of the market.
CURLF.grows: More states and countries allowing medical or adult cannabis use opens new places for it to sell.
CURLF.risk: Wider legalization could flood the market with rivals, and heavy taxes and debt strain its business.

CVI.sells: Gasoline, diesel and farm fertilizer made in Kansas and Oklahoma, sold to retailers, railroads and farm co-ops.
CVI.moat: Its refineries sit near cheap inland crude, but gasoline and fertilizer are the same no matter who makes them.
CVI.grows: Sales rise when fuel and fertilizer prices climb and farmers plant more corn that needs nitrogen.
CVI.risk: Fuel and fertilizer prices swing wildly, and rules on renewable fuel credits can squeeze its profits.

CVNA.sells: Used cars bought and sold online, delivered to your door, with car loans paid by everyday drivers.
CVNA.moat: Its big network of inspection centers, car haulers and loan tools is costly and slow for rivals to build.
CVNA.grows: More people get comfortable buying a car on their phone instead of visiting a dealer lot.
CVNA.risk: It borrows heavily, so a used-car price drop or rising loan defaults could hurt it fast.

CVS.sells: Pharmacy stores, Aetna health insurance and Caremark drug-plan services paid by shoppers, employers and government.
CVS.moat: Being store, insurer and drug-plan manager all at once gives it huge buying power that few rivals match.
CVS.grows: An aging country needs more prescriptions, Medicare plans and nearby clinics for everyday care.
CVS.risk: Higher medical costs in its insurance plans and government limits on drug-plan middlemen could squeeze it.

CVX.sells: Oil, natural gas, gasoline and plastics sold to drivers at Chevron stations, factories and other countries.
CVX.moat: It owns giant oil and gas fields and refineries worldwide that would take decades for a rival to copy.
CVX.grows: The world keeps needing fuel and gas for cars, planes, power plants and factories, especially in Asia.
CVX.risk: Oil is a commodity, so a long price slump or a fast switch to electric power would shrink its profits.

DAL.sells: Plane tickets for travelers and businesses, plus cargo shipping and SkyMiles points sold to credit-card partner Amex.
DAL.moat: Fliers stick with Delta for its on-time reputation, big hubs like Atlanta and the SkyMiles perks they've earned.
DAL.grows: More people traveling abroad and paying extra for comfy seats keeps its premium cabins full.
DAL.risk: A recession, jet fuel spikes or labor strikes can empty seats and wipe out an airline's thin profits.

DAVE.sells: A phone banking app with small paycheck advances called ExtraCash, paid for by fees and tips from users.
DAVE.moat: Members like the quick cash, but many banks and apps like Chime offer similar advances and accounts.
DAVE.grows: More people living paycheck to paycheck look for a cheaper way than overdraft fees to cover gaps.
