DAVE.risk: New rules on paycheck-advance fees or more members failing to repay could break its business model.

DDOG.sells: Dashboards that watch websites and apps for crashes and hackers, paid for by tech teams at companies.
DDOG.moat: Once engineers wire every server and app into Datadog, ripping it out and retraining everyone is painful.
DDOG.grows: Companies move more work to the cloud and build AI apps, and each needs watching and protecting.
DDOG.risk: Big customers may build their own tools or switch to cheaper rivals to cut their monitoring bills.

DE.sells: Green John Deere tractors, combines, mowers and bulldozers sold to farmers, builders and homeowners, plus loans.
DE.moat: Farmers trust the John Deere name and its dealer network, and its smart-farming software keeps them loyal.
DE.grows: Self-driving and precision farming tech helps farmers grow more food with fewer workers and less waste.
DE.risk: When crop prices fall, farmers stop buying expensive new machines, and right-to-repair fights could hurt it.

DGE.L.sells: Drinks like Johnnie Walker, Guinness, Smirnoff, Baileys and Don Julio, bought by bars, shops and adults.
DGE.L.moat: People ask for Johnnie Walker or Guinness by name, and a famous drink brand takes generations to build.
DGE.L.grows: Selling fancier bottles at higher prices and reaching new drinkers in India, Africa and Latin America.
DGE.L.risk: Younger adults drinking less alcohol, or choosing cannabis or cheaper drinks, could shrink demand.

DGX.sells: Blood, urine and other lab tests ordered by doctors and hospitals, paid mostly by health insurers.
DGX.moat: Its huge web of labs and patient centers lets it run tests cheaply and sign deals with big insurers.
DGX.grows: More testing as people age, plus newer tests for cancer, Alzheimer's and genetic health.
DGX.risk: Insurers and the government cutting what they pay per test, or hospitals doing more tests themselves.

DHI.sells: New houses and townhomes across America, bought by families, often with its own home loans.
DHI.moat: Being the biggest builder lets it buy land, lumber and labor cheaper and build homes faster.
DHI.grows: A shortage of homes and many young families wanting starter houses at lower prices.
DHI.risk: High mortgage rates or a weak economy could stop buyers, and land values can fall fast.

DHR.sells: Lab machines, filters and supplies from Beckman Coulter, Pall and Leica, bought by drug makers and labs.
DHR.moat: Once a medicine is approved using its filters and supplies, changing to a rival needs costly re-approval.
DHR.grows: Drug companies making more biotech medicines and hospitals running more diagnostic tests.
DHR.risk: Drug makers cutting spending, or tougher competition and trade fights in China, could slow sales.

DIS.sells: Movies, Disney+ and Hulu streaming, ESPN sports, theme parks and cruises, paid by families and fans.
DIS.moat: Nobody else owns Mickey, Marvel, Star Wars and Pixar, and those characters fill its parks and stores.
DIS.grows: Raising park and cruise prices, adding streaming subscribers, and new hit films that sell toys.
DIS.risk: People cutting cable TV and costly vacations, or a run of movies that flop, could weaken it.

DLR.sells: Space, power and cooling in data center buildings, rented by cloud companies and big businesses.
DLR.moat: Moving servers out is costly and risky, and customers like being plugged in next to their partners.
DLR.grows: Exploding demand for computing power to run AI and cloud services needs more data center space.
DLR.risk: Big tech building its own data centers, or running short of electricity, could limit growth.

DOC.sells: Buildings for medicine, like doctor offices and science labs, rented by hospitals and drug researchers.
DOC.moat: Good locations near hospitals and universities help, but other landlords can build similar buildings.
DOC.grows: An aging population needing more doctor visits and biotech companies needing lab space.
DOC.risk: Biotech companies running low on cash and leaving labs empty, plus high borrowing costs.

DOCN.sells: Simple cloud servers, databases and AI computer chips rented online by small tech companies and coders.
DOCN.moat: Developers like its simple tools and pricing, but giant clouds like Amazon and Google offer the same.
DOCN.grows: Small startups building AI apps that need easy, affordable computing power.
DOCN.risk: Amazon, Microsoft and Google cutting prices or making their own clouds simpler could pull customers.

DOMO.sells: Cloud software that pulls a company's data into dashboards and AI tools, paid for by businesses like banks and hospitals.
DOMO.moat: Once a company builds its reports inside Domo, moving them is a chore, but many bigger rivals offer similar tools.
DOMO.grows: Selling more seats and AI features to existing business customers and signing new ones through partners.
DOMO.risk: Giants like Microsoft, Salesforce and Google bundle similar data tools cheaply and could squeeze it out.

DOV.sells: Pumps, car lifts, fuel station gear, store fridges, product-labeling printers and spare parts for factories and shops.
DOV.moat: Its machines sit inside customers' factories and stations, so they keep buying its parts, refills and repairs.
DOV.grows: Buying smaller niche equipment makers and selling more replacement parts and supplies to its installed machines.
DOV.risk: A slowdown in factory and construction spending could cut orders for new equipment across many of its units.

DOW.sells: Plastics, chemicals, foams and paint ingredients bought by makers of packaging, cars, buildings and household goods.
DOW.moat: Its giant plants make basic chemicals cheaply, but rivals sell nearly identical products, so price decides most sales.
DOW.grows: More demand for packaging, building materials and car parts when the world economy is busy.
DOW.risk: Cheap new plants abroad and weak demand can flood the market with plastic and crush prices for everyone.

DPZ.sells: Pizza, wings and sides sold to hungry families for delivery or pickup through stores run mostly by franchise owners.
DPZ.moat: Its huge store network, dough factories and ordering app let it deliver fast and cheap in a way small shops struggle to.
DPZ.grows: Opening more stores around the world and getting more people to order through its app and loyalty program.
DPZ.risk: Delivery apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats let any local pizza shop reach customers, chipping at its delivery edge.

DRI.sells: Sit-down meals at Olive Garden, LongHorn Steakhouse, The Capital Grille and other restaurants paid for by diners.
DRI.moat: Being one of the biggest restaurant owners lets it buy food, ads and kitchen gear cheaper than smaller chains can.
DRI.grows: Opening new locations, raising menu prices carefully and buying other popular restaurant brands like Chuy's.
DRI.risk: If families cut back on eating out or food and wage costs jump, its restaurants could earn far less.

DTE.sells: Electricity and natural gas delivered to homes and businesses in Michigan, paid for through monthly utility bills.
DTE.moat: The state lets it be the main power and gas company in its area, so customers can't easily switch to a rival.
DTE.grows: Building new power lines, gas pipes and clean energy plants that regulators let it earn a set return on.
DTE.risk: State regulators could refuse rate increases, or big storms could bring costly repairs and angry customers.

DUK.sells: Electricity and natural gas delivered to homes, businesses and towns across the Southeast and Midwest via monthly bills.
DUK.moat: Governments grant it the right to be the local power company, so most customers have no other choice to switch to.
DUK.grows: More people and data centers moving to its fast-growing Southern states and new grid and power plant projects.
DUK.risk: Regulators could limit what it charges, and hurricanes or costly plant projects could eat into its earnings.

DUOL.sells: A fun language-learning app that is free with ads, plus paid Super and Max plans and an English test for students.
DUOL.moat: Its green owl, game-like streaks and friend leagues keep learners coming back daily and make it the name people know.
DUOL.grows: Turning more free users into paying members and adding new subjects like math, music and chess to the app.
DUOL.risk: AI chatbots that can teach languages for free could pull learners away from needing a separate app.

DVA.sells: Kidney dialysis at clinics, in hospitals and at home, paid mostly by Medicare and private insurers.
DVA.moat: Its huge network of nearby clinics, staff and insurer deals is very hard for a newcomer to copy.
DVA.grows: More people with kidney failure from diabetes and aging, plus home dialysis and whole-kidney-care deals.
DVA.risk: Government or insurers cutting what they pay, or new drugs that slow kidney disease and mean fewer patients.

DVN.sells: Oil, natural gas and gas liquids pumped from US fields, sold to refiners, pipelines and utilities.
DVN.moat: Oil and gas are the same no matter who pumps them, so price is set by the market, not by Devon.
DVN.grows: Drilling more wells in its Texas, New Mexico and other basins and getting more out of each one.
DVN.risk: Oil and gas prices falling hard, since Devon cannot control what the world pays for its product.

DXCM.sells: Small skin sensors and apps that track blood sugar all day, used by diabetes patients and paid by insurers.
DXCM.moat: Accurate tiny sensors are hard to build, and doctors and patients get used to its apps and data.
DXCM.grows: More diabetes patients switching from finger pricks, plus Stelo for people not on insulin.
DXCM.risk: Abbott's cheaper Libre sensors and other rivals winning patients, or quality problems with new sensors.

EA.sells: Video games like Madden NFL, EA SPORTS College Football, The Sims, Apex Legends and Battlefield for players.
EA.moat: Exclusive sports league licenses mean rivals cannot make an official NFL football game the same way.
EA.grows: Yearly sports releases plus players paying for extra content, packs and subscriptions inside games.
EA.risk: A big new game flopping, players getting bored, or losing a key sports license to a rival.

EBAY.sells: An online marketplace where people and shops sell new and used items, earning fees from each sale.
EBAY.moat: Lots of sellers attract lots of shoppers and the reverse, so a new site struggles to get both sides.
EBAY.grows: Collectibles like trading cards, used and refurbished goods, plus ads and payment fees from sellers.
EBAY.risk: Amazon, Temu, Facebook Marketplace and others pulling shoppers and sellers away.

ECL.sells: Cleaning, water treatment and pest control services for restaurants, hospitals, hotels and factories.
ECL.moat: Its trained service crews are built into customers' daily routines and safety rules, so few want to switch.
ECL.grows: Factories needing to save water, stricter hygiene rules, and selling more services to each customer.
ECL.risk: Big customers cutting back in a slowdown or cheaper local rivals undercutting its prices.

ED.sells: Electricity, gas and steam delivered to homes and businesses in New York City and nearby areas.
ED.moat: It owns the wires and pipes and holds the government-approved right to serve its area.
ED.grows: Regulators letting it earn a return on new spending for grid upgrades and clean energy lines.
ED.risk: Regulators refusing rate increases, or storms and costly repairs it cannot pass on to customers.

EDIT.sells: Experimental CRISPR gene editing medicines, still in testing, aimed at high cholesterol and blood diseases.
EDIT.moat: It holds CRISPR patents and know-how, but has no approved product yet and rivals are further ahead.
EDIT.grows: Success in clinical trials of its cholesterol therapy and deals with bigger drug partners.
EDIT.risk: Trials failing or the company running short of cash before any medicine reaches patients.

EDU.sells: Tutoring, test-prep classes, study-abroad advice, learning devices and livestream shopping, paid by Chinese families.
EDU.moat: Parents across China know the New Oriental name for exam prep, so many trust it over smaller tutoring shops.
EDU.grows: More students wanting test prep, study-abroad help, non-school classes and products sold on livestreams.
EDU.risk: Chinese government rules on private tutoring can change suddenly and shut down whole parts of the business.

EFX.sells: Credit reports, credit scores and job-and-income checks, paid for by banks, lenders, landlords and employers.
EFX.moat: It holds huge files on people's loans and paychecks that took decades to build, and rivals can't rebuild them.
EFX.grows: Lenders checking more borrowers, mortgage activity, and more employers sharing payroll data for income checks.
EFX.risk: A big data breach or new government rules on personal data could hurt trust and limit what it may sell.

EG.sells: Insurance for other insurance companies plus business property and liability insurance, sold through brokers.
EG.moat: Strong finances and broker ties help, but many big rivals offer similar coverage, so prices stay competitive.
EG.grows: Charging more after costly disasters, and writing more specialty business insurance through brokers.
EG.risk: Huge hurricanes, wildfires or lawsuits could cost far more than it charged for the coverage.

EIX.sells: Electricity delivered over power lines to homes, businesses, farms and cities in southern California.
EIX.moat: The state lets it be the main power-line company in its area, so customers can't easily pick a rival wire.
EIX.grows: Regulators approving new spending on grid upgrades, plus more electric cars and electric homes plugging in.
EIX.risk: Wildfires started by its power lines can bring giant lawsuits and stricter treatment from regulators.

EL.sells: Skin care, makeup and perfume like Clinique, M·A·C, La Mer and Estée Lauder, bought by shoppers worldwide.
EL.moat: Shoppers trust and pay extra for its famous names, and building a luxury beauty brand takes a very long time.
EL.grows: New products, growing demand for fancy perfume, and selling more online and in travel shops.
EL.risk: Weaker spending in China and travel shops, and trendy new brands stealing younger shoppers.

ELV.sells: Health insurance like Anthem Blue Cross plans plus pharmacy services, paid by employers, families and government.
ELV.moat: Being huge lets it get better prices from doctors and drug makers, and the Blue Cross name is widely trusted.
ELV.grows: More members in Medicare and Medicaid plans, and selling pharmacy and care services through Carelon.
ELV.risk: Members using more medical care than expected, or government cutting what it pays for Medicare and Medicaid.

EMN.sells: Specialty plastics, car window film layers, chemicals and fibers, bought by carmakers, builders and factories.
EMN.moat: Some special materials like Tritan plastic and Saflex window layers rely on recipes rivals find hard to copy.
EMN.grows: Selling more specialty materials to carmakers and electronics makers, plus newer plastic recycling efforts.
EMN.risk: Much of what it makes is basic chemicals, so slow factories and cheap rivals can squeeze its profits.

EMR.sells: Valves, sensors, factory control software and RIDGID tools, bought by plants, energy firms and tradespeople.
EMR.moat: Once a plant runs on its control systems and sensors, swapping them out is costly, slow and risky.
EMR.grows: Factories and energy plants adding automation, plus software and testing tools for engineers.
EMR.risk: A slowdown in factory and energy building could make customers delay buying big new equipment.

ENPH.sells: Small boxes called microinverters, home batteries and an app, sold to solar installers and homeowners.
ENPH.moat: Its microinverter chips and software took years to perfect, and installers trust them and are trained on them.
ENPH.grows: More homes adding solar panels, home batteries, EV chargers and backup power for blackouts.
ENPH.risk: Cheaper rivals from abroad and fewer homes buying solar when loans cost more or subsidies shrink.

EOG.sells: Crude oil and natural gas pumped from the ground, sold to refiners, utilities and fuel traders.
EOG.moat: It is known for drilling wells cheaply and picking good rock, so it earns money even when oil is cheap.
EOG.grows: Drilling new wells in its best fields and selling more natural gas as the world uses more of it.
EOG.risk: Oil and gas prices fall hard, since it sells a commodity anyone else can pump too.

EPAM.sells: Teams of software engineers who build apps, websites and cloud systems for banks, stores and drug makers.
EPAM.moat: Once its engineers know a client's systems deeply, swapping them for a new firm is slow and risky.
EPAM.grows: Companies paying for help moving to the cloud, using data and adding AI to their products.
EPAM.risk: AI tools that write code could shrink how many paid engineers clients need, and rivals are many.

EPD.sells: Use of its pipelines, storage caverns and export docks, paid by oil, gas and chemical companies.
EPD.moat: Its giant web of pipes and terminals along the Gulf Coast would be very costly and slow to rebuild.
EPD.grows: More gas and liquids flowing from Texas fields and more fuel and plastics ingredients shipped overseas.
EPD.risk: Less drilling in America or rules that slow fossil fuel use would mean less product flowing through.

EQIX.sells: Space, power and cables inside data centers, rented by cloud giants, banks and internet companies.
EQIX.moat: So many companies connect to each other inside its buildings that new tenants want to be there too.
EQIX.grows: Cloud computing and AI needing more data center space and more direct links between companies.
EQIX.risk: Huge tech firms building their own data centers and power shortages limiting new buildings.

EQR.sells: Apartments for rent in big cities like Boston, New York, Seattle and San Francisco, paid by renters.
EQR.moat: It owns buildings in crowded coastal cities where land is scarce and building new homes is hard.
EQR.grows: Rents rising as people keep moving to big job hubs plus buying more buildings in growing cities.
EQR.risk: Too many new apartments, rent control laws or people leaving big cities could push rents down.

EQT.sells: Natural gas from Appalachia, sold to utilities, factories and gas traders who heat homes and make power.
EQT.moat: It owns huge gas fields and its own pipelines, so it can pull out gas more cheaply than many rivals.
EQT.grows: More gas needed for power plants feeding AI data centers and for shipping gas overseas.
EQT.risk: Gas prices crashing, since gas is a commodity, or pipeline limits that stop it reaching buyers.

ES.sells: Electricity, gas and water delivered to homes and businesses in Connecticut, Massachusetts and New Hampshire.
ES.moat: The government lets it be the only wire and pipe company in its towns, so customers can't switch.
ES.grows: State-approved spending on new power lines and pipes, which it earns a set return on.
ES.risk: Regulators refusing rate increases or blocking costs, plus storms and money lost on side projects.

ESS.sells: Apartments to rent in California and Seattle cities, paid for monthly by the renters who live there.
ESS.moat: Land and permits to build new apartments in coastal California are very hard to get, so few rivals appear.
ESS.grows: Raising rents when tech jobs bring more people, and building or fixing up more apartment buildings.
ESS.risk: Rent control laws or tech layoffs pushing people out of West Coast cities could cut rents.

ESTC.sells: Elasticsearch and Kibana software that lets companies search their data, watch their apps and spot hackers.
ESTC.moat: Once a company's logs and search run on Elastic, moving everything to another tool is slow and risky.
ESTC.grows: Companies building AI chat tools that must search their own data, plus more moving onto Elastic Cloud.
ESTC.risk: Big cloud companies and rivals like Datadog and Splunk offer similar tools, some cheaper or free.

ETR.sells: Electricity to homes and businesses in Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi and Texas, paid on monthly bills.
ETR.moat: The government lets only Entergy run the power lines in its areas, so customers can't pick a rival.
ETR.grows: New factories and data centers along the Gulf Coast need lots of power, so it builds more plants.
ETR.risk: Hurricanes can wreck its power lines, and regulators may refuse to let it raise prices to pay for repairs.

EVGO.sells: Fast charging for electric cars at stations, paid by drivers, carmakers and fleets like ride-share drivers.
EVGO.moat: Its spots at busy stores and the PlugShare app help, but Tesla and others can build chargers nearby.
EVGO.grows: More people driving electric cars and carmakers paying for their drivers to charge on its network.
EVGO.risk: If electric car sales slow or Tesla Superchargers take its drivers, its stations could sit empty.

EW.sells: SAPIEN heart valves doctors put in through a thin tube, plus surgery valves, sold to hospitals.
EW.moat: Doctors trained on SAPIEN trust it, and rival valves need patents and years of safety tests to compete.
EW.grows: More older people with worn-out heart valves, and new PASCAL and EVOQUE valves for other heart parts.
EW.risk: Rival valves from Medtronic or Abbott working as well, or a safety problem hurting doctors' trust.

EWBC.sells: Bank accounts and loans for families and businesses, especially ones that trade between America and Asia.
EWBC.moat: It knows Chinese-American communities and has branches in Asia, and moving all your accounts is a hassle.
EWBC.grows: Making more loans to businesses and holding more deposits as its customers' companies get bigger.
EWBC.risk: Bad real estate loans or fights between America and China could hurt the trade business it serves.

EXC.sells: Electricity and gas delivered to homes and businesses in Chicago, Philadelphia, Baltimore and Washington.
EXC.moat: Each city lets only its local Exelon company run the wires and pipes, so there is no rival line to pick.
EXC.grows: Spending on new power lines for data centers and cities, which regulators let it earn a return on.
EXC.risk: Regulators blocking price increases, or past political scandals making officials less friendly to it.

EXE.sells: Natural gas pulled from shale rock in Pennsylvania, Ohio and Louisiana, sold to utilities and exporters.
EXE.moat: Gas is the same from every driller, though its large low-cost land helps it earn money when prices drop.
EXE.grows: More gas shipped overseas as LNG, and more power plants and data centers burning gas for electricity.
EXE.risk: Gas prices falling hard when too much is drilled, since it cannot control what gas sells for.

EXP.sells: Cement, wallboard, ready-mix concrete and gravel, bought by home builders, contractors and road crews.
EXP.moat: Its cement plants sit on owned limestone quarries, and new plants need hard permits and are costly to build.
EXP.grows: New homes, road and highway repair paid for by governments, and people remodeling their houses.
EXP.risk: A slump in home building or road spending would leave its big plants with less to make and sell.

EXPN.L.sells: Credit reports, credit scores and fraud checks bought by banks, car lenders and shops, plus consumer apps.
EXPN.L.moat: It holds credit histories on huge numbers of people that lenders keep feeding it, which rivals can't rebuild.
EXPN.L.grows: More lenders using its data and AI tools for decisions, plus fraud checks and paid consumer credit services.
EXPN.L.risk: A big data leak or tougher privacy rules could hurt trust and limit how it may use people's data.

EXR.sells: Rentable storage units for boxes, furniture, boats and RVs, paid monthly by households and small businesses.
EXR.moat: Being the biggest storage owner lets it spend less per store on ads, software and managing many locations.
EXR.grows: People moving, downsizing or running out of space, plus buying more stores and raising rents over time.
EXR.risk: Too many new storage buildings nearby could force it to cut rents to keep its units filled.

FAST.sells: Bolts, screws, nuts, safety gear and tools, bought by factories, builders, farms and government agencies.
FAST.moat: Its vending machines and stock bins sit inside customer plants and refill themselves, so leaving is a hassle.
FAST.grows: Putting more vending machines and on-site stores into big factories and winning more large business customers.
FAST.risk: A slowdown in factory work or online rivals selling the same parts cheaper could squeeze its business.

FATE.sells: Nothing for sale yet; it is testing lab-made immune cells meant to fight cancer, lupus and other diseases.
FATE.moat: Its stem-cell know-how is promising, but no treatment is approved and many rivals chase the same idea.
FATE.grows: Good test results, partner deals like the one with Ono Pharmaceutical, and hoped-for future approvals.
FATE.risk: A failed trial or running out of cash before a product is approved could stop the company's plans.

FBIN.sells: Moen faucets, Therma-Tru doors, Master Lock locks and SentrySafe safes, sold to homeowners and builders.
FBIN.moat: Plumbers, builders and shoppers trust names like Moen and Master Lock and pick them off store shelves.
FBIN.grows: People fixing up and remodeling homes, new houses being built, and smart locks like Yale and August.
FBIN.risk: A long slowdown in home remodeling or cheaper store brands could take shelf space and sales away.

FCX.sells: Copper, gold and molybdenum dug from big mines in Arizona, Peru and Indonesia, sold to metal makers.
FCX.moat: It owns giant mines like Grasberg that are rare, but copper is the same metal no matter who digs it up.
FCX.grows: Demand for copper in electric cars, power lines, data centers and buildings around the world.
FCX.risk: A drop in copper prices, mine accidents or political trouble in Indonesia could hurt it a lot.

FDS.sells: Financial data screens and analytics tools bought by fund managers, bankers, wealth advisers and hedge funds.
FDS.moat: Analysts build their daily work, models and reports inside FactSet, so moving to a rival is painful.
FDS.grows: Selling more tools to existing clients, new AI features, and data feeds plugged into clients' own systems.
FDS.risk: Cheaper AI tools or bigger rivals like Bloomberg could pull clients away or push its prices down.

FDX.sells: FedEx flies and trucks packages door to door for online shops, businesses and people who mail things.
FDX.moat: Its giant web of planes, trucks and hubs would take a rival a fortune and many years to rebuild.
FDX.grows: More online shopping and global trade mean more boxes that need to move fast across towns and oceans.
FDX.risk: Amazon delivering its own packages and weaker shipping demand could leave its costly network half full.

FE.sells: FirstEnergy delivers electricity over its power lines to homes and businesses in Ohio, Pennsylvania and nearby.
FE.moat: Government rules let it be the only company running the power lines in its towns, so no rival can move in.
FE.grows: Building and upgrading power lines, which regulators let it earn a set return on, plus rising power use.
FE.risk: Regulators could cut what it may charge, and past bribery scandals have hurt trust with officials.

FERG.sells: Ferguson sells pipes, valves, water heaters and air conditioning parts to plumbers and building contractors.
FERG.moat: Its huge branch network keeps parts in stock near job sites, so pros get what they need fast.
FERG.grows: New homes, repairs of old plumbing, big water projects and data centers all need its pipes and parts.
FERG.risk: A slowdown in building and home repairs would mean contractors order far fewer pipes and parts.

FICO.sells: FICO makes the credit score banks check before giving loans, plus software that spots card fraud.
FICO.moat: Almost every lender's loan rules and systems are built around the FICO score, so changing is painful.
FICO.grows: It keeps raising the price lenders pay per score, and sells more fraud and decision software.
FICO.risk: Regulators pushing lenders toward rival scores like VantageScore, or anger over its price hikes.

FITB.sells: Fifth Third is a bank that takes deposits and lends money to families and businesses in the Midwest and South.
FITB.moat: Customers stick because moving accounts is a hassle, but many banks offer the very same products.
FITB.grows: Opening new branches in fast-growing Southern states and lending more to businesses and homebuyers.
FITB.risk: Bad loans in a recession or depositors moving their cash to banks paying better interest.

FIVE.sells: Five Below sells cheap fun stuff like candy, phone chargers, toys and room decor mostly to kids and teens.
FIVE.moat: Teens love its treasure-hunt stores, but dollar stores, Walmart and online shops sell similar cheap items.
FIVE.grows: Opening many new stores across the country and adding trendy products that kids want right now.
FIVE.risk: Rising costs from tariffs on goods made overseas could squeeze its low price promise.

FLYW.sells: Flywire helps students, patients and travelers pay universities, hospitals and hotels across borders.
FLYW.moat: Its tools plug into a school's or hospital's billing system, so once set up, few want to rip it out.
FLYW.grows: Signing up more colleges, hospitals and travel companies, and handling more payments per customer.
FLYW.risk: Visa limits on foreign students could shrink tuition payments, its biggest source of business.

FMC.sells: FMC sells bug killers, weed killers and fungus sprays that farmers use to protect their crops.
FMC.moat: Its patented chemicals and years of lab research are hard to copy while the patents are still in force.
FMC.grows: New patented sprays and natural biological products that help farmers grow more food per field.
FMC.risk: Cheap copycat versions after key patents expire are already pulling farmers away from its top product.

FOUR.sells: Card payment processing and SkyTab point-of-sale systems paid for by restaurants, hotels, stadiums and stores.
FOUR.moat: Once a restaurant's tablets, menus and staff run on SkyTab, switching to another processor is a big hassle.
FOUR.grows: Signing more restaurants, hotels, sports venues and overseas merchants, and handling more of their payments.
FOUR.risk: Bigger rivals like Square, Toast and Clover fight hard on price for the same small merchants.

FOXA.sells: Fox News, Fox Sports and the FOX TV network, paid for by advertisers and cable and streaming TV providers.
FOXA.moat: Fox News has a very loyal audience, and big live sports like the NFL keep viewers and advertisers coming back.
FOXA.grows: Ad sales around big sports events and elections, fees from TV providers, and growth of the free Tubi app.
FOXA.risk: People cancelling cable bundles, and the rising cost of keeping big sports rights.

FSLR.sells: Thin-film solar panels sold to utilities, power-plant builders and big companies that want clean electricity.
FSLR.moat: Its special thin-film panel recipe differs from Chinese silicon panels and is made largely in American factories.
FSLR.grows: Utilities and data centers needing more electricity, plus US rules that favor American-made panels.
FSLR.risk: Changes to US clean-energy tax credits or tariffs, or cheaper Chinese silicon panels winning on price.

FTNT.sells: FortiGate firewalls and security software subscriptions paid for by businesses, schools and governments.
FTNT.moat: Its own security chips make firewalls fast and cheap, and networks built on its gear are painful to rip out.
FTNT.grows: Selling security subscriptions on top of installed firewalls and replacing older networking gear at companies.
FTNT.risk: Cloud security rivals like Palo Alto Networks and Zscaler pulling customers away from in-office boxes.

FULT.sells: Checking and savings accounts, home and business loans, and wealth advice for people and firms in the Mid-Atlantic.
FULT.moat: Local branches and long customer relationships help, but many banks offer nearly the same products.
FULT.grows: Lending more to local businesses and homeowners and growing its wealth management and deposits.
FULT.risk: Bad loans in a downturn, especially commercial real estate, or interest-rate swings squeezing profits.

FWONK.sells: Formula One racing, paid for by TV and streaming deals, race-hosting cities, sponsors and fans' tickets.
FWONK.moat: It owns the commercial rights to Formula One, so nobody else can sell the world's top racing series.
FWONK.grows: More fans from shows like Drive to Survive, new races in places like Las Vegas, and bigger sponsor deals.
FWONK.risk: Fans losing interest if races get dull, or fights with teams and the FIA over money and rules.

GATX.sells: Leases tank and freight railcars and spare jet engines to oil, chemical, food and railroad companies.
GATX.moat: Its giant fleet and repair shops let it offer railcars plus upkeep that small leasing firms struggle to match.
GATX.grows: Raising lease rates when railcars are in demand, and growing its aircraft engine and overseas rail fleets.
GATX.risk: A slowdown in shipping chemicals and oil by rail, leaving many railcars sitting idle.

GD.sells: Gulfstream jets for wealthy flyers and nuclear submarines, tanks and military tech for the US government.
GD.moat: Only a couple of shipyards can build nuclear submarines, and Gulfstream is a top name in private jets.
GD.grows: Navy submarine orders, demand for new Gulfstream jets, and countries ordering more tanks and ammunition.
GD.risk: Government budget cuts, or shipyard delays and cost overruns on the submarine programs.

GDDY.sells: Domain names, website builders, web hosting and email that small businesses and solo owners pay for.
GDDY.moat: Moving a domain, website and email all at once is a hassle, so small businesses tend to stay put.
GDDY.grows: Selling more add-ons to current customers, like payments, card readers, marketing and AI site tools.
GDDY.risk: Easier or cheaper builders like Wix, Squarespace and Shopify could win new small-business customers.

GDS.sells: Data center space, power and cooling in China, rented by cloud companies, big internet firms and banks.
GDS.moat: Big customers dislike moving servers, but many rivals build similar data centers, so pricing stays tough.
GDS.grows: Chinese internet and cloud firms needing more computer space for AI and online services.
GDS.risk: Heavy borrowing plus Chinese rules and US chip limits could slow customers or squeeze the business.

GE.sells: Jet engines plus repairs and spare parts, bought by airlines, Boeing, Airbus and militaries.
GE.moat: Jet engines take rare know-how and long safety approvals, and each one needs GE parts and repairs for life.
GE.grows: More people flying worldwide means more flight hours, so more engine repairs, spare parts and new orders.
GE.risk: A safety problem, factory slowdowns or a plane maker's troubles could hurt deliveries and trust.

GEHC.sells: CT, MRI, X-ray and ultrasound machines, patient monitors and scan dyes that hospitals and clinics buy.
GEHC.moat: Hospitals train staff on its machines and sign long service deals, so swapping brands is costly.
GEHC.grows: Aging populations need more scans, plus newer AI-assisted imaging and the dyes used in many scans.
GEHC.risk: Tough rivals Siemens and Philips, hospital budget cuts and trade tariffs, especially in China.

GERN.sells: RYTELO, a medicine for a blood cancer called MDS that causes anemia, paid for by insurers and hospitals.
GERN.moat: Its drug is patent-protected, but with just one product and strong rivals, the edge is not proven yet.
GERN.grows: Getting more doctors to prescribe RYTELO, and trials testing it in other blood cancers like myelofibrosis.
GERN.risk: Slow sales, a failed trial or running low on cash could hurt this young one-drug company.

GEV.sells: Gas turbines, wind turbines and power-grid equipment that utilities and governments buy to make electricity.
GEV.moat: Only a few firms can build huge gas turbines, and its giant fleet worldwide needs its service and parts.
GEV.grows: Data centers and AI need much more electricity, so utilities order more turbines and grid gear.
GEV.risk: Money-losing wind projects, cost overruns or a slowdown in power demand could hurt it.

GILD.sells: HIV medicines like Biktarvy, plus hepatitis and cancer drugs, paid for by insurers and governments.
GILD.moat: Patents block copies, and doctors trust its HIV pills that patients take every day for years.
GILD.grows: Yeztugo, an HIV prevention shot given only a few times a year, plus cancer drugs like Trodelvy.
GILD.risk: Patents running out lets cheap copies in, and government drug price cuts could shrink sales.

GL.sells: Life and supplemental health insurance sold to middle-income families, who pay monthly premiums.
GL.moat: Its big agent teams and mail sales reach families others skip, but rivals sell similar policies.
GL.grows: Hiring and keeping more agents to sell new policies, and investing the premiums it collects.
GL.risk: Claims of pushy agent sales practices, or losing agents, could hurt trust and new sales.

GLEN.L.sells: Glencore digs up and trades copper, cobalt, zinc, nickel, coal and oil, selling them to factories and power plants.
GLEN.L.moat: It owns huge mines and a global trading network that took decades to build and is very hard to copy.
GLEN.L.grows: Demand for copper and cobalt in electric cars, batteries and power grids keeps it selling more metal.
GLEN.L.risk: Metal and coal prices swing wildly, and rules against coal or legal trouble could hurt its business.

GM.sells: GM builds Chevrolet, GMC, Cadillac and Buick trucks and cars for families, rental companies and governments.
GM.moat: Loyal truck fans and a huge dealer network keep people coming back to Chevy and GMC pickups and SUVs.
GM.grows: Popular pickups and SUVs, car loans from GM Financial, and software subscriptions add new sales.
GM.risk: Car making is fierce, and cheaper electric cars from rivals or a weak economy could squeeze GM.

GOOG.sells: Google runs Search, YouTube, Android, Gmail and Google Cloud, mostly paid for by advertisers and businesses.
GOOG.moat: Billions use Search and YouTube, so advertisers must be there, and more use makes its results even better.
GOOG.grows: More YouTube viewers, Cloud and Gemini AI tools for companies, and subscriptions like YouTube Premium.
GOOG.risk: AI chatbots could steal search habits, and government lawsuits could force it to change how it works.

GOOGL.sells: Google runs Search, YouTube, Android, Gmail and Google Cloud, mostly paid for by advertisers and businesses.
GOOGL.moat: Billions use Search and YouTube, so advertisers must be there, and more use makes its results even better.
GOOGL.grows: More YouTube viewers, Cloud and Gemini AI tools for companies, and subscriptions like YouTube Premium.
GOOGL.risk: AI chatbots could steal search habits, and government lawsuits could force it to change how it works.

GPC.sells: Genuine Parts runs NAPA stores selling brakes, batteries and filters to repair shops, plus factory parts.
GPC.moat: Its huge web of NAPA stores and warehouses gets the right part to a mechanic fast, which small rivals can't.
GPC.grows: Cars on the road keep getting older and need repairs, and factories keep needing bearings and hoses.
GPC.risk: Electric cars need fewer parts, and online sellers like Amazon could pull mechanics away from NAPA.

GS.sells: Goldman Sachs helps big companies merge and raise money, trades for investors, and manages wealthy people's money.
GS.moat: Top companies trust its famous name and deep connections for their biggest, most secret money deals.
GS.grows: More company mergers, busy trading markets, and more money handed to it to manage for clients.
GS.risk: When markets freeze and deals stop, its fees drop fast, and new banking rules could limit its trading.

GSK.L.sells: GSK makes vaccines like Shingrix for shingles, plus asthma, HIV and cancer medicines paid for by health systems.
GSK.L.moat: Patents protect its medicines, and making vaccines at huge scale takes know-how rivals take years to learn.
GSK.L.grows: New vaccines for shingles and RSV, plus new drugs for cancer, HIV and lung diseases in its research pipeline.
GSK.L.risk: When patents run out, cheap copies arrive, and failed drug trials or lawsuits could leave a hole in sales.

GTBIF.sells: Green Thumb grows and sells cannabis like Rythm and incredibles edibles through its own stores and other shops.
GTBIF.moat: States hand out only a few cannabis licenses, so it is hard for new rivals to open shops and grow farms.
GTBIF.grows: More states allowing adult-use cannabis lets it open new stores and sell its brands to more people.
GTBIF.risk: Cannabis is still illegal at the federal level, and falling prices or more licenses could squeeze it.

GTLB.sells: GitLab sells one web app where coding teams plan, store, test, secure and ship software, paid by companies.
GTLB.moat: Once a company keeps all its code, tests and security checks in GitLab, moving everything out is slow and risky.
GTLB.grows: More companies paying for top plans and the Duo AI helpers that write, check and fix code for developers.
GTLB.risk: Microsoft's GitHub with Copilot is bigger and could keep pulling customers and new coders away from GitLab.

GTX.sells: Garrett makes turbochargers and air compressors that carmakers, truck makers and repair shops pay for.
GTX.moat: Building turbos that spin super fast without breaking takes deep skill, and few rivals besides BorgWarner do it well.
GTX.grows: Turbos in more hybrid cars, plus new electric motors and compressors for fuel cells, cooling and factories.
GTX.risk: If most new cars go fully electric, they no longer need turbochargers, which is Garrett's main product.

GWW.sells: Grainger sells gloves, tools, pumps, cleaning and safety gear to factories, hospitals, schools and governments.
GWW.moat: Its huge warehouses and fast delivery of a giant catalog let it ship almost any part quickly where rivals cannot.
GWW.grows: Winning more mid-size business customers and growing its online stores Zoro in America and MonotaRO in Japan.
GWW.risk: Amazon Business could win over customers by selling the same supplies online at lower prices.

HAL.sells: Halliburton drills, cements and fracks oil and gas wells for energy companies like Exxon and Saudi Aramco.
HAL.moat: Few firms own enough crews, pumping trucks and know-how to run giant fracking jobs around the world.
HAL.grows: More drilling overseas and in deep water, plus electric fracking fleets and digital tools for oil fields.
HAL.risk: When oil and gas prices fall, energy companies drill less and cut what they pay for Halliburton's services.

HALO.sells: Halozyme licenses an enzyme that turns long drug drips into quick shots, paid by drugmakers like Roche and Pfizer.
HALO.moat: Its patented ENHANZE enzyme is built into blockbuster drugs like Darzalex, so partners rarely switch it out.
HALO.grows: Drugmakers putting the enzyme into more cancer and immune drugs, which pays Halozyme a royalty on every sale.
HALO.risk: When its key patents run out, rivals could copy the enzyme and drugmakers might pay Halozyme much less.

HAS.sells: Hasbro sells Magic: The Gathering, Monopoly, Nerf, Play-Doh and Transformers to stores and families.
HAS.moat: Kids and adults have loved Monopoly, Magic and Dungeons & Dragons for ages, and no rival can copy those names.
HAS.grows: Magic card sets, video games built on its brands, and licensing its characters for movies, shows and shirts.
HAS.risk: Kids are trading toys for screens, and if Magic fans lose interest the company's biggest profit maker shrinks.

HBAN.sells: Huntington is a Midwest bank that earns from loans, checking accounts and fees paid by people and businesses.
HBAN.moat: People rarely move their checking account and bill payments, and its overdraft grace perks keep customers loyal.
HBAN.grows: Lending to more businesses, opening branches in new states like Texas and the Carolinas, and buying smaller banks.
HBAN.risk: Banking is very similar everywhere, so bad loans in a recession or rivals paying more on savings could hurt it.

HCA.sells: HCA runs hospitals, ER centers and surgery clinics, paid by insurers, Medicare, Medicaid and patients.
HCA.moat: It owns many hospitals in fast-growing cities, so it buys supplies cheaply and insurers need it in their networks.
HCA.grows: More people moving to Sun Belt cities like Texas and Florida, an aging country, and new outpatient centers.
HCA.risk: Government cuts to Medicaid or Medicare payments, or nurse shortages raising wages, could squeeze its profits.

HCC.sells: Warrior digs coal from Alabama mines and ships it to steel makers in Europe, South America and Asia.
HCC.moat: Its coal is good for making steel, but coal is a commodity and steel makers can switch to other mines.
HCC.grows: More steel being made in Asia and new mines opening raise how much coal it can sell.
HCC.risk: Steel demand or coal prices can fall hard, and mine accidents or floods can stop work for months.

HD.sells: Home Depot sells lumber, tools, paint, garden supplies and installs, paid for by homeowners and contractors.
HD.moat: Its huge store network and supply deals let it stock more, deliver faster and charge less than small rivals.
HD.grows: Old homes needing repairs and pros like roofers and plumbers ordering big job loads keep sales coming.
HD.risk: When people move less and housing slows, fewer big remodels happen and store sales can shrink.

HDB.sells: HDFC Bank holds savings and lends money for homes, cars and businesses, earning interest from Indian borrowers.
HDB.moat: Millions of Indians trust it with their savings, giving it cheap deposits that newer banks struggle to match.
HDB.grows: More Indians opening accounts, using cards and phone payments, and taking first loans keeps it growing.
HDB.risk: If many borrowers stop repaying loans or rules from India's central bank tighten, profits could get squeezed.

HHH.sells: Howard Hughes sells land to homebuilders in giant planned towns and rents out offices, shops and apartments.
HHH.moat: It owns huge blocks of land in towns like The Woodlands and Summerlin that rivals cannot easily get.
HHH.grows: As families move into its towns, nearby land gets more valuable and it builds more shops and offices.
HHH.risk: High mortgage rates or a housing slump could slow land sales and leave its offices half empty.

HIG.sells: The Hartford sells car, home, workers' comp and business insurance plus group benefits paid for by employers.
HIG.moat: Its long ties with insurance agents and deep claims data help it price small business policies well.
HIG.grows: More small businesses needing coverage and employers adding disability and life plans grow its premiums.
HIG.risk: Big storms, lawsuits or pricing mistakes can make claims cost more than the premiums it collects.

HII.sells: Huntington Ingalls builds and repairs warships, aircraft carriers and submarines paid for by the US Navy.
HII.moat: It runs the only shipyard in America that builds nuclear aircraft carriers, which takes decades to copy.
HII.grows: The Navy wanting more submarines and ships, plus defense tech work, keeps its order book full.
HII.risk: Worker shortages, cost overruns or cuts to the Navy's budget could squeeze profits on fixed-price ships.

HIK.L.sells: Hikma makes generic medicines and hospital injections, paid for by hospitals, pharmacies and health systems.
HIK.L.moat: Making clean, safe injectable drugs is hard, and its large factories supply hospitals that need steady stock.
HIK.L.grows: Drug shortages, new generic launches and growth in Middle East and North Africa markets push sales.
HIK.L.risk: Generic drug prices can drop fast when rivals enter, and a failed factory inspection could stop supply.

HIMS.sells: Hims & Hers sells online doctor visits and treatments for hair, skin, sex health and weight loss.
HIMS.moat: Its well-known brand and easy app make getting private treatments simple, so many people keep subscriptions.
HIMS.grows: Adding new treatments like weight loss and hormone care and entering new countries brings more subscribers.
HIMS.risk: Rules on copied weight-loss drugs or drug makers selling direct could cut off a key part of its business.

HLT.sells: Hotel owners pay Hilton fees to run Hampton, DoubleTree and Waldorf Astoria hotels under its famous names.
HLT.moat: Hilton Honors members keep booking Hilton hotels, so owners want the name and rivals struggle to match it.
HLT.grows: Owners keep opening new Hilton-branded hotels around the world, and Hilton earns fees from each one.
HLT.risk: A travel slump or a recession means fewer guests, so room sales and Hilton's fees both shrink.

HON.sells: Factory controls, building fire and security systems, sensors and refinery tech for plants and buildings.
HON.moat: Once a refinery or building is wired with Honeywell controls, ripping them out is costly and risky.
HON.grows: Factories and buildings keep adding automation, software and energy-saving upgrades, plus service contracts.
HON.risk: A slowdown in factory and building spending, or a messy breakup of the company, could weaken it.

HONA.sells: Cockpit electronics, small engines, navigation gear and brakes for plane makers, airlines and the military.
HONA.moat: Its parts are certified onto each plane model, so airlines keep using Honeywell for repairs and spares.
HONA.grows: More flights and more defense and space spending mean more new planes and more repair work.
HONA.risk: Plane-making delays, cuts to military budgets, or a rival winning spots on new aircraft designs.

HOOD.sells: An app for trading stocks, options and crypto; it earns from trading, margin loans, interest and Gold plans.
HOOD.moat: Its simple app and well-known name pull in young investors who then move savings and retirement money there.
HOOD.grows: New products like retirement accounts, credit cards, prediction markets and more countries bring in money.
HOOD.risk: Trading dries up when markets fall, and regulators could limit how it earns money from trades.

HRL.sells: SPAM, Skippy, Planters, Jennie-O turkey and bacon sold to grocery stores, restaurants and convenience stores.
HRL.moat: Shoppers trust and recognize SPAM, Skippy and Planters, so stores keep them on shelves.
HRL.grows: New flavors, snack nuts and ready-to-eat meals, plus sales to restaurants and overseas shoppers.
HRL.risk: Rising meat costs, turkey disease, and cheaper store brands could squeeze its profits.

HSBA.L.sells: Bank accounts, home loans, wealth advice and global payments for families in Hong Kong, the UK and big firms.
HSBA.L.moat: Its huge network across Asia and Europe lets big companies move money between countries in one place.
HSBA.L.grows: More wealthy savers in Asia and companies trading across borders need its banking and investing help.
HSBA.L.risk: Trouble in Hong Kong's property market, falling interest rates, or tension between China and the West.

HSIC.sells: Gloves, fillings, dental chairs, implants and office software sold to dentists and doctors' offices.
HSIC.moat: Dentists rely on its fast delivery of many supplies and its practice software, which is hard to switch.
HSIC.grows: Dental offices keep needing supplies, plus more implants, digital equipment and software subscriptions.
HSIC.risk: Big rivals, online sellers and dental groups bargaining for lower prices could squeeze its thin profits.

HST.sells: It owns fancy hotels like Ritz-Carlton, Westin and Hyatt; guests and event groups pay for rooms and meetings.
HST.moat: Its hotels sit in prime city and resort spots that are very hard and costly for rivals to build again.
HST.grows: Renovating its hotels, more business travel and events, and raising room rates help sales rise.
HST.risk: A recession or travel shock empties hotel rooms, and high borrowing costs hurt real estate owners.

HSY.sells: Candy like Reese's, Kit Kat and Twizzlers plus SkinnyPop popcorn, sold to grocery, drug and corner stores.
HSY.moat: Shoppers grab the names they grew up with, and stores give the best shelf spots to snacks that sell most.
HSY.grows: New flavors, holiday treats like Halloween candy, and salty snacks like pretzels and popcorn.
HSY.risk: Expensive cocoa, or people eating less sugar because of diets and weight-loss drugs.

HUBG.sells: It moves goods for retailers and car makers using trucks, trains, shipping containers and warehouses.
HUBG.moat: It owns lots of containers and works closely with railroads, but many rivals offer similar shipping.
HUBG.grows: More goods shipped across the country and more companies handing it their warehousing and delivery.
HUBG.risk: A slow economy with fewer goods to ship, and cheap rival trucking pulling prices down.

HUM.sells: Medicare health plans for seniors, paid by members and the government, plus CenterWell senior clinics.
HUM.moat: It is one of the biggest Medicare plan companies, with doctor networks and clinics that are hard to build.
HUM.grows: More people reaching Medicare age and more seniors using its CenterWell clinics and home health care.
HUM.risk: The government paying less per member, or members using more care than the company planned for.

HUT.sells: Bitcoin mining plus power and data center space rented to companies running computers and AI.
HUT.moat: It controls power sites, but bitcoin mining is a commodity business and many rivals do the same.
HUT.grows: AI companies needing big power-hungry data centers, and more income from mining if bitcoin holds value.
HUT.risk: A drop in the bitcoin price or higher power costs could wipe out mining profits fast.

HWM.sells: Jet engine blades, fasteners and metal parts for plane makers like Boeing and Airbus, plus truck wheels.
HWM.moat: Engine parts take years of testing to get approved, so plane and engine makers rarely switch suppliers.
HWM.grows: Airlines ordering new planes and older engines needing replacement parts during repairs.
HWM.risk: Plane makers slowing production, or a serious quality problem with a part flying on jets.

IBCP.sells: Checking and savings accounts, home loans and money advice for families and businesses in Michigan.
IBCP.moat: Local customers like knowing their bankers, but many banks and apps offer the same accounts.
IBCP.grows: Making more loans to Michigan homeowners and small businesses and adding wealth management clients.
IBCP.risk: Borrowers failing to repay loans in a bad economy, or savers moving cash to higher-paying accounts.

IBKR.sells: Online trading of stocks, options, futures and currencies worldwide for individuals, funds and advisors.
IBKR.moat: Its highly automated system lets it charge low fees and still earn more than rivals with bigger staffs.
IBKR.grows: More people around the world opening trading accounts and keeping cash and loans with the broker.
IBKR.risk: Lower interest rates cut what it earns on client cash, and quiet markets mean fewer trades.

IBM.sells: Software, cloud and AI tools, consulting and big mainframe computers for banks, governments and large firms.
IBM.moat: Big banks and airlines run key systems on IBM software and mainframes, and switching is costly and risky.
IBM.grows: Companies adding AI and hybrid cloud software, plus new mainframe models and consulting projects.
IBM.risk: Faster cloud rivals like Amazon and Microsoft drawing customers away from older IBM systems.

IBN.sells: Bank accounts, loans, cards, insurance and investing apps for families and companies across India.
IBN.moat: A huge branch and app network collects cheap savings deposits that smaller lenders struggle to match.
IBN.grows: More Indians open bank accounts, take home and car loans, and pay digitally as incomes rise.
IBN.risk: Bad loans piling up in a weak economy, or tougher competition from rival banks and payment apps.

IBP.sells: Crews that install insulation, garage doors, gutters, shower doors and fireproofing for home builders.
IBP.moat: As a national installer it gets better material prices and dependable crews that big builders rely on.
IBP.grows: More new homes being built, stricter energy rules needing more insulation, and acquiring local installers.
IBP.risk: A housing slowdown, since fewer new homes means far less installation work.

ICE.sells: Trading floors like the New York Stock Exchange, market data, and mortgage software paid for by banks and lenders.
ICE.moat: Traders go where other traders already are, and banks build their daily work around its data and tools.
ICE.grows: More trading, more demand for bond and index data, and lenders moving mortgage paperwork fully online.
ICE.risk: Regulators limiting fees, or a long freeze in home sales hurting the mortgage software business.

IDXX.sells: Blood and urine testing machines, SNAP test kits and lab services that vets use to check pets.
IDXX.moat: Vet clinics own its machines and software, so they keep paying for its test supplies year after year.
IDXX.grows: Owners spending more on pet health and vets running more tests during each checkup.
IDXX.risk: Fewer pet visits to the vet, or rivals offering cheaper machines and tests that clinics switch to.

IEP.sells: A grab bag of businesses: an oil refinery, fertilizer, car repair shops, real estate and investment funds.
IEP.moat: It is a collection of unrelated businesses run by one investor, without one clear edge holding it together.
IEP.grows: Results depend on fuel prices, fertilizer demand and how well the founder's investments perform.
IEP.risk: Heavy reliance on one founder's bets, swings in oil prices, and paying out more cash than it earns.

IEX.sells: Specialty pumps, valves, meters, seals, fire truck pumps and rescue tools sold to factories and labs.
IEX.moat: Its small precise parts are designed into customers' machines, so swapping them out is costly and risky.
IEX.grows: Demand from medical labs, chip makers and water systems, plus adding small niche companies.
IEX.risk: A factory slowdown where customers order fewer parts and delay new equipment projects.

IFF.sells: Secret flavor and scent recipes plus food ingredients bought by soda, snack, perfume and soap makers.
IFF.moat: Once its flavor is in a famous drink or snack, changing it risks customers noticing the taste is off.
IFF.grows: Food makers launching new healthier products and brands needing fresh flavors, probiotics and scents.
IFF.risk: Big food brands squeezing prices or making flavors themselves, plus heavy debt from past mergers.

ILMN.sells: DNA reading machines and the chemical kits they use, paid for by hospitals, labs and research centers.
ILMN.moat: Labs build their work and software around its machines and keep paying for its kits to run them.
ILMN.grows: More DNA testing for cancer, rare diseases and pregnancy screening as reading DNA gets cheaper.
ILMN.risk: Cheaper rival DNA machines, especially in China, and cuts to government research funding.

IMAX.sells: Giant-screen theater systems and movie remastering, paid for by cinemas and the studios that release films.
IMAX.moat: Moviegoers pay extra for the IMAX name, and big directors shoot with its special cameras.
IMAX.grows: New theaters around the world, more blockbusters filmed for IMAX, and live concerts on its giant screens.
IMAX.risk: A stretch with few big movies, or people choosing to stream at home instead of going to theaters.

IMB.L.sells: Cigarettes like Davidoff, Winston and JPS, rolling tobacco and Blu vapes, paid for by smokers at shops.
IMB.L.moat: Smokers stick with a favorite brand, and ad bans make it very hard for a new brand to get noticed.
IMB.L.grows: Raising prices on fewer smokers, and selling more vapes, heated tobacco and nicotine pouches.
IMB.L.risk: Fewer people smoking, tougher laws and taxes, and rivals winning the new vape and pouch market.

INCY.sells: Jakafi and other medicines for blood cancers and immune diseases, paid for by insurers and hospitals.
INCY.moat: Patents stop others from copying Jakafi for now, and doctors trust it for these rare blood diseases.
INCY.grows: Newer drugs like Niktimvo and Opzelura cream for skin diseases, plus a pipeline of cancer medicines.
INCY.risk: Jakafi's patent running out lets cheaper copies in, and new drugs could fail in testing.

INFY.sells: Tech help like running software, cloud and AI projects, paid for by big banks, stores and factories.
INFY.moat: Once Infosys runs a company's key systems, swapping to a new team is slow, risky and costly.
INFY.grows: Companies wanting help with AI, cloud moves and updating old software, with Infosys's low-cost engineers.
INFY.risk: AI tools doing coding work cheaply, clients cutting tech budgets, and rivals like TCS and Accenture.

INSM.sells: Arikayce, an inhaled drug for a rare lung infection, and brensocatib for bronchiectasis, paid by insurers.
INSM.moat: Patents and hard-won approvals protect its drugs, and few rivals treat these rare lung diseases.
INSM.grows: More patients starting its bronchiectasis pill, plus new lung and gene therapy drugs in testing.
INSM.risk: Drugs failing in testing, slower sales of the new pill than hoped, or insurers refusing to pay.

INSP.sells: A small implant that gently pulses a tongue nerve so sleep apnea patients breathe at night, paid by insurers.
INSP.moat: It is the main approved device of its kind, and surgeons trained on it tend to keep using it.
INSP.grows: More doctors offering it to people who can't stand wearing a CPAP mask at night.
INSP.risk: Weight-loss drugs that ease sleep apnea, a rival implant, or insurers paying less per surgery.

INTC.sells: Core chips for laptops and Xeon chips for servers, paid for by PC makers like Dell and cloud companies.
INTC.moat: Its huge chip factories and decades of software built for its chips are very hard to copy.
INTC.grows: Making chips for other companies in its own factories, and new AI and PC chips.
INTC.risk: AMD, Nvidia and Apple's own chips taking share, and its costly new factories falling behind TSMC.

IONQ.sells: Time on its quantum computers through Amazon, Microsoft and Google clouds, paid by labs and governments.
IONQ.moat: It is still early, and big rivals like IBM and Google are racing to build better quantum machines.
IONQ.grows: Government and research contracts, taking over other quantum firms, and selling whole machines.
IONQ.risk: Quantum computers may take far longer to be useful, and it spends much more cash than it earns.

IONS.sells: RNA medicines like Spinraza, Wainua and Tryngolza for rare diseases, paid for by insurers and hospitals.
IONS.moat: Long know-how in designing RNA drugs plus patents on each medicine make its approach hard to copy.
IONS.grows: New launches like Tryngolza and Dawnzera, and late-stage drugs like olezarsen for wider heart patients.
IONS.risk: A failed late-stage trial or a rival drug that works better could shrink sales of its key medicines.

IP.sells: Cardboard boxes and containerboard, paid for by food, drink, shipping and factory companies that pack goods.
IP.moat: Its huge network of mills and box plants near customers lets it make and deliver boxes cheaply.
IP.grows: More online shopping and shipped food need boxes, plus cutting costs by closing weaker mills.
IP.risk: Boxes are much the same everywhere, so a slowdown in shipping or cheaper rivals can squeeze profits.

IQ.sells: Streaming shows, movies and micro dramas in China, paid for by member subscriptions and advertisers.
IQ.moat: Popular original Chinese dramas help, but fans can easily switch to Tencent Video, Youku or short-video apps.
IQ.grows: Hit original series, short micro dramas, and licensing its shows and characters for games and merchandise.
IQ.risk: Short-video apps like Douyin stealing viewing time and China's content rules limiting what it can show.

IQV.sells: Runs drug trials and sells health sales data and software, paid for by drug, biotech and device makers.
IQV.moat: Its giant store of prescription and patient data took decades to gather and drug makers rely on it daily.
IQV.grows: Drug makers keep testing new medicines and want more data, AI tools and help bringing drugs to market.
IQV.risk: Biotech funding drying up can cut trial spending, and rival trial firms compete hard on price.

IREN.sells: Data centers and rented Nvidia GPU computers for AI companies, plus Bitcoin mining in Australia and Canada.
IREN.moat: Owning land and big power hookups helps it build fast, but many rivals also race to build AI data centers.
IREN.grows: Big AI customers like Microsoft renting more GPU capacity as it fills new data center sites.
IREN.risk: AI spending slowing, chips getting outdated fast, or heavy borrowing to build sites could hurt it.

IRM.sells: Stores and shreds paper records, runs data centers and recycles old IT gear for big companies worldwide.
IRM.moat: Moving millions of stored boxes elsewhere is costly and slow, so most customers simply stay for years.
IRM.grows: Raising storage prices, renting data center space to tech firms, and wiping and reselling old computers.
IRM.risk: Companies going paperless shrinks box storage, and data centers need heavy borrowing to keep building.

IRTC.sells: Zio heart-monitor patches that doctors prescribe to catch irregular heartbeats, paid for by insurers.
IRTC.moat: Its huge library of recorded heartbeats trains its software, and doctors trust the easy, long-wear patch.
IRTC.grows: More doctors switching from bulky monitors to Zio, plus new uses like spotting hidden heart issues earlier.
IRTC.risk: Lower insurance payments for heart monitoring or rivals and smartwatches offering cheaper heart checks.

ISRG.sells: da Vinci surgery robots and Ion lung systems for hospitals, plus the tools they pay for on each operation.
ISRG.moat: Surgeons spend years training on da Vinci and hospitals invest heavily, so switching to rival robots is hard.
ISRG.grows: More kinds of surgery done by robot, the newest da Vinci model, and recurring sales of tools and service.
ISRG.risk: Rival robots from Medtronic and J&J, or hospitals cutting spending, could slow new robot sales.

ITUB.sells: Itaú runs bank accounts, loans, credit cards and insurance for people and businesses across Brazil.
ITUB.moat: As one of Brazil's biggest banks, its huge branch and app network spreads costs over millions of customers.
ITUB.grows: More Brazilians and small firms using its app for loans, cards, investing and insurance keeps sales rising.
ITUB.risk: A weak Brazilian economy or nimble digital banks like Nubank could pull away customers and cause bad loans.

ITW.sells: ITW makes car parts, kitchen dishwashers, welding gear, glues and nails that factories, builders and restaurants buy.
ITW.moat: It builds many small, carefully engineered products that customers rely on and then keep rebuying supplies for.
ITW.grows: Repeat purchases of welding wire, fluids and fasteners plus new designed-in parts keep orders coming.
ITW.risk: A slowdown in car making, construction or factories could shrink orders across many of its businesses.

IVZ.sells: Invesco runs mutual funds and ETFs like the QQQ fund, and charges savers and pension funds a small fee to manage money.
IVZ.moat: Well-known funds such as QQQ attract investors, and big investors rarely move huge sums without good reason.
IVZ.grows: More money flowing into its popular ETFs and rising markets increase the fees it collects.
IVZ.risk: Fee wars with giant cheap-fund firms like Vanguard and BlackRock could squeeze what it can charge.

JACK.sells: Jack in the Box and Del Taco sell burgers, tacos and late-night fast food, mostly through franchise owners.
JACK.moat: Its brands are known in the West, but diners can easily switch to many other cheap fast-food chains.
JACK.grows: Franchise fees, new restaurants, menu deals and drive-thru and delivery orders help sales grow.
JACK.risk: Tough competition, rising food and worker costs and struggling franchise owners could hurt the business.

JBHT.sells: J.B. Hunt moves goods for stores and factories by truck and train containers, plus delivers big items to homes.
JBHT.moat: Its giant fleet of containers and trucks plus close railroad partnerships are very hard for rivals to rebuild.
JBHT.grows: Shippers moving more freight from highways onto cheaper train routes keeps its container business growing.
JBHT.risk: A freight slump or trouble with its railroad partners could leave trucks and containers sitting empty.

JCI.sells: Johnson Controls makes and services heating, cooling, fire alarm and security systems for offices, hospitals and data centers.
JCI.moat: Once its systems are built into a building, owners tend to keep calling it for repairs and upgrades.
JCI.grows: Data centers needing powerful cooling and buildings upgrading to save energy keep demand rising.
JCI.risk: A slowdown in new building projects or strong rivals like Carrier and Trane could take away orders.

JD.sells: JD.com sells phones, appliances, groceries and more online to shoppers in China and delivers with its own trucks.
JD.moat: Its own nationwide warehouses and delivery network get packages to shoppers fast, which is costly to copy.
JD.grows: Selling more everyday goods, renting out its delivery network and adding services keeps sales growing.
JD.risk: Fierce price fights with Alibaba, PDD and Meituan plus weak Chinese spending could squeeze its profits.

JNJ.sells: Johnson & Johnson sells prescription medicines and surgery tools, hip implants and ACUVUE contact lenses to hospitals.
JNJ.moat: Patented medicines and trusted surgical products that doctors are trained on are hard for rivals to replace.
JNJ.grows: New cancer and immune-system drugs plus newer surgery robots and medical devices keep sales growing.
JNJ.risk: Patents running out on top drugs, cheaper copies and big lawsuits could cut into its earnings.

JOBY.sells: Joby builds electric air taxis that take off straight up, and plans to sell rides to travelers and flights to the military.
JOBY.moat: Its early work with air safety regulators and its partner deals could help, but the business is still young.
JOBY.grows: Getting its air taxi approved to carry paying riders and opening routes in cities like Dubai and New York.
JOBY.risk: Approval delays, high building costs, or riders not paying enough could drain cash before rides pay off.

JOE.sells: St. Joe sells home lots to builders and runs hotels, golf clubs, marinas and rentals in the Florida Panhandle.
JOE.moat: It owns a huge block of land near the Gulf beaches that no rival can simply buy or build again.
JOE.grows: More people moving to the Florida Panhandle buy homes, join its clubs, and stay in its hotels.
JOE.risk: A housing slowdown, a big hurricane, or fewer people moving to Florida could shrink lot sales and visits.

JPM.sells: JPMorgan runs Chase bank accounts, credit cards and loans for families, and big deal and trading help for companies.
JPM.moat: Its giant size lets it spend more on apps and safety, and customers trust it with paychecks and company cash.
JPM.grows: More customers using Chase cards and the app, plus fees from helping companies raise money and invest.
JPM.risk: A deep recession where many borrowers can't repay loans, or stricter banking rules, could hurt profits.

KEY.sells: KeyBank offers checking accounts, mortgages and business loans to families and companies, mostly in the Midwest.
KEY.moat: Moving all your bills, paychecks and business payments to a new bank is a hassle, so many customers stay put.
KEY.grows: Lending more to local businesses and earning fees from advising companies and managing people's money.
KEY.risk: Bad loans in a downturn, especially office buildings, or customers moving savings to banks that pay more.

KEYS.sells: Keysight sells testing tools like oscilloscopes and software that phone, chip, car and defense engineers use.
KEYS.moat: Engineers trust its precise tools and train on its software, and the deep measuring know-how is hard to copy.
KEYS.grows: New tech like faster wireless, AI data centers, and electric cars all need fresh testing gear and software.
KEYS.risk: If chip and phone makers cut back on new products, they buy fewer test tools for a while.

KHC.sells: Kraft Heinz makes Heinz ketchup, Kraft Mac & Cheese, Oscar Mayer, Lunchables and Capri Sun for grocery shoppers.
KHC.moat: Shoppers know and reach for its famous names, and stores give these big brands good shelf space.
KHC.grows: Raising prices on loved brands and selling more of them in restaurants and in countries outside America.
KHC.risk: Cheaper store brands and shoppers choosing fresher, healthier food could keep pulling buyers away.

KIM.sells: Kimco owns shopping centers with grocery stores and collects rent from stores, gyms and restaurants in them.
KIM.moat: Its centers sit in busy suburbs where there is little open land left to build new shopping centers nearby.
KIM.grows: Raising rents as leases renew and filling empty spaces with stores people visit every week.
KIM.risk: Store chains closing or more shopping moving online could leave spaces empty and lower its rent income.

KKR.sells: KKR runs investment funds that buy whole companies, buildings and lend money, paid in fees by pensions and the rich.
KKR.moat: Big investors trust its long record and name, so they hand it money again for each new fund.
KKR.grows: Raising bigger funds, selling to more wealthy families, and growing its insurance and lending businesses.
KKR.risk: If its deals do poorly or borrowing gets costly, investors may give less money and fees could shrink.

KLAC.sells: KLA sells machines that spot and measure tiny flaws on computer chips to chipmakers like TSMC and Samsung.
KLAC.moat: Its defect-finding tools take decades of optics and software know-how, and factories build their lines around them.
KLAC.grows: Chips keep getting smaller and more complex for AI and phones, so factories need more checking at every step.
KLAC.risk: A slowdown in chip factory spending or export limits on selling tools to China could shrink orders.

KMB.sells: Kimberly-Clark sells Huggies diapers, Kleenex tissues, Scott paper towels and Kotex pads to shoppers and stores.
KMB.moat: Parents and shoppers trust names like Huggies and Kleenex, and stores give those familiar brands prime shelf space.
KMB.grows: People everywhere keep needing diapers, tissues and toilet paper, plus small price raises and new markets abroad.
KMB.risk: Cheaper store brands from Walmart, Costco and Target could pull shoppers away from the famous names.

KMI.sells: Kinder Morgan charges energy companies fees to move and store natural gas, fuel and chemicals in its pipelines.
KMI.moat: Its huge web of pipelines and terminals is already built, and new pipelines are very hard to get permits for.
KMI.grows: Rising demand for natural gas from power plants, data centers and gas shipped overseas fills its pipes.
KMI.risk: A long-term shift away from oil and gas, or tougher rules on fossil fuels, could slowly reduce what it carries.

KMX.sells: CarMax sells used cars and trucks to drivers, plus car loans, repair plans and buying cars people want to sell.
KMX.moat: Its nationwide stores and pricing data let it buy, fix and sell lots of used cars more smoothly than small lots.
KMX.grows: More people choosing used cars, buying online and trading in cars helps it sell more and lend more.
KMX.risk: Online rivals like Carvana and car loans going bad when buyers can't pay could hurt sales and profits.

KRC.sells: Kilroy rents office and lab buildings on the West Coast to tech, media and life science companies.
KRC.moat: It owns nice modern buildings in good cities, but tenants can move to other landlords when their leases end.
KRC.grows: Filling empty space, finishing new projects and signing tech and science tenants could raise its rent income.
KRC.risk: More people working from home leaves many offices empty, which could keep rents and occupancy weak.

KSPI.sells: Kaspi runs a super-app in Kazakhstan where people shop, pay bills, send money and get loans from shops and users.
KSPI.moat: Almost everyone and nearly every shop in Kazakhstan uses the app, so new users and merchants keep joining.
KSPI.grows: Adding more shopping, travel, grocery and money services, plus expanding into new countries like Turkey.
KSPI.risk: Trouble in the economy or new government rules in Kazakhstan could hurt lending and payments.

KTOS.sells: Kratos sells jet drones, rocket engines, satellite ground software and missile parts to the US military and allies.
KTOS.moat: It has years of experience building cheap, fast drones and defense electronics with secret government approvals.
KTOS.grows: Militaries want more low-cost drones, hypersonic test vehicles and satellite systems as defense budgets focus there.
KTOS.risk: Losing big government contracts, budget cuts or bigger defense companies building similar drones could hurt it.

KYMR.sells: Kymera is testing pills that break down disease-causing proteins, aiming at eczema, asthma, lupus and cancer patients.
KYMR.moat: Its protein-breaking science is patented and partnered with Sanofi, but none of its pills are approved yet.
KYMR.grows: Good results in human trials and new deals with big drug companies could bring in money and future products.
KYMR.risk: If trials fail or show safety problems, the company could have little to sell and need to raise more money.

LCID.sells: Lucid sells pricey electric cars like the Air sedan and Gravity SUV to drivers who buy online or in stores.
LCID.moat: Its motors, batteries and software are well made, but many bigger carmakers also build strong electric cars.
LCID.grows: Sales grow if more people buy the Gravity SUV and if Lucid can launch cheaper models that more families afford.
LCID.risk: It spends far more cash than it earns, so it relies on its big owner and investors to keep it running.

LCII.sells: LCI makes parts like axles, awnings, windows, doors and steps that RV and boat builders put in their vehicles.
LCII.moat: It makes so many parts in huge volumes that RV builders find it easier and cheaper to buy most from one supplier.
LCII.grows: Sales grow when more RVs are built and when owners buy replacement awnings, covers and parts in the aftermarket.
LCII.risk: RV sales drop hard when money is tight or loans get pricey, and few builders buy most of its parts.

LDOS.sells: Leidos sells tech, cyber and defense services to the US government, plus airport scanners and air traffic systems.
LDOS.moat: Government work needs security clearances, trusted track records and approvals that new rivals take years to earn.
LDOS.grows: Sales grow as governments spend more on cyber defense, missile defense, space and upgrading old computer systems.
LDOS.risk: Most money comes from the government, so budget cuts or losing big contracts to rivals could hurt badly.

LEN.sells: Lennar builds and sells new houses to first-time, move-up and retired buyers, and offers mortgages and closing help.
LEN.moat: As one of the biggest builders, it buys land, lumber and labor in bulk, so it can build homes cheaper than small rivals.
LEN.grows: Sales grow when more families need homes and when it opens new neighborhoods in growing towns in the South and West.
LEN.risk: High mortgage rates or a weak economy can stop people from buying homes, forcing price cuts and lower profits.

LH.sells: Labcorp runs blood and medical tests that doctors order, paid by insurers, Medicare and patients, plus drug testing for pharma.
LH.moat: Its huge network of labs and patient centers lets it run tests cheaply and quickly, and insurers already list it.
LH.grows: Sales grow as people get older and need more tests, and as drug makers pay it to test new medicines in studies.
