LH.risk: Government and insurers can cut how much they pay per test, and hospitals or new tech could take some testing.

LI.sells: Li Auto sells big electric and hybrid family SUVs and minivans to car buyers in China through stores and online.
LI.moat: Its roomy family cars are popular, but China has dozens of electric carmakers fighting hard with very similar cars.
LI.grows: Sales grow if Chinese families keep picking its new models and if it can start selling cars in other countries.
LI.risk: Fierce price wars in China's car market and government rule changes could squeeze its sales and profits.

LII.sells: Lennox makes furnaces, air conditioners and heat pumps for homes and stores, sold mostly through local installers.
LII.moat: Homeowners trust the Lennox name, and its own network of dealers and parts stores keeps installers loyal to it.
LII.grows: Sales grow as old units wear out and get replaced, and as new rules push people to switch to efficient heat pumps.
LII.risk: Fewer new homes or weaker spending could slow sales, while big rivals like Carrier and Trane fight for installers.

LIN.sells: Linde sells oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen and other gases to hospitals, chip makers, steel mills and chemical plants.
LIN.moat: It builds gas plants and pipelines right next to big customers on long contracts, which rivals can't easily match.
LIN.grows: Sales grow as factories, chip plants and clean hydrogen projects need more gas, and as it raises prices over time.
LIN.risk: A slowdown in factories and heavy industry could cut how much gas customers use, and big projects can get delayed.

LKQ.sells: Used, recycled and new car parts like bumpers, lights and engines, paid for by repair shops and dealers.
LKQ.moat: Its huge network of salvage yards and warehouses can deliver almost any part to a body shop fast.
LKQ.grows: More older cars on the road need repairs, and insurers like cheaper recycled parts over new ones.
LKQ.risk: Electric and safer self-braking cars could crash less and need fewer of the parts it sells.

LLOY.L.sells: Bank accounts, mortgages, credit cards and car loans for British families and small businesses.
LLOY.L.moat: Millions of Britons keep their everyday accounts at Lloyds and Halifax, giving it cheap money to lend.
LLOY.L.grows: Interest earned on mortgages and loans, plus pensions and insurance from Scottish Widows.
LLOY.L.risk: A UK recession or falling house prices could mean many borrowers fail to repay their loans.

LLY.sells: Medicines like Mounjaro and Zepbound for diabetes and weight loss, paid for by patients, insurers and governments.
LLY.moat: Patents block copies of its drugs, and inventing new medicines takes years of research rivals lack.
LLY.grows: Huge demand for its weight-loss and diabetes shots, plus new cancer and Alzheimer's drugs.
LLY.risk: Patents expire, governments push drug prices down, and rival weight-loss pills could take customers.

LLYVK.sells: Concert promotion, artist management and event tickets, paid for by fans, venues and sponsors.
LLYVK.moat: Artists want the venues and ticket systems fans already use, and venues want the biggest artists.
LLYVK.grows: People keep spending more on live shows, festivals and premium seats than on recorded music.
LLYVK.risk: Government antitrust action against its ticketing business, or a slowdown in concert spending.

LMND.sells: Renters, home, car, pet and life insurance sold through an app to young customers.
LMND.moat: Its app and fast claims are friendly, but big insurers can copy the tech and have far more money.
LMND.grows: Young renters graduating into homeowners and car owners who add more policies in the same app.
LMND.risk: Paying out more in claims than it collects, especially after storms, before it ever earns steady profits.

LNT.sells: Electricity and natural gas for homes, farms and factories in Iowa and Wisconsin.
LNT.moat: It is the approved local power company, so no rival can string competing wires to its customers.
LNT.grows: New factories and data centers needing power, plus approved spending on wind and solar farms.
LNT.risk: Regulators refusing to let it raise rates enough to pay for its big building plans.

LOW.sells: Tools, lumber, paint, appliances and garden supplies for homeowners and contractors.
LOW.moat: Its giant buying power and stores nationwide let it stock more items at lower prices than small shops.
LOW.grows: Older homes needing repairs, more pro contractor customers, and online orders with store pickup.
LOW.risk: High mortgage rates slowing home sales and remodeling, and Home Depot competing for the same shoppers.

LPLA.sells: Gives independent financial advisors trading, tools and paperwork; paid by advisors and their clients.
LPLA.moat: Moving thousands of client accounts to another firm is slow and painful, so advisors tend to stay put.
LPLA.grows: More advisors leave big banks to work for themselves, and LPL takes over advisor teams from other firms.
LPLA.risk: Lower interest rates shrink what it earns on client cash, and rivals like Schwab compete hard for advisors.

LRCX.sells: Makes giant machines that etch and coat chips; paid by chipmakers like Samsung, TSMC, Micron and Intel.
LRCX.moat: Its etch and coating tools take years of know-how, and chip factories rarely swap a proven tool.
LRCX.grows: Chips for AI need more layers, especially stacked memory, and each layer needs more etching and coating.
LRCX.risk: Chipmakers cut factory spending in downturns, and export rules can block sales to China, a big customer.

LSEG.L.sells: Sells market data, FTSE Russell indexes and World-Check screening to banks, and runs the London exchange.
LSEG.L.moat: Banks build their daily work around its data feeds, indexes and clearing, so ripping them out is costly.
LSEG.L.grows: Customers want more data, AI tools and fraud checks, and fund managers pay to track FTSE Russell indexes.
LSEG.L.risk: Bloomberg is a tough data rival, and fewer companies listing in London weakens the exchange.

LSTR.sells: Arranges truck, rail, air and ocean shipping for factories and stores using independent agents and drivers.
LSTR.moat: Its big network of agents and owner-drivers helps, but many brokers offer the same trucks to shippers.
LSTR.grows: More factory output and store restocking means more freight to move, plus trade with Mexico and Canada.
LSTR.risk: Freight slumps cut demand and rates, and digital brokers can win shippers by matching loads more cheaply.

LULU.sells: Sells yoga pants, leggings, tops, shoes and jackets to shoppers through its own stores and website.
LULU.moat: Shoppers pay extra for the lululemon logo and the feel of its fabrics, and they keep coming back for them.
LULU.grows: Opening more stores in China and abroad, plus selling more men's clothing and shoes.
LULU.risk: Cheaper copycats and rivals like Alo and Vuori are pulling shoppers away, dulling the brand.

LUNR.sells: Builds Nova-C moon landers and space data links; paid mostly by NASA and other government space agencies.
LUNR.moat: It has real moon landing experience, but it is early-stage and leans on a few government contracts.
LUNR.grows: NASA and the military want more trips to the moon, plus data networks and rovers for moon bases.
LUNR.risk: A failed landing or a NASA budget cut could hurt badly, and bigger space firms chase the same contracts.

LUV.sells: Flies travelers around the US and nearby beach countries; paid through tickets, bag fees and upgrades.
LUV.moat: Its Rapid Rewards fans are loyal, but rivals fly the same routes and its old cost edge has mostly faded.
LUV.grows: Charging for assigned seats, extra legroom and bags, and adding routes where travelers want to go.
LUV.risk: Fuel costs, Boeing delays on new planes, and price wars with other airlines can wipe out its profits.

LVS.sells: Runs giant casino hotels like The Venetian Macao and Marina Bay Sands; paid by gamblers, guests and shoppers.
LVS.moat: Macao and Singapore allow only a few casino licenses, and its huge resorts would be very hard to rebuild.
LVS.grows: More tourists visiting Macao and Singapore to gamble, shop, stay and attend big conventions.
LVS.risk: China's government can change Macao rules or squeeze travel, and governments must renew its licenses.

LYB.sells: Plastic pellets and chemicals like polyethylene and propylene that factories turn into packaging and car parts.
LYB.moat: Its giant plants and licensed process know-how help, but its main plastics are commodities rivals also make.
LYB.grows: More demand for food packaging, car parts, paints and home goods, plus fees from licensing its plant designs.
LYB.risk: Too many new plastic plants worldwide pushing prices down, and swings in oil and gas costs that squeeze profits.

LYV.sells: Concert tickets through Ticketmaster, live shows and festivals it promotes, and sponsorships sold to brands.
LYV.moat: Big venues use Ticketmaster because fans and artists are there, and artists tour with it because it owns venues.
LYV.grows: Fans spending more on live concerts and festivals, more shows around the world, and more brand sponsorship deals.
LYV.risk: Government antitrust cases could force it to split Ticketmaster from concerts, and angry fans push for new rules.

MA.sells: A payment network that lets shoppers pay with Mastercard cards; banks and stores pay it a small fee per swipe.
MA.moat: Nearly every store takes Mastercard because shoppers carry it, and shoppers carry it because stores take it.
MA.grows: More people paying by card and phone instead of cash, more travel spending abroad, and selling fraud and data tools.
MA.risk: Laws that cap swipe fees, plus new payment systems run by governments or apps that skip card networks.

MAA.sells: Apartments for rent in Sun Belt cities across the Southeast and Southwest; renters pay it monthly rent.
MAA.moat: Owning many buildings in growing cities helps it run them cheaply, but renters can easily move to rival complexes.
MAA.grows: People and jobs moving to warm southern cities, raising rents over time, and building new apartment communities.
MAA.risk: Lots of new apartment buildings opening nearby can force it to cut rents, and higher borrowing costs hurt it.

MAR.sells: Hotel brands like Ritz-Carlton, Westin, Sheraton and Courtyard; hotel owners pay it fees and travelers pay for rooms.
MAR.moat: Travelers trust its famous names and earn Marriott Bonvoy points, so hotel owners pay to wear its brands.
MAR.grows: Opening more hotels around the world under its brands, more people traveling, and fees from its rewards credit cards.
MAR.risk: A downturn or crisis that stops people from traveling, and booking sites like Expedia taking a cut of each stay.

MARA.sells: It runs computers that mine Bitcoin and sells the coins, and is starting to rent computing power for AI apps.
MARA.moat: Mining is a race anyone can join with machines and cheap power, so there is little to stop rivals from copying it.
MARA.grows: Adding more mining machines, finding cheaper electricity, and moving into AI computing for paying customers.
MARA.risk: A drop in the Bitcoin price or rising mining difficulty can wipe out profits, and its AI plans are still unproven.

MAS.sells: Delta and Hansgrohe faucets, Behr paint and Hot Spring spas, sold through Home Depot, plumbers and builders.
MAS.moat: Homeowners and plumbers trust names like Delta and Behr, and its strong spot at Home Depot is hard to win away.
MAS.grows: People fixing up and remodeling older homes, new home building, and new products like smart and filtered faucets.
MAS.risk: Relying heavily on Home Depot for paint sales, plus slow housing markets that make people put off remodels.

MATX.sells: Container shipping to Hawaii, Alaska and Guam, plus fast ocean service from China to California for retailers.
MATX.moat: US law requires ships between US ports be US-built and crewed, and it owns the port terminals islands rely on.
MATX.grows: Steady demand for food and goods on the islands, plus online shoppers wanting fast shipping from China to the US.
MATX.risk: Trade fights and tariffs that shrink its China route, or a change to the shipping law that protects its island routes.

MCK.sells: Ships medicines and medical supplies to pharmacies, hospitals and clinics, who pay for each delivery.
MCK.moat: Its giant warehouse and truck network moves medicine cheaper and faster than a newcomer could.
MCK.grows: More prescriptions, pricey cancer and specialty drugs, and pharmacy tech services keep volumes rising.
MCK.risk: Big pharmacy customers or drugmakers could squeeze its thin fees or ship medicine around it.

MCO.sells: Rates bonds for the companies and governments that borrow, and sells risk data to banks and insurers.
MCO.moat: Rules and investors expect a rating from a few trusted agencies, so new raters struggle to be accepted.
MCO.grows: More borrowing by companies and governments, plus banks paying yearly for its data and software.
MCO.risk: A big ratings mistake or tougher rules could hurt trust, and quiet bond markets mean fewer ratings.

MDLN.sells: Makes and delivers gloves, gowns, surgery kits and wound care to hospitals, clinics and nursing homes.
MDLN.moat: Its huge factory and delivery network lets hospitals get almost everything from one supplier cheaply.
MDLN.grows: More surgeries and older patients need supplies, and hospitals hand it more of their supply chain work.
MDLN.risk: Supplies like gloves are easy to copy, so hospitals could switch to cheaper rivals or squeeze prices.

MDLZ.sells: Makes Oreo, Ritz, Cadbury, Milka and Toblerone snacks sold in stores, paid for by shoppers worldwide.
MDLZ.moat: People reach for favorite names like Oreo and Cadbury, and stores give those famous brands shelf space.
MDLZ.grows: Selling more snacks in growing countries and raising prices on loved brands keeps sales climbing.
MDLZ.risk: Pricier cocoa, cheaper store brands, or people eating fewer sweets could shrink its profits.

MDT.sells: Makes pacemakers, heart valves, spine stimulators, surgical staplers and robots used by hospitals.
MDT.moat: Doctors train on its devices, and patents plus long safety approvals make new rivals slow to catch up.
MDT.grows: Aging patients, new heart treatments like ablation, and surgery robots keep demand rising.
MDT.risk: Rival device makers moving faster or a big product recall could steal doctors and hospital orders.

MELI.sells: Runs a giant Latin American online store and Mercado Pago app, earning fees from sellers and users.
MELI.moat: More shoppers draw more sellers, and its own delivery and payment app make it hard for rivals to match.
MELI.grows: More people shopping and paying online in Brazil and Mexico, plus loans and ads on its platform.
MELI.risk: Rivals like Amazon and Shopee, bad loans, or money troubles in Argentina could hurt its edge.

MET.sells: Sells life, dental and disability insurance and retirement income, mostly through employers' benefit plans.
MET.moat: Big employers like one huge insurer to cover all their workers, and changing benefit plans is a hassle.
MET.grows: More companies offering worker benefits and retirees wanting steady income keep premiums rising.
MET.risk: Falling interest rates, bad investments or rivals cutting prices could squeeze what it earns.

META.sells: Runs Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp for free, earning money from businesses that pay to show ads.
META.moat: Your friends and family are already there, so leaving means losing them, and advertisers follow people.
META.grows: Better AI ad targeting, more Reels video ads, and businesses selling through WhatsApp keep sales growing.
META.risk: Users drifting to TikTok, privacy rules, or huge AI and glasses spending that never pays back.

MFG.sells: Loans, deposits, bond and stock deals, and money advice for big Japanese companies, governments and families.
MFG.moat: It is one of Japan's biggest banks, so giant companies trust it with huge loans few rivals can handle.
MFG.grows: Higher interest rates in Japan let it earn more on loans, plus more deal advice work overseas.
MFG.risk: Bad loans in a slowdown, or interest rates falling back, would squeeze what it earns.

MGM.sells: Casino games, hotel rooms, shows and meals in Las Vegas and Macau, plus online betting through BetMGM.
MGM.moat: Casino licenses are hard to get, especially in Macau, and giant Strip resorts take years to build.
MGM.grows: Conventions, concerts, visitors returning to Macau, a new resort in Japan, and online betting.
MGM.risk: A recession or travel slump empties its hotels, and heavy debt and rent make bad years hurt more.

MKC.sells: Spices, seasonings and sauces like McCormick, Frank's RedHot, French's and Old Bay for shoppers and food makers.
MKC.moat: Shoppers trust its red-cap spices, and food companies build secret recipes around its custom flavors.
MKC.grows: More home cooking, love of hot sauce and global flavors, and making flavors for snack companies.
MKC.risk: Cheaper store-brand spices and rising costs for peppers and other crops could squeeze its edge.

MKTX.sells: An online marketplace where big investment firms and banks trade bonds, paying a fee on each trade.
MKTX.moat: Traders go where other traders already are, so a crowded marketplace keeps pulling in more firms.
MKTX.grows: More bond trading moving from phone calls to screens, new bond types, and selling its price data.
MKTX.risk: Rivals like Tradeweb and banks' own systems are winning share, especially in big bundled trades.

MLM.sells: Crushed stone, sand, gravel, concrete and asphalt sold to builders of roads, buildings and homes.
MLM.moat: Rock is heavy and costly to haul, and new quarries near cities are nearly impossible to get approved.
MLM.grows: Government road and bridge spending, new factories and data centers, and raising prices over time.
MLM.risk: A big slowdown in building and road projects would cut how much stone builders need.

MMM.sells: Post-it Notes, Scotch tape, safety masks, sandpaper and road-sign films for shoppers, factories and builders.
MMM.moat: Decades of science in glues, films and coatings plus famous brands like Post-it are hard to copy.
MMM.grows: New materials for chips, data centers and cars, plus steady demand for safety gear and office supplies.
MMM.risk: Huge lawsuits over 'forever chemicals' and earplugs, plus slow growth, could drain cash for years.

MNDY.sells: Online tools teams use to plan projects, track sales and run help desks, paid for by monthly subscriptions.
MNDY.moat: Once a company builds its daily work on its boards, moving everything to a new tool is a big hassle.
MNDY.grows: Companies adding more users, moving up to its CRM, dev and service tools, and new AI features.
MNDY.risk: Rivals like Asana, Microsoft and new AI tools could make simple work apps cheap and easy to copy.

MNST.sells: Monster, Reign and Bang energy drinks sold through Coca-Cola bottlers to stores, gas stations and shoppers.
MNST.moat: Its edgy brand plus Coca-Cola's huge delivery network keep its cans in nearly every store cooler.
MNST.grows: New flavors, sugar-free Ultra drinks, and selling more in countries where energy drinks are new.
MNST.risk: Hot rivals like Celsius and health worries about caffeine and sugar could pull drinkers away.

MO.sells: Marlboro cigarettes, Copenhagen and Skoal dip, on! nicotine pouches and NJOY vapes, sold through US stores.
MO.moat: Smokers stick with the Marlboro brand they know, and strict ad rules make it hard for new brands to get noticed.
MO.grows: Raising prices each year and selling more smoke-free products like on! pouches and NJOY vapes.
MO.risk: Fewer people smoke every year, and new laws or lawsuits could hurt sales of cigarettes and vapes.

MOH.sells: Health insurance plans for low-income families through Medicaid, Medicare and the state marketplaces.
MOH.moat: Winning state Medicaid contracts takes licenses, local doctor networks and years of experience running them.
MOH.grows: Winning new state contracts and signing up more members in Medicaid, Medicare and marketplace plans.
MOH.risk: States can rebid contracts and the government can cut payments while members' doctor bills keep rising.

MOS.sells: Phosphate and potash fertilizer that farmers, co-ops and farm stores in the US and Brazil use to grow crops.
MOS.moat: It owns big mines that are hard to build, but fertilizer is a commodity so farmers pick whoever is cheapest.
MOS.grows: Farmers needing more fertilizer to feed a growing world, especially in Brazil, plus extras like MicroEssentials.
MOS.risk: Fertilizer prices swing a lot, so a drop in crop prices or cheap rival supply can shrink its profits fast.

MPC.sells: Gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and asphalt made from crude oil, sold to fuel stations like Marathon and ARCO.
MPC.moat: Its refineries and pipelines are very hard to build, but fuel is a commodity sold mostly on price.
MPC.grows: Running its refineries well, earning steady fees from its pipelines, and selling renewable diesel.
MPC.risk: The gap between crude oil cost and fuel prices swings wildly, and electric cars could cut gasoline demand.

MPWR.sells: Tiny power chips that control electricity inside AI servers, laptops, cars and home appliances.
MPWR.moat: Its chips are designed into customers' products early and its power know-how is hard for rivals to match.
MPWR.grows: Booming demand for AI data center servers and more electronics inside cars, each needing power chips.
MPWR.risk: A big AI customer could switch suppliers or rivals could catch up, and chip demand can drop suddenly.

MRK.sells: Medicines like Keytruda for cancer and Gardasil vaccines for people, plus Bravecto pet and livestock medicines.
MRK.moat: Patents block copies of its medicines, and building new drugs takes huge research skill and approvals.
MRK.grows: New drugs like Winrevair, new cancer medicines from partners, and a strong animal health business.
MRK.risk: When the Keytruda patent ends, cheaper copies can take a big chunk of its biggest seller's sales.

MRNA.sells: mRNA vaccines like Spikevax for COVID and mRESVIA for RSV, paid for by governments, pharmacies and insurers.
MRNA.moat: It has deep mRNA know-how, but rivals like Pfizer also make mRNA vaccines and demand has faded.
MRNA.grows: Getting new vaccines approved for flu, combo shots and other viruses, plus mRNA cancer treatments.
MRNA.risk: Fewer people getting COVID shots and new products failing trials could keep sales shrinking.

MRVL.sells: Custom chips and networking chips that move data inside giant data centers run by big cloud companies.
MRVL.moat: Designing custom AI chips and fast data links takes rare skills and years of work with each customer.
MRVL.grows: Cloud companies building more AI data centers that need custom chips and faster optical connections.
MRVL.risk: A few huge cloud customers drive most demand, so losing one or them making chips in-house would hurt.

MS.sells: Deal advice and trading for big companies, plus advisers who manage savings for wealthy families.
MS.moat: Families stay with advisers they trust, and companies want a famous bank leading their biggest deals.
MS.grows: More savers move money into its advice accounts, and deal-making picks up when markets are busy.
MS.risk: A market slump or a big trading mistake could dry up deals and scare off clients.

MSCI.sells: Stock market indexes and risk tools that fund companies pay to use, like the scoreboards many ETFs copy.
MSCI.moat: Huge funds are built to follow its indexes, so switching to a rival index would be costly and confusing.
MSCI.grows: More money flowing into index funds and ETFs means more fees for the indexes those funds follow.
MSCI.risk: Big fund firms building their own cheaper indexes, or fee cuts across the index fund world.

MSFT.sells: Windows, Office, Teams and the Azure cloud to businesses and people, plus Xbox games and LinkedIn.
MSFT.moat: Companies run their whole workday on Office, Teams and Azure, so moving everything elsewhere is a huge pain.
MSFT.grows: Businesses renting more Azure cloud power for AI and paying extra for Copilot helpers in their apps.
MSFT.risk: Spending heavily on AI data centers that customers might not pay enough for, plus strong cloud rivals.

MSI.sells: Two-way radios, emergency networks, cameras and dispatch software for police, firefighters and schools.
MSI.moat: Cities build their whole emergency radio system on its gear, and replacing it is slow, costly and risky.
MSI.grows: Selling yearly software, support and video security services on top of the radio systems already in place.
MSI.risk: Government budget cuts or cheaper phone-based networks replacing dedicated police and fire radios.

MSTR.sells: Mostly it holds a giant pile of bitcoin and sells shares and bonds to investors who want bitcoin exposure.
MSTR.moat: Its small analytics software business has loyal users, but holding bitcoin is something anyone can copy.
MSTR.grows: Raising more money to add bitcoin, so its value mostly rises and falls with the bitcoin price.
MSTR.risk: A deep bitcoin crash could leave it with heavy debts and payments that are hard to cover.

MTB.sells: Checking accounts, home and car loans, and business loans to families and companies mainly in the Northeast.
MTB.moat: Families and local businesses rarely move banks because switching paychecks, bills and loans is a hassle.
MTB.grows: Making more loans to local businesses and earning more on deposits when interest rates are favorable.
MTB.risk: Losses on office building loans or a local economic slump that leaves borrowers unable to repay.

MTCH.sells: Dating apps like Tinder and Hinge, where singles pay for subscriptions and extra features to meet people.
MTCH.moat: People join the apps where the most other singles already are, which makes big apps hard to beat.
MTCH.grows: Hinge winning new users and getting more people to pay for premium features on Tinder.
MTCH.risk: Younger people getting tired of swiping and moving to newer apps or meeting people other ways.

MTD.sells: Precision lab scales, pipettes and testing tools, plus factory and grocery scales, for drug and food makers.
MTD.moat: Labs trust its exact scales for rules-heavy work, and its service teams keep the machines running for years.
MTD.grows: Selling service plans and software with each instrument and helping factories automate their checks.
MTD.risk: Cutbacks in drug and lab spending, or weaker demand from factories in China.

MTZ.sells: MasTec builds and fixes cell towers, fiber lines, power lines, pipelines and solar farms for phone and power companies.
MTZ.moat: Few rivals have enough trained crews and heavy equipment to take on huge projects across many states at once.
MTZ.grows: Power companies, data centers and phone carriers keep needing new lines, fiber and energy projects built.
MTZ.risk: Big projects can lose money if costs run over, and work dries up when customers cut back on spending.

MU.sells: Micron makes memory chips that store data in phones, PCs, cars and the AI servers run by cloud companies.
MU.moat: Only a few companies on earth know how to make advanced memory chips like high-bandwidth memory at scale.
MU.grows: AI data centers need huge amounts of fast memory, and phones and cars keep holding more data.
MU.risk: Memory chips are close to a commodity, so prices crash when Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron overbuild.

NDAQ.sells: Nasdaq runs a stock exchange and sells market data, index licenses and anti-fraud software to banks and firms.
NDAQ.moat: Buyers and sellers trade where everyone else trades, and banks rarely rip out fraud software like Verafin.
NDAQ.grows: More banks buy its anti-crime and risk software, and more funds pay to track Nasdaq-branded indexes.
NDAQ.risk: Rival exchanges and new trading venues could pull away trades, and regulators could cap what it charges.

NEE.sells: NextEra sells electricity to millions of Florida homes through FPL and builds wind, solar and battery farms.
NEE.moat: Florida Power & Light is the approved power company for its area, so homes there cannot pick a rival.
NEE.grows: More people move to Florida, and power-hungry data centers and utilities want new clean energy farms.
NEE.risk: Rising borrowing costs, angry regulators blocking rate hikes, or cuts to clean energy support could hurt it.

NEM.sells: Newmont digs gold, plus some copper and silver, out of mines around the world and sells it to buyers and banks.
NEM.moat: Gold is the same no matter who mines it, so Newmont mostly wins by owning big, long-lasting mines.
NEM.grows: Sales rise when the gold price goes up and when it finds or opens new mines with more metal in them.
NEM.risk: A falling gold price, rising mining costs, or trouble with governments in the countries it mines in.

NET.sells: Cloudflare sells website speed-up, hacker protection and developer tools to businesses of all sizes.
NET.moat: Its giant global network sees so much internet traffic that it spots attacks faster than smaller rivals.
NET.grows: Companies keep adding more Cloudflare products, like Zero Trust security and Workers AI, once they join.
NET.risk: Big cloud giants like Amazon, Microsoft and Google could offer similar tools bundled at lower prices.

NFLX.sells: Netflix sells monthly memberships to stream shows, movies, games and live events, plus ads on cheaper plans.
NFLX.moat: With so many members it can spend more on hit shows than rivals, and spread that cost across the world.
NFLX.grows: Ad-supported plans, live sports and events, price increases and stopping password sharing bring more money.
NFLX.risk: Viewers could cancel if hits dry up or if YouTube, Disney and other streamers win more of their time.

NG.L.sells: National Grid runs the power lines and gas pipes in England, Wales, New York and New England for homes and firms.
NG.L.moat: It holds government licenses to run these networks, and nobody else can build a second set of power lines.
NG.L.grows: Countries need bigger grids to connect wind farms, electric cars and data centers, and regulators allow returns on that.
NG.L.risk: Regulators could cut the returns it is allowed to earn, and huge building plans need lots of borrowed money.

NI.sells: Natural gas for homes and businesses in Ohio, Pennsylvania and nearby states, plus electricity in northern Indiana.
NI.moat: Government lets it be the only pipe and wire company in its towns, and rivals can't lay a second gas network.
NI.grows: Regulators let it earn a set return on new pipes, power plants and upgrades, so building more raises sales.
NI.risk: Regulators could refuse rate increases, or homes could switch from gas heat to electric heat pumps.

NIO.sells: Electric SUVs and sedans sold to drivers in China and Europe, plus battery swaps and charging services.
NIO.moat: Its battery-swap stations are unusual, but many Chinese carmakers sell similar electric cars at low prices.
NIO.grows: New car models, cheaper sub-brands, more swap stations and selling into more countries.
NIO.risk: Brutal price wars with BYD, Tesla and others could keep it losing money and needing fresh cash.

NKE.sells: Sneakers, clothes and sports gear under Nike, Jordan and Converse, sold to shoppers and stores worldwide.
NKE.moat: The swoosh and Jordan name, built by star athletes for decades, make people pay extra for the same shoe.
NKE.grows: New shoe launches, athlete deals, women's and kids' lines, and selling direct through its app and stores.
NKE.risk: Hot rivals like On and Hoka could keep stealing runners if Nike's new designs stop feeling exciting.

NOW.sells: Cloud software big companies and governments use to handle IT help tickets, HR requests and support tasks.
NOW.moat: Once a company runs its daily work on ServiceNow, ripping it out is slow, risky and expensive.
NOW.grows: Selling more apps and AI helpers to existing customers, who keep adding new teams and workflows.
NOW.risk: AI tools from rivals could make building these workflows so easy that customers need ServiceNow less.

NRG.sells: Electricity to homes and businesses through Reliant and Green Mountain, plus Vivint home security.
NRG.moat: Power is the same from any seller, so customers can switch providers easily when prices look better elsewhere.
NRG.grows: Rising power demand from data centers, new gas plants, and bundling home security with electricity.
NRG.risk: Swings in natural gas and power prices, or extreme weather like Texas freezes, can hurt its profits.

NSC.sells: Rail shipping of grain, chemicals, coal, cars and shipping containers for companies across the eastern US.
NSC.moat: Its rail lines and land through the eastern US are nearly impossible for anyone to build again today.
NSC.grows: Moving more containers off trucks and onto trains, and raising shipping prices over time.
NSC.risk: Train accidents like East Palestine, tougher safety rules, or trucks winning freight could hurt it.

NTAP.sells: Data storage machines and ONTAP software that businesses use to store files, plus storage inside big clouds.
NTAP.moat: Companies store years of critical data on NetApp, and moving it all to another system is risky and painful.
NTAP.grows: Fast all-flash storage, built-in deals with Amazon, Microsoft and Google clouds, and storing AI data.
NTAP.risk: Customers could move data straight into cloud storage, or rivals like Pure Storage could win on price.

NTLA.sells: Experimental CRISPR gene-editing medicines for rare diseases, paid for by partners like Regeneron for now.
NTLA.moat: It has deep gene-editing know-how and patents, but no approved medicine yet and strong rivals in CRISPR.
NTLA.grows: Getting its liver disease and swelling-attack treatments approved and then sold to hospitals.
NTLA.risk: A failed trial, a safety problem, or running out of cash before any medicine reaches patients.

NTRA.sells: Blood tests like Panorama for pregnancy and Signatera for cancer, paid by insurers, doctors and patients.
NTRA.moat: Its huge pile of past test results makes its tests sharper, and doctors already order them by habit.
NTRA.grows: More cancer doctors using Signatera to check if cancer is coming back, plus more insurers paying for it.
NTRA.risk: Insurers refusing to pay, patent fights, or rivals making cheaper blood tests that work just as well.

NTRS.sells: Safekeeping and managing money for pension funds, foundations and very rich families, who pay fees.
NTRS.moat: Moving huge piles of money and records to another bank is slow and risky, so big clients rarely leave.
NTRS.grows: Winning new wealthy families and big funds, and earning more when the money it holds grows in value.
NTRS.risk: Fee fights with bigger rivals, low interest rates squeezing earnings, or a costly tech or trust mistake.

NUE.sells: Steel beams, sheets, bars and building parts sold to builders, carmakers and factories in North America.
NUE.moat: It melts recycled scrap in electric furnaces, which is cheaper and more flexible than old-style mills.
NUE.grows: Demand for new buildings, factories, bridges, power lines and solar farms that all need steel.
NUE.risk: Steel is a commodity, so cheap imports or a building slowdown can crush prices quickly.

NUVL.sells: Experimental pills for certain lung cancers that reach the brain; no approved product sold yet.
NUVL.moat: Its drugs are designed to hit cancer targets more precisely, but they still need approval to prove it.
NUVL.grows: Winning approval for its lung cancer pills and having cancer doctors choose them over older drugs.
NUVL.risk: A trial letdown, a regulator saying no, or a big drug company making a better pill first.

NVAX.sells: Vaccines like its COVID shot Nuvaxovid, sold through partners like Sanofi to governments and pharmacies.
NVAX.moat: Its Matrix-M booster ingredient is special know-how, but much bigger vaccine makers dominate the market.
NVAX.grows: Partner payments and royalties from Sanofi, plus using Matrix-M in other companies' vaccines.
NVAX.risk: Falling demand for COVID shots and leaning heavily on partners to sell its vaccine.

NVCR.sells: Optune wearable devices that send gentle electric fields to fight brain and lung tumors, paid by insurers.
NVCR.moat: It invented tumor treating fields and holds patents, so no rival sells the same kind of device.
NVCR.grows: Getting the device approved for more cancers like pancreatic and lung and used by more doctors.
NVCR.risk: Trials that fail, patents expiring, or patients finding the device hard to wear every day.

NVDA.sells: Chips and systems that power AI and gaming, bought by cloud giants like Microsoft and by PC gamers.
NVDA.moat: Developers build AI on its CUDA software, so leaving NVIDIA chips means rewriting lots of code.
NVDA.grows: Companies racing to build AI data centers, plus networking gear, self-driving car chips and gaming cards.
NVDA.risk: Big customers designing their own chips, export limits to China, or an AI spending slowdown.

NVR.sells: Ryan Homes, NVHomes and Heartland Homes houses and townhomes, plus mortgages to the families buying them.
NVR.moat: It rents the right to buy land lots instead of owning piles of land, but other builders can copy that.
NVR.grows: More families needing homes in its East Coast and Midwest towns, plus earning on each buyer's mortgage.
NVR.risk: High mortgage rates or a housing slump could stop buyers from signing up for new homes.

NWG.L.sells: Bank accounts, mortgages, loans and savings for British families and businesses, who pay interest and fees.
NWG.L.moat: Millions of Brits keep their pay and savings there, and moving all your bills to a new bank is a hassle.
NWG.L.grows: Lending more for homes and businesses and earning more on deposits when interest rates sit higher.
NWG.L.risk: A weak British economy could mean borrowers stop paying back loans, while app banks steal young customers.

NWS.sells: The Wall Street Journal, Barron's, HarperCollins books and realestate.com.au, paid for by readers and home sellers.
NWS.moat: Readers trust the Journal for business news, and Australian home sellers list where all the buyers look.
NWS.grows: More paid digital subscribers, business data products like Factiva, and real-estate agents paying for ads.
NWS.risk: Free news online and AI summaries could shrink what people will pay for, and print papers keep fading.

NWSA.sells: The Wall Street Journal, Barron's, HarperCollins books and realestate.com.au, paid for by readers and home sellers.
NWSA.moat: Readers trust the Journal for business news, and Australian home sellers list where all the buyers look.
NWSA.grows: More paid digital subscribers, business data products like Factiva, and real-estate agents paying for ads.
NWSA.risk: Free news online and AI summaries could shrink what people will pay for, and print papers keep fading.

NXPI.sells: Chips that run cars, factory machines and tap-to-pay phones, bought by carmakers like Volkswagen and gadget makers.
NXPI.moat: Once a carmaker designs an NXP chip into a model, swapping it out means costly redesign and safety testing.
NXPI.grows: Cars needing more chips for electric motors, radar and safety, plus more smart devices that connect wirelessly.
NXPI.risk: Car and factory slowdowns cut orders, and chipmakers in China could undercut it on price.

O.sells: It owns stores and buildings and rents them on long leases to tenants like pharmacies, grocers and dollar stores.
O.moat: Its huge size lets it borrow money cheaper than smaller landlords, so it can win more property deals.
O.grows: Buying more buildings in America and Europe and slowly raising the rent tenants pay each year.
O.risk: High interest rates make borrowing costly, and online shopping could hurt the store tenants paying rent.

OCSL.sells: Loans to mid-sized private companies, which pay it interest that it passes to its own shareholders.
OCSL.moat: The Oaktree name helps it find deals, but many other lenders offer the same kind of loans.
OCSL.grows: Making more loans to growing companies and earning more interest when rates stay higher.
OCSL.risk: If the companies it lends to struggle in a downturn, they may not pay back their loans.

ODFL.sells: Trucking for shippers who send pallet-sized loads too small to fill a whole truck, like factories and stores.
ODFL.moat: Its big web of truck terminals took decades to build and it delivers on time with very little damage.
ODFL.grows: Winning shippers who pay extra for reliable service and filling its terminals as the economy picks up.
ODFL.risk: A long slump in factory and store shipping leaves trucks half empty while costs keep running.

OKE.sells: Drillers, utilities and refiners pay it fees to move, process and store natural gas and fuels.
OKE.moat: Giant pipeline networks take years and government permits to build, so rivals can't easily lay new ones.
OKE.grows: More drilling in Texas and the Rockies sends more gas and liquids through its pipes and plants.
OKE.risk: If drilling slows or energy prices crash, less fuel flows through its system and fees shrink.

OKLO.sells: It is designing small nuclear power plants to supply electricity to data centers and other big users.
OKLO.moat: Nothing proven yet; no plant runs, though nuclear permits and fuel recycling know-how are hard to copy.
OKLO.grows: AI data centers hungry for steady, clean power are the customers it hopes to sign as plants get built.
OKLO.risk: Regulators could delay approval, or the first reactors could cost far more and take much longer to build.

OLLI.sells: Shoppers pay low prices for brand-name leftovers like food, toys, home goods and books it scoops up cheaply.
OLLI.moat: Its buyers grab other companies' extra stock at deep discounts, so it can price below normal stores.
OLLI.grows: Opening new stores in new towns and growing its Ollie's Army rewards club brings in more shoppers.
OLLI.risk: If closeout deals dry up or bargain hunters shift online, its treasure-hunt shopping trips lose their pull.

OMC.sells: Big brands pay it to make ads, plan where ads run, run PR and handle social media and marketing data.
OMC.moat: Its huge size gets better ad deals and data, but clients can and do switch agencies, so the edge is modest.
OMC.grows: Brands keep spending on ads across TV, online shops and social apps, and want its data-driven help.
OMC.risk: AI tools and tech giants like Google and Meta let brands make and place ads themselves without an agency.

OMER.sells: It develops medicines like narsoplimab for rare immune problems that can follow stem-cell transplants.
OMER.moat: Drug patents could protect it if a medicine wins approval, but nothing is proven to sell well yet.
OMER.grows: Getting regulators to approve narsoplimab and moving other drugs through trials would bring first real sales.
OMER.risk: A failed trial or a rejection from regulators could leave it with little to sell and running short of cash.

ON.sells: Carmakers, factories and data centers pay for its power chips and image sensors, like the eyes in car cameras.
ON.moat: Once its chips are designed into a car model, carmakers rarely swap them out until the next model.
ON.grows: Electric cars, self-driving safety cameras, factory robots and AI data centers all need more of its chips.
ON.risk: A slowdown in electric car sales or cheaper chips from Chinese rivals could cut its sales and profits.

OPEN.sells: It makes cash offers on homes online, fixes them up, then resells them, earning on the gap plus closing fees.
OPEN.moat: Other real estate firms can make online offers too, and nothing locks sellers in to come back.
OPEN.grows: More people choosing a fast, easy online sale over a slow listing with an agent means more homes to flip.
OPEN.risk: If home prices fall while it holds lots of houses, it can lose money on every one it resells.

ORCL.sells: Oracle Database, Java, cloud servers and Fusion and NetSuite business apps, paid for by companies and governments
ORCL.moat: Big companies run their money, staff and records on Oracle, so moving off it is slow, costly and scary
ORCL.grows: Companies renting Oracle cloud computers to train and run AI, plus moving old software into its cloud
ORCL.risk: Spending heavily on AI data centers that may not pay off if Amazon, Microsoft or Google win those customers

ORLY.sells: Car parts like batteries, brakes, oil and wipers to home fixers and repair shops that need them fast
ORLY.moat: Its huge web of stores and warehouses gets the right part to a mechanic within hours, which rivals struggle to match
ORLY.grows: Cars on the road keep getting older and need more repairs, and it keeps opening stores and winning repair shops
ORLY.risk: Electric cars need fewer parts, and online sellers like Amazon could win more parts orders

OTIS.sells: Elevators, escalators and moving walkways for buildings, plus the repair and upkeep building owners pay for
OTIS.moat: It services a giant base of its own elevators worldwide, and owners rarely switch who keeps them safe and running
OTIS.grows: Steady maintenance fees from elevators already installed, plus upgrading old elevators in aging buildings
OTIS.risk: A slump in new building, especially in China, and cheaper local repair firms taking service work

OXY.sells: Oil, natural gas and gas liquids pumped from its wells, sold to refiners, utilities and chemical makers
OXY.moat: Oil is the same no matter who pumps it, so it has good land in Texas but no lasting edge customers pay extra for
OXY.grows: Drilling more wells on its land and new projects that capture and store carbon dioxide underground
OXY.risk: Oil and gas prices falling, which it cannot control, plus the heavy debt it took on to buy rivals

OZK.sells: Checking, savings and loans for people and businesses, and big loans that pay for building projects
OZK.moat: It is known for skill at big real estate construction loans, but many banks offer the same accounts and loans
OZK.grows: Gathering more deposits from new branches and making more large loans to builders and developers
OZK.risk: Many of its loans are tied to commercial real estate, so a property slump could cause big loan losses

PANW.sells: Firewalls and security software like Prisma and Cortex that companies and governments pay to block hackers
PANW.moat: Once its tools guard a company's whole network and cloud, ripping them out is risky and a lot of work
PANW.grows: More attacks and AI use push companies to buy more of its subscriptions and bundle everything on one platform
PANW.risk: Tough rivals like CrowdStrike, Microsoft and Zscaler, or a big hack that hurts trust in its products

PARA.sells: Small marketing apps like Demio webinars, OpenReel video and Vidello hosting that small businesses rent monthly
PARA.moat: These are small tools in a crowded field, and customers can easily switch to many similar apps
PARA.grows: Buying other small software companies and adding AI features to its video and webinar tools
PARA.risk: It is a small, early company, so running short of cash or losing customers to bigger apps could hurt it

PAYC.sells: Online payroll, hiring, time clock and benefits software that small and mid-sized companies pay for
PAYC.moat: Changing payroll systems risks paying workers wrong, so companies tend to stay once set up
PAYC.grows: Winning new companies and selling more add-on tools to the businesses already using it
PAYC.risk: Rivals like ADP, Paychex and Rippling, and fewer workers to pay if hiring slows in a weak economy

PCAR.sells: Kenworth, Peterbilt and DAF big rig trucks plus spare parts and truck loans for trucking companies and drivers.
PCAR.moat: Drivers prize the Kenworth and Peterbilt names, and a wide dealer network keeps parts and repairs nearby.
PCAR.grows: Every truck on the road needs parts and service for years, and fleets replace old trucks over time.
PCAR.risk: Truck orders drop hard when the economy slows, and electric or self-driving trucks could reshuffle leaders.

PCOR.sells: An online app where builders, contractors, architects and owners plan, track and pay for construction jobs.
PCOR.moat: Once a builder keeps all project files, photos and payments in Procore, moving it all out is a big hassle.
PCOR.grows: More construction firms move off paper and spreadsheets, and current customers add more of its tools.
PCOR.risk: A construction slowdown or cheaper rival software from bigger tech firms could slow new signups.

PDD.sells: Pinduoduo in China and Temu worldwide sell cheap goods online straight from factories to everyday shoppers.
PDD.moat: Linking shoppers directly to factories cuts out middlemen, so its prices stay lower than most rivals match.
PDD.grows: Temu keeps adding shoppers in new countries while Pinduoduo signs up more farmers and factories.
PDD.risk: Trade fights, new taxes on small imports and safety rules could raise costs and shut doors in key countries.

PEG.sells: Electricity and natural gas delivered to New Jersey homes and businesses, plus power from nuclear plants.
PEG.moat: Regulators let it be the only company running the power lines and gas pipes in its service area.
PEG.grows: Rising demand for electricity, including data centers, and approved upgrades to its grid and pipes.
PEG.risk: Regulators could limit the rates it charges, and storms or nuclear plant problems could bring big costs.

PEP.sells: Pepsi, Gatorade, Mountain Dew, Lay's, Doritos and Quaker oats sold to stores and restaurants worldwide.
PEP.moat: Famous brands plus trucks that deliver straight to store shelves make it hard for new snacks to win space.
PEP.grows: Raising prices on loved brands, new flavors and healthier options, and selling more in countries abroad.
PEP.risk: Shoppers cutting back on chips and soda, weight-loss drugs, and cheaper store brands could shrink sales.

PFE.sells: Medicines and vaccines like Eliquis, Prevnar, Paxlovid and cancer drugs, paid for by insurers and governments.
PFE.moat: Patents make it the only seller of a drug for years, and its labs and drug-testing skill are hard to copy.
PFE.grows: New cancer medicines, vaccines and drugs from buying smaller biotech companies replace older products.
PFE.risk: Patents on big sellers run out, letting cheap copycat versions in, plus government limits on drug prices.

PFG.sells: Retirement plans, investment funds and dental, life and disability insurance for employers and their workers.
PFG.moat: Once a company sets up its workers' retirement plan with Principal, changing providers is slow and messy.
PFG.grows: More small and medium businesses offer retirement plans, and savings grow as markets and paychecks rise.
PFG.risk: Falling stock markets shrink its fees, and cheap index funds and rivals keep pushing down what it can charge.

PFGC.sells: Food, kitchen supplies, snacks and drinks delivered to restaurants, schools and convenience stores.
PFGC.moat: A huge network of warehouses and trucks lets it deliver cheaply, which small distributors find hard to match.
PFGC.grows: Signing up more independent restaurants and convenience stores, and buying smaller food distributors.
PFGC.risk: Thin profit on each order means fuel costs, food price swings or less eating out can hurt it quickly.

PG.sells: Everyday home and body goods like Tide, Pampers, Gillette, Crest and Charmin, paid for by shoppers worldwide.
PG.moat: Shoppers trust names like Tide and Pampers, and stores give these famous brands the best shelf space.
PG.grows: New product upgrades, slightly higher prices over time, and more families in growing countries using its goods.
PG.risk: Cheaper store brands that look just as good could pull shoppers away from paying extra for the famous names.

PGR.sells: Car, motorcycle, boat, home and small-truck insurance, paid for by drivers, homeowners and small businesses.
PGR.moat: It is very good at pricing each driver's risk from data, so it can charge fair prices and still make money.
PGR.grows: More drivers switching to it online, higher insurance prices as car repairs cost more, and new home policies.
PGR.risk: Big storms, costly accidents or rivals catching up on pricing skill could make claims cost more than it charges.

PHM.sells: New houses and townhomes under Pulte, Centex and Del Webb, paid for by families and retirees, plus home loans.
PHM.moat: It owns lots of land ready to build on and is known for retiree towns, but other builders can do similar work.
PHM.grows: More people needing homes, retirees moving to Del Webb towns, and building more homes on land it already owns.
PHM.risk: High mortgage rates or a weak economy could stop people from affording new homes, and home sales could drop fast.

PINS.sells: A free app where people save ideas like recipes and home decor, paid for by companies that show ads there.
PINS.moat: Years of pins saved by many users make its idea boards useful, which keeps people coming back to plan and shop.
PINS.grows: More shoppable ads, better ad tools for stores, and earning more from each user outside the United States.
PINS.risk: Users and advertisers could spend more time and money on TikTok, Instagram, Google or Amazon instead.

PKG.sells: Cardboard boxes and office paper, paid for by food, drink and factory companies that need to ship their goods.
PKG.moat: It runs efficient mills that make its own boxboard, but cardboard is a basic product many rivals can also make.
PKG.grows: More goods being shipped in boxes, online shopping, and running its mills well to keep costs low.
PKG.risk: A slowdown in shipping or too many rival mills could push box prices down and squeeze its earnings.

PLD.sells: Huge warehouses rented to companies like Amazon, stores and shippers that need space to store and move goods.
PLD.moat: It owns warehouses on scarce land near big cities and ports, and that land is very hard for rivals to get now.
PLD.grows: Raising rents when old leases end, building new warehouses, and adding solar power and data centers on its land.
PLD.risk: If online shopping slows or too many new warehouses get built, rents could fall and buildings could sit empty.

PLTR.sells: Data and AI software like Gotham, Foundry and AIP, paid for by armies, spy agencies and big companies.
PLTR.moat: Once an army or company runs its daily work on Palantir, ripping it out would be slow, costly and risky.
PLTR.grows: Companies racing to use AI with its AIP software, plus more defense contracts with the US and its allies.
PLTR.risk: Government budgets could shrink, or cheaper AI tools from big tech firms could do the same job well enough.

PM.sells: Marlboro cigarettes plus smoke-free IQOS heated sticks and ZYN nicotine pouches, paid for by adult smokers.
PM.moat: Smokers stick with brands they know, and strict tobacco rules make it very hard for new rivals to start up.
PM.grows: Smokers switching to IQOS and ZYN, which sell well in many countries, plus raising cigarette prices.
PM.risk: Fewer people smoking, tougher health laws or bans on nicotine pouches and flavors could shrink its sales.

PNC.sells: Checking accounts, home and car loans, credit cards and business loans for families, shops and big companies.
PNC.moat: Moving your paychecks, bills and business payments to a new bank is a hassle, so most customers just stay.
PNC.grows: Opening branches in new cities and lending more to businesses and families as they grow.
PNC.risk: Many loans going bad in a recession, or customers moving savings to banks paying better interest.

PNR.sells: Pool pumps and filters, water softeners, ice machines and industrial pumps for homeowners, restaurants and farms.
PNR.moat: Pool pros and plumbers trust brands like Pentair, Everpure and Fleck and keep installing the parts they know.
PNR.grows: More backyard pools needing repairs and upgrades, and people wanting cleaner water at home and work.
PNR.risk: Fewer new pools and home projects when money is tight, plus rivals selling cheaper equipment.

PNW.sells: Electricity for homes and businesses across Arizona, made from nuclear, gas, coal and solar plants.
PNW.moat: The state lets it be the main power company in its area, so no rival can string its own wires there.
PNW.grows: More people, houses and data centers moving to sunny Arizona and using lots of air conditioning.
PNW.risk: State regulators refusing to let it raise prices enough to pay for new plants and power lines.

PODD.sells: Omnipod, a tubeless stick-on insulin pump for people with diabetes, paid for mostly through pharmacies and insurers.
PODD.moat: Its tubeless pod and auto-dosing software are hard to copy, and users who learn it rarely want to switch.
PODD.grows: More people with diabetes, including kids and adults on daily shots, moving to an easy wearable pump.
PODD.risk: New weight-loss and diabetes drugs or rival pumps reducing how many people need its pods.

POOL.sells: Pool chemicals, pumps, filters and building supplies sold to pool builders, repair crews and pool stores.
POOL.moat: It is the biggest pool supply middleman, with warehouses near most customers so pros get parts fast.
POOL.grows: Every existing pool needs chemicals and repairs each year, plus new pools and backyard makeovers.
POOL.risk: A housing slowdown cutting new pools and remodels, or makers selling straight to pool pros.

PPG.sells: Paints and coatings for houses, new cars, airplanes, ships, food cans and road markings.
PPG.moat: Car and plane makers test coatings for years before approving them, so switching suppliers is slow.
PPG.grows: More cars, planes and buildings being made and repainted, plus new coatings that last longer.
PPG.risk: Costly raw materials and weaker factory and car production squeezing what it earns per can.

PPL.sells: Electricity and natural gas for millions of homes and businesses in Pennsylvania, Kentucky and Rhode Island.
PPL.moat: Governments give it the right to be the main power company in its areas, so rivals can't build wires.
PPL.grows: Upgrading power lines and plants, and new factories and data centers needing more electricity.
PPL.risk: Regulators blocking price increases, or storms and costly plant changes eating into profits.

PRCT.sells: AquaBeam and HYDROS robots that use a water jet to treat enlarged prostates, sold to hospitals.
PRCT.moat: Its water-jet robot is patented and doctors train on it, but the company is still young and unproven.
PRCT.grows: More hospitals adding the robot and more men choosing the treatment, which uses a new kit each time.
PRCT.risk: Hospitals cutting spending, insurers paying less, or cheaper prostate treatments winning doctors over.

PRGO.sells: Store-brand cold, allergy and pain medicines plus Mederma and Compeed, paid for by shoppers at drugstores.
PRGO.moat: Big chains lean on its huge factories and medicine approvals to fill their store-brand shelves.
PRGO.grows: Shoppers picking cheaper store brands and new shelf medicines like the Opill birth control pill.
PRGO.risk: Factory quality problems, like its past infant formula troubles, or stores pushing it on price.

PRU.sells: Life insurance, retirement plans and money management sold to families, employers and big investors.
PRU.moat: Its trusted old name and huge size make people feel safe counting on payouts far in the future.
PRU.grows: More people retiring who want steady income, plus fees from managing money through PGIM.
PRU.risk: A big stock or bond crash, or people living longer than planned, could squeeze what it owes.

PSA.sells: Self-storage units rented month to month to families and small businesses that need extra space.
PSA.moat: Its huge network of sites sits in crowded cities where land is scarce and new storage is hard to build.
PSA.grows: Raising rents over time, adding new sites, and people moving, downsizing or running out of room.
PSA.risk: Too many new storage buildings nearby, or a slow housing market, could force lower rents.

PTC.sells: Design software like Creo and Onshape plus Windchill, which factories and engineers pay for each year.
PTC.moat: Engineers' product designs and records live inside its tools, so moving to a rival is slow and risky.
PTC.grows: Customers moving to cloud versions, adding more users, and smarter factories needing connected software.
PTC.risk: Big rivals like Siemens and Dassault, or new AI design tools, could win over its customers.

PTON.sells: Home exercise bikes, treadmills and rowers plus monthly class memberships paid for by fitness fans.
PTON.moat: Fans love its instructors, but rivals and free workout apps can copy connected classes fairly easily.
PTON.grows: Keeping members paying monthly, the cheaper Peloton App, rentals and selling to gyms and hotels.
PTON.risk: Members canceling and fewer people wanting pricey home machines could shrink the business.

PVH.sells: Tommy Hilfiger and Calvin Klein clothes, underwear and jeans sold to shoppers in stores and online.
PVH.moat: People pay extra for famous names like Calvin Klein and Tommy Hilfiger that rivals can't copy.
PVH.grows: Selling more in Europe and Asia, its own stores and websites, and items like underwear and fragrance.
PVH.risk: The brands going out of style or department stores shrinking could cut sales.

PYPL.sells: Online checkout, Venmo and money transfers, mostly paid for by stores taking a small fee on each sale.
PYPL.moat: Millions of shoppers and stores already use it, so each side keeps the other coming back.
PYPL.grows: More online shopping, Venmo turning into a way to pay at stores, and Braintree processing for big sites.
PYPL.risk: Apple Pay, Google, Shopify and card-checkout rivals could pull shoppers away at checkout.

PZZA.sells: Papa Johns pizzas for delivery and carryout, paid for by hungry families and by franchise owners paying fees.
PZZA.moat: People know the Papa Johns name and app, and its own kitchens supply dough and sauce to every store.
PZZA.grows: Opening new stores abroad, more app and online orders, and new menu items like special crust pizzas.
PZZA.risk: Pizza is easy to copy, and Domino's, Pizza Hut and local shops fight hard on price and delivery speed.

QBTS.sells: Quantum computers and Leap cloud access that companies, schools and governments rent to solve scheduling puzzles.
QBTS.moat: It has built special annealing quantum machines for a long time, but the tech is still early and unproven.
QBTS.grows: More companies trying quantum tools for routing, factory schedules and drug research through its cloud service.
QBTS.risk: Normal computers or rivals like IBM and Google may solve the same problems better, and money could run short.

QCOM.sells: Snapdragon chips for phones, cars and gadgets, plus patent licenses that phone makers like Samsung pay for.
QCOM.moat: Almost every phone uses its wireless patents, so makers must pay it even when they use other chips.
QCOM.grows: Putting chips into cars, laptops and smart devices, plus new AI features running right on gadgets.
QCOM.risk: Apple building its own modem chips, Chinese phone makers switching, and fights with regulators over licenses.

QSR.sells: Burger King, Tim Hortons, Popeyes and Firehouse Subs food, mostly run by franchise owners who pay it fees.
QSR.moat: Famous names like the Whopper and Tims coffee bring people back, and owners pay to use those brands.
QSR.grows: Opening more Popeyes and Tim Hortons stores around the world and fixing up older Burger King restaurants.
QSR.risk: Struggling franchise owners and tough rivals like McDonald's and Chick-fil-A could pull customers away.

QUBT.sells: Light-based chips, sensors and early quantum machines sold to companies, labs and government agencies.
QUBT.moat: It works on special lithium niobate chips, but sales are tiny and its products are not proven yet.
QUBT.grows: Hoping more labs and government groups try its photonic chips, sensors and optimization machines.
QUBT.risk: It may never sell enough to pay its bills, and bigger, richer quantum and chip rivals could win instead.

RBC.sells: Precision bearings and gears that airplane makers, the military and factories use to keep parts spinning.
RBC.moat: Its parts are approved for jets and submarines, and switching to an untested part is slow and risky.
RBC.grows: More airplanes being built, repair parts for planes already flying, and defense spending on ships and jets.
RBC.risk: A slowdown in airplane building or factory work, or losing approval on a key aircraft program.

RBLX.sells: A free game world where kids play games made by other players and spend money on Robux for avatar items.
RBLX.moat: Millions of players draw creators, and the creators' games draw more players, so it feeds itself.
RBLX.grows: More older players, more countries, more spending on Robux, and new ads inside popular games.
RBLX.risk: Safety worries about kids online could bring strict rules, lawsuits or parents keeping kids away.

RCKT.sells: Gene therapies in testing for rare heart and blood diseases, aimed at patients, hospitals and insurers.
RCKT.moat: Its gene treatments are hard to make and protected by patents, but none is widely sold yet.
RCKT.grows: Getting a treatment approved by regulators so doctors can start using it for patients with rare diseases.
RCKT.risk: A failed trial, a safety problem, or a regulator saying no could leave it with nothing to sell.

RCL.sells: Cruise vacations on Royal Caribbean, Celebrity and Silversea ships, paid for by families and travelers.
RCL.moat: Huge fleets, private islands like CocoCay and big ship orders spread costs that small rivals cannot match.
RCL.grows: New bigger ships, private beach destinations and more people choosing cruises over land trips.
RCL.risk: A recession, pandemic or fuel spike can empty cabins while the big ship debts still need paying.

RDDT.sells: Ads shown to people in Reddit's interest forums, plus data licenses sold to AI firms like Google.
RDDT.moat: Millions of people keep posting in communities because everyone else is already there answering questions.
RDDT.grows: Google search sends more visitors, advertisers learn to target hobbies, and AI firms pay to use its posts.
RDDT.risk: If Google sends less traffic or users and volunteer moderators leave, the crowd that makes it useful shrinks.

RDW.sells: Star trackers, solar arrays, cameras and drones sold to NASA, the military and satellite builders.
RDW.moat: It has flight-proven gear, but bigger defense firms make similar parts, so there is no clear lock-in yet.
RDW.grows: More satellites, moon missions and military drone spending create new orders for its parts and systems.
RDW.risk: Losing money, government budget delays or a big contract going to a rival could strain the company.

REG.sells: Rents space in suburban shopping centers to grocers like Publix and Kroger, restaurants and shops.
REG.moat: Its centers sit in busy, wealthy neighborhoods where land is scarce and new centers are hard to get approved.
REG.grows: Raising rents as leases renew, filling empty spaces, and building new centers anchored by grocery stores.
REG.risk: Online shopping, struggling tenants or high interest rates could squeeze rents and property values.

REGN.sells: Medicines like Dupixent for eczema and asthma and EYLEA for eye disease, paid for mostly by insurers.
REGN.moat: Patents protect its drugs, and its mouse-based lab system helps it invent new antibody medicines quickly.
REGN.grows: Dupixent being approved for more diseases, plus new drugs in cancer, cholesterol and gene editing.
REGN.risk: Cheaper copycat versions of EYLEA are arriving, and drug price rules or failed trials could cut sales.

REL.L.sells: Elsevier journals, LexisNexis legal search, risk checks and trade shows, paid for by firms and universities.
REL.L.moat: Lawyers, insurers and scientists build their daily work around its unique data, so switching is painful.
REL.L.grows: Adding AI tools to its data, raising subscription prices and selling more risk checks to banks and insurers.
REL.L.risk: Free AI tools or open-access science could make people less willing to pay for its databases.

RELY.sells: An app that lets immigrants send money home to family abroad, earning fees and currency exchange margins.
RELY.moat: Its app is easy and trusted, but rivals like Wise and Western Union offer similar transfers.
RELY.grows: More immigrants switching from cash shops to apps, new sending countries, and extra services like wallets.
RELY.risk: Price wars, stricter immigration or tax rules on money sent abroad could shrink the business.

RF.sells: Checking accounts, mortgages, credit cards and business loans for people and companies across the South.
RF.moat: People rarely move their checking account and auto-pay bills, so deposits stay put and cost little.
RF.grows: Fast-growing Southern states like Florida and Texas bring new families and businesses that need banking.
RF.risk: Bad loans in a recession, especially office real estate, or customers moving cash for higher rates elsewhere.

RGTI.sells: Rigetti builds quantum computer chips and rents time on its quantum machines over the cloud to labs and companies.
RGTI.moat: Its chip-making know-how is rare, but big rivals like IBM and Google build similar machines with deeper pockets.
RGTI.grows: Government labs, universities and defense research buying chips, systems and cloud time as quantum tech matures.
RGTI.risk: Useful quantum computers may take far longer to arrive, and richer rivals could pull ahead first.

RIO.L.sells: Rio Tinto digs up iron ore, aluminium, copper and lithium and sells them to steel mills and factories worldwide.
RIO.L.moat: It owns huge, rich mines plus its own railways and ports in Australia that newcomers cannot easily build.
RIO.L.grows: Demand for steel in growing cities and copper and lithium for electric cars, power grids and batteries.
RIO.L.risk: Metal prices swing with China's economy, so a slowdown there can shrink what it earns from every ton.

RIOT.sells: Riot runs giant computer farms that mine bitcoin and also makes electrical gear for data centers and utilities.
RIOT.moat: Cheap power deals and big sites help, but any miner with machines and electricity can do the same job.
RIOT.grows: More mining machines, higher bitcoin prices, and renting its power-ready sites to data center customers.
RIOT.risk: A fall in the bitcoin price or a rise in electricity costs can wipe out the profit from mining.

RIVN.sells: Rivian makes electric pickup trucks and SUVs for families and electric delivery vans for Amazon.
RIVN.moat: Its adventure-style trucks have loyal fans, but big carmakers and Tesla also sell electric trucks and SUVs.
RIVN.grows: A cheaper new SUV model, more delivery vans for business fleets, and software and charging services.
RIVN.risk: It still loses money on cars, so slow sales or running short on cash could break the business.

RJF.sells: Raymond James gives families investing advice through financial advisors and helps companies raise money.
RJF.moat: People trust their own advisor and rarely move their savings, so clients tend to stay for many years.
RJF.grows: Recruiting more advisors who bring their clients, plus fees that rise as clients' savings grow.
RJF.risk: Falling markets or lower interest rates shrink its fees, and top advisors can leave and take clients.

RKLB.sells: Rocket Lab launches small satellites on its Electron rocket and builds spacecraft parts for governments and firms.
RKLB.moat: Very few companies can reliably launch rockets and build satellites, which takes years of hard-won skill.
RKLB.grows: Its bigger Neutron rocket, satellite-building contracts, and more space missions for defense agencies.
RKLB.risk: A failed launch or delays on the new rocket could hurt trust, and SpaceX competes hard on price.

RKT.sells: Rocket lends home mortgages online, runs the Redfin home search site and the Rocket Money budgeting app.
RKT.moat: Rocket Mortgage is a well-known name with fast online loans, but many banks offer the same mortgages.
RKT.grows: More people buying or refinancing homes, and linking Redfin home shoppers straight to its loans.
RKT.risk: High interest rates slow home buying and refinancing, which can sharply cut how many loans it makes.

RMD.sells: ResMed sells CPAP machines and masks for sleep apnea, paid by patients, insurers and home care suppliers.
RMD.moat: Millions of its connected machines feed doctors data, and patients keep reordering ResMed masks.
RMD.grows: Many people with sleep apnea are still undiagnosed, plus steady mask refills and care software.
RMD.risk: New weight-loss drugs could shrink the number of people with sleep apnea who need a machine.

ROK.sells: Allen-Bradley controllers, motor drives and factory software, bought by carmakers, food makers and warehouses.
ROK.moat: Factories build whole lines around its controllers, so rewiring and retraining workers is costly.
ROK.grows: More factories adding robots and automation, plus software and service contracts on machines already installed.
ROK.risk: Factory spending slumps, or rivals like Siemens and cheaper Asian makers win the new plants.

ROL.sells: Orkin pest, termite and wildlife control for homes, restaurants, hospitals and warehouses that pay for visits.
ROL.moat: Orkin is a famous name, and busy local routes let its techs serve more customers per day than small rivals.
ROL.grows: Buying small local pest companies and signing homes and businesses up for repeat service plans.
ROL.risk: Local pest companies are easy to start, and bad service or termite damage lawsuits could hurt trust.

ROOT.sells: Car and renters insurance sold through its app, website and partners like car sellers and online shops.
ROOT.moat: Many insurers sell car coverage and drivers can switch easily, so a lasting edge is not clear yet.
ROOT.grows: Partner deals that offer Root insurance at checkout, plus pricing based on how carefully people drive.
ROOT.risk: Big accident costs or bad pricing could make claims cost more than the money drivers pay in.

ROP.sells: Niche software for schools, insurers, freight brokers and pharmacies, plus water meters and medical gear.
ROP.moat: Customers run daily work on these tools, so moving data and retraining staff makes switching painful.
ROP.grows: Buying more small software companies and raising subscription prices with loyal customers.
ROP.risk: Overpaying for deals, or AI tools making it easier for new rivals to copy niche software.

ROST.sells: Discount brand-name clothes, shoes and home goods at Ross and dd's, bought by budget-minded families.
ROST.moat: Big buying power and plain, lean stores let it buy leftover brand goods cheap and sell below department stores.
ROST.grows: Opening new stores and drawing deal hunters, especially when family budgets are tight.
ROST.risk: Fewer leftover brand goods to buy, or online discount sellers pulling shoppers away.

RR.L.sells: Jet engines for big airliners, military and submarine engines and mtu generators, bought by airlines and navies.
RR.L.moat: Building jet engines takes decades of know-how, and airlines pay Rolls-Royce for care over each engine's life.
RR.L.grows: More flying means more paid engine service, plus defense orders and backup power for data centers.
RR.L.risk: An engine safety or durability problem could bring costly repairs and make airlines pick rival engines.

RSG.sells: Trash and recycling pickup plus landfills, paid for by households, towns and businesses.
RSG.moat: New landfills are very hard to get approved, so owning them and dense local routes keeps rivals out.
RSG.grows: Steady price raises, buying smaller trash haulers, and more recycling and special waste work.
RSG.risk: Stricter environmental rules or rising fuel and labor costs it cannot pass on to customers.

RTX.sells: Pratt & Whitney engines, Collins plane parts and Raytheon missiles, bought by airlines, Boeing and governments.
RTX.moat: Planes and weapons are certified with its parts for years, and building them takes rare know-how and approvals.
RTX.grows: More air travel needs engine repairs and spare parts, and governments are buying more missile defense.
RTX.risk: Engine defects that ground planes and cost billions in fixes, or cuts to government defense budgets.

RUN.sells: Rooftop solar panels and home batteries, mostly leased to homeowners who pay a monthly bill.
RUN.moat: Long home power contracts keep customers paying, but many installers can sell similar solar panels.
RUN.grows: Homeowners wanting lower power bills and backup batteries that keep the lights on in blackouts.
RUN.risk: Higher borrowing costs or cuts to government solar tax credits could make its deals less attractive.

RVMD.sells: Experimental cancer pills that block a faulty RAS protein; it has no approved product to sell yet.
RVMD.moat: Its drug patents and lab know-how look strong, but nothing is approved, so the edge is still unproven.
RVMD.grows: Sales could start only if trial results win approval for pancreatic, lung and other RAS cancers.
RVMD.risk: A failed trial or a regulator saying no could stop its lead drugs before they ever reach patients.

RYAN.sells: Helps regular insurance agents find coverage for tricky risks; insurers and agents pay it commissions.
RYAN.moat: Agents rely on its specialists and trusted ties to insurers to place risks most brokers cannot handle.
RYAN.grows: More unusual risks like big storms, lawsuits and cyber attacks push business into specialty insurance.
RYAN.risk: If insurance prices fall or insurers handle this work themselves, its fees and commissions could shrink.

SAIA.sells: Trucking that carries part-load freight for businesses whose shipments don't fill a whole truck.
SAIA.moat: Its large network of terminals near cities is slow and costly for new rivals to build or buy.
SAIA.grows: Opening new terminals in new regions lets it carry more freight for more shippers.
SAIA.risk: A slowdown in factories and shopping means less freight, and rivals may cut prices to win loads.

SBAC.sells: Space on cell towers that it rents to phone carriers like Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile for antennas.
SBAC.moat: Towers are hard to permit and build, and carriers sign long leases and rarely move their antennas.
SBAC.grows: More phone data and new network upgrades push carriers to add antennas to towers it already owns.
SBAC.risk: A few big carriers are its main renters, so a merger or carriers cutting spending would hurt it.

SBUX.sells: Coffee, tea and snacks in its cafes, plus bagged coffee and bottled drinks sold in grocery stores.
SBUX.moat: Its famous name and rewards app keep people coming back for the same drink they already love.
SBUX.grows: New stores abroad, mobile ordering, and new drinks and food items that bring in more customers.
SBUX.risk: Cheaper coffee chains and slow, crowded stores could push customers away and weaken the brand's pull.

SCHW.sells: Investing accounts, banking and advice for savers and financial advisers; it earns on cash and fees.
SCHW.moat: Its huge size lets it offer free trading cheaply, and moving accounts elsewhere is a hassle for customers.
SCHW.grows: More savers opening accounts and more advisers bringing their clients' money onto its platform.
SCHW.risk: If interest rates fall or customers move cash out, the money it earns on customer cash drops.

SE.sells: Shopee online shopping, Garena video games like Free Fire, and Monee loans and digital wallets.
SE.moat: More shoppers draw more sellers to Shopee, which draws more shoppers, making it hard to knock off.
SE.grows: More people in Southeast Asia and Latin America shopping, paying and borrowing on their phones.
SE.risk: Rivals like TikTok Shop and Lazada spending heavily to win shoppers, plus bad loans in its lending arm.

SEDG.sells: Boxes that turn rooftop solar power into usable home electricity, plus home batteries, sold to installers.
SEDG.moat: Installers learn its apps and tools, but rival inverter makers sell very similar gear, often cheaper.
