SEDG.grows: More homes and businesses adding solar panels, batteries and car chargers that need its gear.
SEDG.risk: Cheaper inverters from rivals in China and Enphase could keep pushing installers away from its products.

SGI.sells: Tempur-Pedic and Sealy mattresses and pillows, sold to sleepers through Mattress Firm stores and other shops.
SGI.moat: Famous mattress names people trust, plus owning Mattress Firm stores puts its beds right in front of shoppers.
SGI.grows: People replacing old beds, upgrading to fancier adjustable bases, and more stores selling its brands.
SGI.risk: Cheap online bed-in-a-box rivals and shoppers delaying big purchases when money is tight.

SHAK.sells: Burgers, crinkle fries, chicken and frozen custard shakes, paid for by diners at its Shake Shack restaurants.
SHAK.moat: A fun, trendy name that fans seek out, though anyone can open a burger shop nearby.
SHAK.grows: Opening new Shacks in more cities and countries, plus drive-thrus and ordering through its app.
SHAK.risk: Rising food and worker costs, and lots of burger rivals like Five Guys competing for the same diners.

SHEL.L.sells: Oil, natural gas, fuel at Shell gas stations, motor oil and chemicals, bought by drivers, airlines and factories.
SHEL.L.moat: Its giant network of gas fields, ships, refineries and stations is too costly for a newcomer to build.
SHEL.L.grows: Selling more liquefied natural gas to countries that need it, plus fuel, lubricants and EV charging.
SHEL.L.risk: Oil and gas prices swing wildly, and a long-term shift away from fossil fuels could shrink demand.

SHLS.sells: Wiring kits and connector boxes that link solar panels and batteries, bought by companies building solar farms.
SHLS.moat: Its plug-together wiring saves builders labor, but rival wiring suppliers can offer similar setups.
SHLS.grows: More big solar farms and battery sites being built by utilities and power developers.
SHLS.risk: Product quality problems, rivals cutting prices, or fewer solar farms being built would hurt sales.

SHOP.sells: Software to run an online store and take payments, paid for by merchants from tiny shops to big brands.
SHOP.moat: Shops build their whole business on its store, apps and payments, so moving away is a big headache.
SHOP.grows: More merchants selling online, bigger brands joining, and more stores using Shopify Payments.
SHOP.risk: Amazon or other platforms offering merchants a cheaper or easier way to sell online.

SHW.sells: Paint, stains and coatings, bought mainly by professional painters at its own stores and by factories.
SHW.moat: Its huge chain of its own paint stores near every painter makes it fast and handy for pros to buy.
SHW.grows: Painters repainting homes and offices, new buildings, and opening more Sherwin-Williams stores.
SHW.risk: A slowdown in home sales and building could cut how much paint painters need.

SIRI.sells: Satellite radio and the Pandora music app, paid for by listeners' monthly fees and by advertisers.
SIRI.moat: It holds the satellite radio licenses and comes built into most new cars, which rivals can't easily copy.
SIRI.grows: New car buyers trying the free trial and staying, plus exclusive shows and ad sales.
SIRI.risk: Drivers switching to Spotify, Apple Music and podcasts through their phones in the car instead.

SITE.sells: Sprinklers, plants, pavers, fertilizer and outdoor lights, sold to landscaping crews who build and tend yards.
SITE.moat: Hundreds of branches near job sites mean crews get everything in one quick stop, with expert help too.
SITE.grows: Opening and adding more branches, plus new homes, parks and golf courses that need lawns and patios.
SITE.risk: A housing slowdown, or big stores like Home Depot chasing the same pro landscapers, could squeeze sales.

SJM.sells: Folgers and Dunkin' coffee, Jif peanut butter, Uncrustables, Milk-Bone treats and Hostess snacks for grocers.
SJM.moat: Shoppers trust familiar names like Jif and Folgers, and stores give those brands the best shelf spots.
SJM.grows: Uncrustables and Café Bustelo winning new fans, plus raising prices when coffee beans cost more.
SJM.risk: Cheaper store brands, pricey coffee beans and weak Hostess snack sales could eat into profits.

SKHY.sells: Memory chips for servers, phones and PCs, plus special stacked AI memory that goes next to Nvidia chips.
SKHY.moat: Making the stacked high-speed memory AI chips need is very hard, and only a few factories can do it well.
SKHY.grows: AI data centers needing huge amounts of fast memory to train and run chatbots and other AI tools.
SKHY.risk: Memory swings from boom to bust; Samsung or Micron catching up, or too many chips, could crash prices.

SLB.sells: Drilling tools, well data and equipment that oil and gas companies like Saudi Aramco pay to find and pump fuel.
SLB.moat: Its drilling tech, data software and worldwide crews are hard for smaller rivals to match on tough jobs.
SLB.grows: Big offshore and Middle East oil projects, digital software for oil fields, and carbon capture work.
SLB.risk: If oil prices fall, energy companies drill less and cut what they spend on SLB's services.

SMCI.sells: Computer servers, many packed with Nvidia AI chips and liquid cooling, sold to cloud firms and data centers.
SMCI.moat: It ships new server designs fast, but Dell and HPE sell similar machines built on the same chips.
SMCI.grows: Companies racing to build AI data centers that need racks full of powerful, cool-running servers.
SMCI.risk: Thin profits, fierce price fights with Dell and HPE, and past accounting troubles that shook trust.

SMR.sells: Designs for small nuclear power plants, plus licensing help, training and support, for power companies.
SMR.moat: It holds a rare US safety approval for its reactor design, but has not yet built a working power plant.
SMR.grows: Rising demand for clean, steady power from AI data centers and utilities replacing old coal plants.
SMR.risk: Plants may never get built if costs run too high, as happened when an early Utah project was canceled.

SN.L.sells: Knee and hip implants, tools for joint surgery, and advanced wound dressings that hospitals pay for.
SN.L.moat: Surgeons train on its implants and robots and tend to stick with them, and new devices need approval.
SN.L.grows: More older people needing new knees and hips, plus sports injury repairs and care for hard-to-heal wounds.
SN.L.risk: Rivals like Stryker and Zimmer Biomet winning surgeons, and hospitals pushing hard for lower prices.

SNA.sells: Wrenches, tool chests and car diagnostic scanners sold from vans straight to mechanics at their shops.
SNA.moat: Mechanics prize the Snap-on name, and van dealers visit every week and let pros pay for tools over time.
SNA.grows: Cars getting more complex and needing new diagnostic tools, plus repair shops and factories worldwide.
SNA.risk: Cheaper tool brands, or mechanics struggling to pay off tool loans when money gets tight.

SNAP.sells: The Snapchat app is free; brands pay to show ads, and some fans pay for Snapchat+ extras.
SNAP.moat: Friends chat with friends there, so leaving means losing your group, and young users love its camera lenses.
SNAP.grows: More users, better ad tools that help shops sell, and more people paying for Snapchat+.
SNAP.risk: Teens could move to TikTok or Instagram, and advertisers could spend more on bigger rival apps.

SNDK.sells: Flash memory chips, SSDs and memory cards bought by PC and phone makers, data centers and shoppers.
SNDK.moat: Its flash know-how and big factories help, but memory is a commodity sold mostly on price.
SNDK.grows: AI data centers, phones and cars all need more storage to hold photos, videos and data.
SNDK.risk: Memory prices swing wildly when rivals like Samsung and Micron build too many chips.

SNDR.sells: Trucks, trailers and rail containers that move goods for stores and factories, who pay per load.
SNDR.moat: Its big fleet and long shipper relationships help, but many trucking firms offer similar service.
SNDR.grows: More goods shipped, more dedicated fleet deals, and moving freight from highways onto trains.
SNDR.risk: Freight slumps cut prices, and fuel, driver pay and new rivals squeeze what it earns.

SNOW.sells: A cloud place where companies like banks and stores keep and study their data, paying for what they use.
SNOW.moat: Once a company moves its data and daily reports onto Snowflake, moving everything out is hard work.
SNOW.grows: Companies storing more data and running new AI tools on it, which means using Snowflake more.
SNOW.risk: Databricks, Amazon, Microsoft and Google offer similar tools and could win customers on price.

SNPS.sells: Software and ready-made chip parts that chip makers like Nvidia, Apple and Intel pay for to design chips.
SNPS.moat: Chip engineers learn its tools for years, and switching mid-project risks costly chip mistakes.
SNPS.grows: AI chips keep getting more complex, so designers need more design software and ready-made chip parts.
SNPS.risk: Rival Cadence could win key customers, and trade rules could limit sales to China.

SO.sells: Electricity and natural gas for homes and businesses across the Southeast, who pay monthly bills.
SO.moat: Governments let it be the only power company in its areas, in return for overseeing its prices.
SO.grows: New data centers, factories and families moving South all need more electricity.
SO.risk: Regulators could deny price raises, and costly power plant projects could run over budget.

SOFI.sells: Loans, bank accounts, investing and credit cards for members, plus banking software for other firms.
SOFI.moat: Its all-in-one app helps keep members, but many banks and fintech apps offer similar products.
SOFI.grows: Adding members who use more products, and more firms running on its Galileo banking software.
SOFI.risk: Loan losses in a weak economy and tough competition from big banks could hurt profits.

SOLV.sells: Wound care, surgical supplies, dental braces and coding software bought by hospitals and dentists.
SOLV.moat: Doctors and nurses trust its long-known products, like Littmann stethoscopes, and stick with them.
SOLV.grows: More surgeries and dental care as people age, plus new wound care and dental products.
SOLV.risk: Cheaper rival supplies and heavy debt from its split from its old parent company could slow it.

SOUN.sells: Voice AI that carmakers, TV makers and restaurants pay for, like assistants that take drive-thru orders.
SOUN.moat: Once a carmaker builds its voice helper on Houndify switching is work, but giant tech rivals offer the same.
SOUN.grows: More restaurants using voice ordering and more companies using AI agents to answer customer calls.
SOUN.risk: Google, Amazon and OpenAI offer strong voice AI too, and SoundHound still loses money.

SPCE.sells: Rides to the edge of space on its own spaceplanes, paid for by wealthy travelers and research groups.
SPCE.moat: Building safe crewed spaceships is very hard, but it is still early and other companies fly tourists too.
SPCE.grows: Getting its new Delta spaceships flying so it can run many more flights for paying passengers.
SPCE.risk: Delays, accidents or running out of cash before the new ships fly could stop the business.

SPCX.sells: Rocket launches for NASA and businesses, plus Starlink space internet for homes, airlines and the military.
SPCX.moat: Its reusable rockets land and fly again, so it can launch far cheaper than rivals who throw rockets away.
SPCX.grows: More Starlink customers worldwide, bigger Starship rockets, and its Grok AI and X businesses.
SPCX.risk: A big Starship failure, rival satellite networks, or heavy spending on AI could hurt the edge.

SPG.sells: Space in big shopping malls and outlet centers, rented out to stores and restaurants that pay rent.
SPG.moat: Its top malls sit in prime spots that are hard to rebuild, so popular brands want to stay inside them.
SPG.grows: Raising rents at busy malls, adding hotels, homes and restaurants, and filling empty store spots.
SPG.risk: More shoppers ordering online could leave stores empty and weaken demand for mall space.

SPGI.sells: Credit ratings, market data and the S&P stock indexes, paid for by banks, companies and investment funds.
SPGI.moat: Lenders and rules expect an S&P or Moody's rating, and funds pay to track its famous stock indexes.
SPGI.grows: More companies borrowing money that needs a rating, and more funds built to copy its indexes.
SPGI.risk: A big mistake in its ratings, like before the housing crash, or new rules could hurt trust.

SPOT.sells: Music, podcasts and audiobooks streaming, paid by Premium subscribers and advertisers on the free version.
SPOT.moat: Saved playlists and smart picks tuned to each listener make people stay, though rivals have the same songs.
SPOT.grows: More paying subscribers worldwide, price increases, and more podcasts, audiobooks and video.
SPOT.risk: Record labels own the music and take most of the money, and Apple, Amazon and YouTube compete hard.

SRE.sells: Electricity and gas delivered to homes and businesses in California and Texas, paid for on monthly bills.
SRE.moat: Governments let only one utility run the wires and gas pipes in each area, so customers have no rival.
SRE.grows: Texas is growing fast and data centers need power, so it builds more lines that regulators let it earn on.
SRE.risk: Wildfires in California, or regulators cutting the money it may earn, could squeeze profits.

SRPT.sells: Duchenne muscular dystrophy medicines like gene therapy Elevidys, paid for by insurers and governments.
SRPT.moat: Patents and hard-won skill making gene therapy for a rare disease make it slow for rivals to copy.
SRPT.grows: Treating more Duchenne patients and getting new medicines for other rare muscle diseases approved.
SRPT.risk: Safety worries after patient deaths with Elevidys, and regulators limiting who can get it, hurt trust.

SSD.sells: Metal connectors, screws and anchors that hold wood, concrete and steel together, bought by builders and stores.
SSD.moat: Builders and inspectors trust the Strong-Tie name and its tested parts, so they keep asking for it by name.
SSD.grows: New homes, remodeling jobs and stricter building rules for storms and earthquakes keep demand coming.
SSD.risk: A big slowdown in home building or cheaper rival connectors winning over store shelves.

SSE.L.sells: Electricity from wind farms and dams, plus the power lines that carry it to homes and businesses in Britain.
SSE.L.moat: It holds government licenses to run the power lines in its areas, and nobody else can build a second set.
SSE.L.grows: Britain wants more clean power, so SSE builds more wind farms and bigger power lines to carry it.
SSE.L.risk: Regulators could cut what it may charge, or windless weather and costly projects could squeeze it.

STE.sells: Machines, chemicals and services that clean and sterilize surgical tools, sold to hospitals and drug makers.
STE.moat: Hospitals build their cleaning rooms around STERIS machines and keep buying its supplies and repair plans.
STE.grows: More surgeries and more medical products needing sterilization keep the supplies and services flowing.
STE.risk: Safety problems at a sterilizing plant or new health rules could force costly changes or shutdowns.

STEM.sells: Software and battery systems that help solar and storage owners like utilities run their power plants.
STEM.moat: Its PowerTrack software helps, but many rivals offer similar tools and the business is still finding its footing.
STEM.grows: More solar farms and big batteries being built need software to watch and manage them.
STEM.risk: Losing money for long, plus tough rivals, could leave it short of cash to keep going.

STM.sells: Computer chips and sensors for cars, factory machines and phones, bought by carmakers and gadget makers.
STM.moat: It owns chip factories and years of design skill, and carmakers rarely swap a chip once it is in a model.
STM.grows: Electric cars, smarter factories and gadgets with more sensors all need more of its chips.
STM.risk: Car and factory sales slowing down, plus strong chip rivals in Asia, could leave its factories half empty.

STT.sells: Safekeeping, record keeping and funds like SPDR ETFs for big money managers, pension plans and insurers.
STT.moat: Moving huge piles of investments and records to another bank is slow and risky, so clients rarely leave.
STT.grows: As markets rise and more money goes into funds, the assets it looks after and earns fees on grow.
STT.risk: Fee wars with rivals and falling markets could shrink what it earns on the money it guards.

STX.sells: Hard drives and storage gear, bought mostly by cloud companies, computer makers and stores.
STX.moat: Only a couple of companies can make hard drives at this size, which takes huge factories and know-how.
STX.grows: Cloud companies and AI tools store ever more data and need big, cheap drives to hold it.
STX.risk: Cheaper flash memory chips could replace hard drives, and cloud buyers can suddenly stop ordering.

SUPN.sells: Medicines like SUBLOCADE shots and SUBOXONE film that help people recover from opioid addiction.
SUPN.moat: Its medicines are protected by patents and doctors trust them, while new rivals need long approval steps.
SUPN.grows: More patients getting addiction treatment and doctors moving to monthly shots like SUBLOCADE.
SUPN.risk: Cheaper copycat drugs, rival shots, or new drugs failing in trials could shrink its sales.

SW.sells: Cardboard boxes, paperboard and paper packaging that food, drink and shop brands pay for to ship goods.
SW.moat: Owning many paper mills and box plants near customers lets it make boxes cheaply and deliver them fast.
SW.grows: More online shopping, food deliveries and brands swapping plastic for paper keep box demand rising.
SW.risk: Boxes are mostly a commodity, so a slow economy or too many mills can push box prices down.

SWK.sells: DEWALT, CRAFTSMAN and STANLEY tools sold at stores like Lowe's and Home Depot to builders and homeowners.
SWK.moat: Builders trust DEWALT, and once they own its batteries they keep buying tools that fit them.
SWK.grows: Home repairs, new construction and the switch to cordless tools keep pros and DIY fans buying.
SWK.risk: Cheaper rival brands and slow home building could make shoppers pick other tools.

SYF.sells: Store credit cards for shops like Dick's Sporting Goods and CareCredit for doctor bills; users pay interest.
SYF.moat: Its card systems are built into big stores' checkouts and apps, so stores rarely switch lenders.
SYF.grows: Signing new store partners and more people paying for vets, dentists and big buys over time.
SYF.risk: If many shoppers stop paying back loans in a downturn, losses could pile up fast.

SYK.sells: Hip and knee implants, Mako surgery robots and hospital beds that hospitals and surgeons pay for.
SYK.moat: Surgeons train on its Mako robot, and hospitals that bought the robot keep buying its implants.
SYK.grows: More older people needing new joints and more hospitals adding robot-helped surgery.
SYK.risk: Hospitals cutting spending or a rival robot beating Mako could slow its implant sales.

SYY.sells: Food, napkins, pots and cleaning supplies delivered to restaurants, schools, hospitals and hotels.
SYY.moat: Its huge fleet of trucks and warehouses lets it buy cheap and deliver almost anything a kitchen needs.
SYY.grows: More people eating out, plus restaurants buying more items from it in each delivery.
SYY.risk: It earns little per order, so a drop in dining out or food price swings can hurt fast.

T.sells: Phone plans, AT&T Fiber home internet and Cricket prepaid service paid for by families and businesses.
T.moat: Its cell towers, airwaves and fiber cables took decades to build and are very costly to copy.
T.grows: Laying fiber to more homes and selling phone plus home internet bundles to the same families.
T.risk: Price wars with Verizon, T-Mobile and cable companies, plus big debt from building networks.

TAL.sells: After-school classes, online courses and learning gadgets in China that parents pay for.
TAL.moat: Parents know the Xueersi name, but Chinese rules on tutoring can change what it is allowed to sell.
TAL.grows: Selling learning devices and allowed courses to Chinese families who spend a lot on school.
TAL.risk: China's government could tighten tutoring rules again, as it did before, and shrink the business.

TAP.sells: Beers like Coors Light, Miller Lite and Blue Moon sold through stores and bars to adult drinkers.
TAP.moat: Famous beer names and distributor deals give it shelf and tap space that new brands struggle to win.
TAP.grows: Pricier drinks like Peroni, plus hard seltzers, spirits and energy drinks beyond plain beer.
TAP.risk: Fewer young adults drinking beer, and drinkers moving to spirits or alcohol-free options.

TCOM.sells: Trip.com, Ctrip, Qunar and Skyscanner sell hotel stays, flights and train tickets to travelers and businesses.
TCOM.moat: Lots of travelers attract lots of hotels and airlines, and that big choice keeps pulling in more travelers.
TCOM.grows: More people in China and Asia taking trips abroad and booking hotels, flights and tours on their phones.
TCOM.risk: A slowdown in China's economy, government rules, or a travel shutdown could empty hotels and planes.

TDS.sells: TDS sells home internet, fiber, TV and phone service to families and small businesses, and rents tower space.
TDS.moat: In some small towns it owns the only good lines, but bigger cable and wireless rivals can still move in.
TDS.grows: Laying new fiber cables to more homes and renting space on its towers to wireless phone companies.
TDS.risk: Big rivals like cable and wireless giants, plus the heavy cost of building fiber, could squeeze its money.

TDY.sells: Teledyne sells thermal cameras, sensors, test gear and defense electronics to armies, factories and scientists.
TDY.moat: Its special cameras and sensors are hard to build, and militaries trust gear that has already been tested.
TDY.grows: Defense and space spending, factory automation, and buying smaller tech companies that fit its lineup.
TDY.risk: Cuts in government defense budgets or a bad buyout could hurt a big part of its business.

TEAM.sells: Atlassian sells Jira, Confluence, Trello and Loom software that teams pay for monthly to plan and track work.
TEAM.moat: Once a company's projects, notes and workflows live in Jira and Confluence, moving them all out is painful.
TEAM.grows: More companies moving to its cloud versions, adding more users, and new AI helpers like Rovo.
TEAM.risk: Rivals like Microsoft or new AI tools could do the same job cheaper and pull teams away.

TEL.sells: TE Connectivity sells connectors, wires and sensors to carmakers, factories, data centers and plane builders.
TEL.moat: Its parts are designed into cars and machines for years, so swapping them means costly redesign and testing.
TEL.grows: Electric cars that need more wiring, AI data centers that need fast connections, and smart factories.
TEL.risk: A slump in car and factory sales would mean fewer parts ordered across many of its customers.

TER.sells: Teradyne sells machines that test computer chips to chipmakers, plus Universal Robots arms for factories.
TER.moat: Its chip testers are very complex, and chipmakers build their testing programs around its machines.
TER.grows: More powerful AI and phone chips that need more testing, and factories adding helper robots.
TER.risk: Chip spending goes up and down in big swings, and a slump would cut testing machine orders fast.

TFC.sells: Truist offers checking, savings, mortgages and business loans to families and companies in the Southeast.
TFC.moat: Its many branches and customer deposits give it cheap money to lend, and people rarely switch their bank.
TFC.grows: Growing Southern cities, more loans to businesses, and selling wealth management to its customers.
TFC.risk: A recession could make borrowers stop paying loans back, and rate changes can squeeze lending profits.

TGT.sells: Target sells clothes, groceries, toys, beauty and home goods to shoppers in its stores and on Target.com.
TGT.moat: Shoppers like its stylish store brands and friendly stores, which make it feel nicer than other big shops.
TGT.grows: Same-day pickup and delivery, new own-brand products, and design partnerships that bring shoppers back.
TGT.risk: Walmart and Amazon selling cheaper, plus shoppers cutting back on extras, could pull customers away.

THO.sells: Travel trailers, fifth wheels and motorhomes like Airstream and Jayco, sold to families through RV dealers.
THO.moat: As the biggest RV maker it gets parts cheaply and fills dealer lots, but rivals can build similar campers.
THO.grows: More people camping and road-tripping, fresh new models, and its European campervan brands.
THO.risk: RVs are luxury purchases, so costly loans or a weak economy can make families put off new RVs for years.

TJX.sells: Name-brand clothes and home goods at bargain prices in T.J. Maxx, Marshalls and HomeGoods stores for shoppers.
TJX.moat: Its huge sourcing team grabs brands' extra stock cheaply, and treasure-hunt shopping keeps people coming back.
TJX.grows: Opening more stores at home and abroad and drawing shoppers who want famous brands for less.
TJX.risk: If brands make less extra stock or online bargain sites win shoppers, its cheap deals get harder to find.

TLN.sells: Electricity from nuclear, gas and coal power plants, sold to power markets and big users like data centers.
TLN.moat: Building a new nuclear plant takes huge money and many years, so its existing plants are very hard to copy.
TLN.grows: Tech companies need lots of steady power for AI data centers and sign long deals to get it.
TLN.risk: Power prices can drop, rules can change, and an outage or accident at a big plant would hurt badly.

TLRY.sells: Cannabis, craft beers like Shock Top and SweetWater, and hemp foods, sold to stores, pharmacies and patients.
TLRY.moat: It owns many brands, but cannabis and beer are crowded markets where shoppers switch easily.
TLRY.grows: Selling more craft beer and drinks, and entering new countries as medical cannabis becomes legal.
TLRY.risk: Cannabis prices keep falling, laws can change, and beer sales are shrinking in many places.

TMDX.sells: The Organ Care System, a box that keeps donor hearts, lungs and livers alive, paid for by transplant hospitals.
TMDX.moat: Its special machines, approvals and own planes for flying organs took decades to build and are hard to copy.
TMDX.grows: More hospitals using it so more donated organs can be saved and transplanted instead of thrown away.
TMDX.risk: A rival organ machine, a safety problem, or fewer hospitals using its flying service could slow it down.

TME.sells: QQ Music, Kugou and Kuwo music apps plus WeSing karaoke, paid for by Chinese subscribers and advertisers.
TME.moat: It ties into Tencent's WeChat and holds huge song libraries, so fans and artists stay where everyone else is.
TME.grows: Getting more listeners to pay for subscriptions and premium extras like special artist content.
TME.risk: Strict Chinese government rules, and short-video apps like Douyin pulling music fans' time away.

TMO.sells: Lab machines, test kits and supplies, used by drug makers, hospitals, universities and science labs.
TMO.moat: Labs build their work around its tools and keep reordering its supplies, so switching is a big hassle.
TMO.grows: New medicines and vaccines need more research and testing, which uses more of its tools and supplies.
TMO.risk: Drug makers or governments cutting research budgets, which means fewer orders for its products.

TMUS.sells: Phone, data and home internet plans under T-Mobile, Metro and Mint Mobile, paid for by customers monthly.
TMUS.moat: Its government airwave licenses and huge tower network are scarce, so few new rivals can build a network.
TMUS.grows: Adding phone customers and selling home internet over its wireless network to people tired of cable.
TMUS.risk: Fierce price fights with Verizon, AT&T and cable companies selling cheap phone plans.

TOL.sells: Toll Brothers builds and sells fancy houses and condos to families with lots of money to spend.
TOL.moat: Its luxury name and owned land, design and mortgage teams make buyers trust it over smaller local builders.
TOL.grows: Opening new neighborhoods, selling upgrades like nicer kitchens, and renting out apartments it builds.
TOL.risk: When loans get pricey or people feel poorer, wealthy buyers can stop buying new homes fast.

TOST.sells: Toast sells cash registers, ordering apps, payroll and card payment tools that restaurants pay for.
TOST.moat: Once a restaurant runs orders, staff and payments on Toast, ripping it all out mid-service is painful.
TOST.grows: Signing up more restaurants and selling each one extra tools like payroll, online ordering and AI help.
TOST.risk: Rivals like Square and Clover can undercut prices, and many small restaurants close in hard times.

TPR.sells: Tapestry sells Coach and Kate Spade handbags, wallets, shoes and accessories to shoppers worldwide.
TPR.moat: Shoppers pay more for a Coach or Kate Spade bag because they know and like the name.
TPR.grows: Winning younger shoppers with trendy Coach bags, selling online, and growing in China and Asia.
TPR.risk: Fashion tastes change fast, and a brand that stops feeling cool can lose shoppers quickly.

TREX.sells: Trex makes decking and railings from recycled plastic and wood that homeowners and builders buy.
TREX.moat: Trex is the best-known name in fake-wood decks, and stores and contractors already stock and trust it.
TREX.grows: More people swapping wood decks for low-care boards, plus railings, lighting and other add-ons.
TREX.risk: Rival composite brands can copy the product, and people delay deck projects when money is tight.

TRMB.sells: Trimble sells GPS gear, machine guidance and software to construction crews, surveyors and truck fleets.
TRMB.moat: Builders and fleets build their whole workflow around Trimble tools, so changing means retraining everyone.
TRMB.grows: Moving customers to monthly software plans and linking design, job site and trucking tools together.
TRMB.risk: Big software rivals like Autodesk could win the job site, and a construction slowdown hurts demand.

TROW.sells: T. Rowe Price runs mutual funds and retirement plans and earns fees from savers and companies.
TROW.moat: A long record of careful investing and sticky retirement accounts keep many savers from moving money.
TROW.grows: Rising markets lift the money it manages, plus selling new products like ETFs and private investments.
TROW.risk: Savers keep moving to cheap index funds from Vanguard and BlackRock, squeezing its fees.

TRU.sells: TransUnion keeps credit reports and scores that banks, landlords and shoppers pay to check.
TRU.moat: Its giant file on how people pay bills took decades to build, and only a few rivals have one like it.
TRU.grows: Selling fraud checks, identity tools and data to more industries and growing credit bureaus abroad.
TRU.risk: A big data breach or new government rules on credit data could hurt trust and profits.

TSCO.sells: Tractor Supply sells animal feed, pet food, fencing, tools and work clothes to rural families and farmers.
TSCO.moat: Its many stores in small towns carry heavy feed and farm gear that online sellers struggle to ship cheap.
TSCO.grows: Opening more stores, selling pet food and its own store brands, and loyalty perks that bring folks back.
TSCO.risk: Amazon, Walmart and Chewy chasing pet and farm shoppers, plus rural families cutting back when money is short.

TSCO.L.sells: Groceries in big stores, corner shops and online, plus phone plans and insurance, paid for by everyday shoppers.
TSCO.L.moat: Being the biggest UK grocer lets Tesco get lower prices from suppliers, and its Clubcard keeps shoppers coming back.
TSCO.L.grows: More online orders, more convenience stores, and selling food to other shops through its wholesale arm.
TSCO.L.risk: Discount chains like Aldi and Lidl can undercut its prices and pull shoppers away.

TSLA.sells: Electric cars, home and grid batteries like Powerwall and Megapack, and solar panels for families and utilities.
TSLA.moat: Huge factories and its own Supercharger network help it build cars cheaply and keep drivers in its system.
TSLA.grows: More big batteries for power companies, software upgrades in its cars, and self-driving work if it succeeds.
TSLA.risk: Cheaper electric cars from rivals like BYD could win buyers away and squeeze what Tesla earns per car.

TSM.sells: It builds the most advanced computer chips for companies like Apple and Nvidia that design but do not make them.
TSM.moat: Making the tiniest chips takes decades of skill and giant factories that almost no rival can match.
TSM.grows: Demand for chips that power AI data centers, smartphones, and cars keeps its factories busy.
TSM.risk: Tension between China and Taiwan could disrupt its factories, which sit mostly in one place.

TT.sells: Heating, cooling, and refrigeration systems for offices, data centers, homes, trucks, and trains under Trane and Thermo King.
TT.moat: Once its big chillers and controls are built into a building, owners keep paying Trane for service and parts.
TT.grows: New data centers that need heavy cooling, plus rules pushing buildings to use less energy.
TT.risk: A slowdown in new building and data center construction could shrink orders for its big systems.

TTC.sells: Lawn mowers, snow throwers, sprinklers, and digging machines for golf courses, landscapers, cities, and homeowners.
TTC.moat: Golf courses and pro landscapers trust the Toro name and its dealer network for tough, long-lasting gear.
TTC.grows: Golf course upkeep, underground utility work with its drilling machines, and replacing worn-out equipment.
TTC.risk: When homeowners and contractors tighten budgets, they put off getting new mowers and machines.

TTWO.sells: Video games like Grand Theft Auto, Red Dead Redemption, and NBA basketball games, plus mobile games like Words With Friends.
TTWO.moat: Hit game worlds like Grand Theft Auto take years and huge teams to make, and fans wait eagerly for each one.
TTWO.grows: New releases in its big series, plus in-game purchases that players keep paying for after launch.
TTWO.risk: Delays or a flop on a major game could hurt badly, since a few hit series bring in much of the money.

TXN.sells: Simple chips that manage power and read sensors, used by makers of cars, factory machines, and gadgets.
TXN.moat: It owns its own large chip factories, making basic chips cheaper, and engineers design its parts in for years.
TXN.grows: More electronics in cars and factory equipment, each needing many of its small chips.
TXN.risk: Chinese chipmakers making similar basic chips cheaply could take customers and pressure its prices.

TXRH.sells: Steak dinners, ribs, and fresh rolls at Texas Roadhouse and its sports bar Bubba's, paid for by families eating out.
TXRH.moat: Diners love its good food at fair prices and lively feel, so its restaurants stay packed when others are quiet.
TXRH.grows: Opening new restaurants in new towns and keeping more guests coming through the door.
TXRH.risk: Rising beef prices and worker pay could squeeze its profits if it keeps menu prices low to stay popular.

TYL.sells: Software that cities, counties, courts and schools pay for to run taxes, payroll, courts and police records.
TYL.moat: Swapping out a county's court or tax system is risky, slow and costly, so governments rarely leave.
TYL.grows: Moving governments to cloud subscriptions and handling online payments for permits, fees and parks.
TYL.risk: Tight government budgets or a big failed rollout that hurts its name with public buyers.

U.sells: Tools game makers use to build games, plus ads that help them find players and earn money.
U.moat: Studios and students learn Unity and build whole games on it, so switching engines means redoing work.
U.grows: More mobile games, ad tools for app makers, and use outside games in cars, films and factories.
U.risk: Rivals like Unreal and free Godot, plus angry developers after past pricing changes, could pull users away.

UAL.sells: Plane tickets for travelers and businesses, plus cargo flights and MileagePlus miles sold to card banks.
UAL.moat: Scarce gates at busy hubs like Newark and Chicago, plus MileagePlus miles, keep flyers coming back.
UAL.grows: More people flying overseas, pricier premium seats, and banks paying for miles on United credit cards.
UAL.risk: Fuel costs, recessions and price wars hit every airline hard, and flyers can easily compare seat prices.

UAN.sells: Nitrogen fertilizer like ammonia and UAN that farmers and factories pay for.
UAN.moat: Fertilizer is a commodity; it helps that its plants sit near Corn Belt farms, cutting shipping costs.
UAN.grows: Farmers planting more corn and higher fertilizer prices when world supply is tight.
UAN.risk: Fertilizer and natural gas prices swing wildly, so a price slump can shrink profits quickly.

UBER.sells: Rides and food or grocery delivery that riders pay for, with drivers, restaurants and shippers on the app.
UBER.moat: More riders draw more drivers, which means shorter waits, which draws even more riders.
UBER.grows: Uber Eats grocery orders, Uber One memberships, ads in the app, and new cities and trip types.
UBER.risk: Robotaxi rivals like Waymo or Tesla, or laws that make drivers employees, could squeeze its model.

UDR.sells: Apartment homes in major U.S. cities that renters pay monthly rent to live in.
UDR.moat: Renters can move to rival buildings, though good locations and smart management keep many renewing.
UDR.grows: Raising rents over time, adding fees and services, and building or acquiring new apartment communities.
UDR.risk: Lots of new apartments being built nearby or a weak job market could force rent cuts.

UHS.sells: Hospital care and mental health treatment, paid by insurers, Medicare, Medicaid and patients.
UHS.moat: New hospitals need state permits and huge sums, and UHS runs one of the biggest mental health networks.
UHS.grows: More demand for mental health care, aging patients, and new hospitals and outpatient centers.
UHS.risk: Cuts to Medicaid or insurer payments, nurse shortages, or lawsuits over patient care.

ULTA.sells: Makeup, skincare, hair products and salon services that shoppers pay for in stores and online.
ULTA.moat: Ultimate Rewards keeps shoppers coming back, and it carries drugstore and luxury brands in one place.
ULTA.grows: New stores, more loyalty members, new beauty brands, wellness products and growth outside the U.S.
ULTA.risk: Sephora inside Kohl's, Amazon and brands selling direct could pull its shoppers away.

ULVR.L.sells: Dove soap, Hellmann's mayo, Knorr soup and OMO detergent that families buy at stores around the world.
ULVR.L.moat: Shoppers trust Dove and Vaseline and reach for them by habit, so stores keep them on the best shelves.
ULVR.L.grows: Selling more in fast-growing countries in Asia and Africa and pushing pricier beauty lines like Nutrafol.
ULVR.L.risk: Cheaper store brands and new online beauty brands could pull shoppers away from its famous names.

UNH.sells: Health insurance paid for by employers, families and the government, plus Optum doctors and drug delivery.
UNH.moat: Its huge size lets it bargain hard with hospitals and drug makers, which small rivals can't match.
UNH.grows: More older people joining its Medicare plans and more patients using Optum clinics and pharmacies.
UNH.risk: Government rule changes or rising medical bills could squeeze what it earns from each member.

UNM.sells: Disability, life and dental insurance that employers buy for their workers through Unum and Colonial Life.
UNM.moat: Its long record of handling disability claims helps it price policies well, and employers rarely switch.
UNM.grows: More employers adding extra benefits like dental, vision and cancer coverage to keep workers happy.
UNM.risk: A recession that cuts jobs, or more workers filing disability claims than it expected.

UNP.sells: Train shipping for grain, chemicals, coal, cars and shipping containers, paid for by farms and factories.
UNP.moat: Its tracks across the western US took ages to build, and nobody can easily lay a new rival railroad.
UNP.grows: Moving more goods off trucks onto trains and carrying more freight as factories and farms ship more.
UNP.risk: Trucks winning back freight, less coal to haul, or a slowdown that leaves fewer goods to move.

UPS.sells: Package delivery by brown trucks and planes, paid for by online stores, businesses and people sending gifts.
UPS.moat: Its giant network of planes, hubs and drivers reaches almost every address, which is very costly to copy.
UPS.grows: More online shopping, healthcare deliveries and help for small businesses shipping overseas.
UPS.risk: Amazon delivering its own packages and rising driver costs could shrink its business and profit.

UPST.sells: An AI website that helps banks decide who gets personal and car loans, and banks pay a fee per loan.
UPST.moat: It says its AI spots good borrowers better, but rivals can build similar tools, so the edge is unproven.
UPST.grows: More banks and credit unions using its platform and new products like car loans and home equity lines.
UPST.risk: If borrowers stop paying back loans or lenders stop funding them, its loan volume can dry up fast.

URI.sells: Rents lifts, forklifts, diggers and generators to builders, factories, utilities and cities.
URI.moat: With the biggest fleet and branches everywhere, it can get the right machine to a job fast and buy cheaper.
URI.grows: Big projects like factories, roads and data centers, and more firms choosing to rent rather than buy.
URI.risk: A building slowdown would leave many machines sitting idle while it still owes money on them.

USB.sells: Checking accounts, loans, credit cards and card payment processing for people and businesses across the US.
USB.moat: Moving your paychecks, bills and business payments to a new bank is a hassle, so most customers stay.
USB.grows: Signing up more card-payment merchants, growing wealth management and lending more as the economy grows.
USB.risk: Loans going bad in a recession, or customers moving deposits to higher-paying rivals and apps.

USFD.sells: Trucks fresh, frozen and dry food plus supplies to restaurants, hospitals, hotels, schools and the military.
USFD.moat: Huge warehouses and truck fleets let it deliver almost anything cheaply, and the MOXe ordering app keeps chefs loyal.
USFD.grows: More independent restaurants ordering through it, plus its own store brands and help-your-kitchen services.
USFD.risk: Restaurants cutting back when diners spend less, and rivals like Sysco fighting hard on price.

V.sells: Runs the network that moves money when people tap or swipe Visa cards; banks and stores pay small fees.
V.moat: Almost every store takes Visa and almost every bank issues it, so each side keeps the other side hooked.
V.grows: More shopping moving from cash to cards and phones, plus money transfers through Visa Direct.
V.risk: Governments capping card fees, or new instant-payment systems letting shoppers skip card networks.

VFC.sells: Makes The North Face jackets, Vans sneakers, Timberland boots and JanSport backpacks sold in stores and online.
VFC.moat: Shoppers seek out famous names like The North Face and Vans, which helps it charge more than plain brands.
VFC.grows: Selling more directly to shoppers online and in its own stores, and growing outdoor gear around the world.
VFC.risk: Brands like Vans falling out of style, as fashion tastes change fast and cool can fade.

VKTX.sells: An early-stage drug company testing pills and shots for weight loss and fatty liver; no products on sale yet.
VKTX.moat: Its patents on test drugs only matter if trials succeed, and giant drug makers already sell weight-loss shots.
VKTX.grows: Good trial results could lead to approval or a deal with a big drug company to sell its medicines.
VKTX.risk: A failed trial or bigger rivals like Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly winning the weight-loss market.

VLO.sells: Turns crude oil into gasoline, diesel and jet fuel sold to gas stations, airlines and truckers.
VLO.moat: Its big efficient refineries help, but fuel is a commodity and profits swing with oil and fuel prices.
VLO.grows: Strong demand for diesel and jet fuel, plus cleaner fuels from its Diamond Green Diesel plants.
VLO.risk: Electric cars cutting gasoline demand and wild swings in the gap between oil and fuel prices.

VLTO.sells: Sells Hach water-testing tools, ChemTreat chemicals, Videojet package printers and Pantone color guides.
VLTO.moat: Customers keep rebuying its test kits, inks and parts, and designers everywhere speak in Pantone colors.
VLTO.grows: Stricter water-safety rules and more packaged food and medicine that needs codes printed on it.
VLTO.risk: Cities and factories delaying spending, or cheaper rival printers and water tools winning customers.

VMC.sells: Digs crushed stone, sand and gravel and sells it with asphalt and concrete to road and home builders.
VMC.moat: Rock is heavy to haul, and new quarries near growing cities are very hard to get permits for.
VMC.grows: Government road and bridge spending plus new homes, warehouses and factories in fast-growing states.
VMC.risk: A slowdown in building and road spending, which leaves fewer trucks hauling its stone.

VNOM.sells: Owns land rights in Texas oil fields and collects a slice of what oil companies earn pumping there.
VNOM.moat: Its owned rights under busy oil land are useful, but its income rises and falls with oil prices.
VNOM.grows: More wells drilled on its land, often by its parent Diamondback, and buying more royalty rights.
VNOM.risk: Falling oil and gas prices or drillers slowing down on its land, which shrinks its checks.

VOD.L.sells: Phone and home internet plans for families and companies in Europe and Africa, plus M-Pesa phone money.
VOD.L.moat: Running a phone network needs government airwave licenses and costly towers, so few rivals can start one.
VOD.L.grows: More business internet and connected-device plans, and more people in Africa paying and saving with M-Pesa.
VOD.L.risk: Price wars with rival carriers in Europe could keep squeezing what Vodafone can charge for its plans.

VRSK.sells: Insurance companies pay Verisk for data, policy forms and tools to price policies, model storms and spot fraud.
VRSK.moat: It holds decades of shared claims data from insurers that a newcomer could not rebuild, and its forms are built in.
VRSK.grows: Insurers pay more each year for new tools on storms, fraud and repair estimates as their risks get more complex.
VRSK.risk: Big insurers or AI firms could build their own data tools and stop needing Verisk's shared database.

VRSN.sells: Website owners pay a small yearly fee through sellers like GoDaddy to keep every .com and .net name working.
VRSN.moat: It holds the official government-backed contract to run .com, so no rival is allowed to run that list.
VRSN.grows: More websites and the right to slowly raise the yearly fee per name under its contract keep sales rising.
VRSN.risk: Regulators could cap its fees or hand the .com contract to someone else, or fewer people may want new websites.

VRTX.sells: Medicines like Trikafta for cystic fibrosis and Casgevy for sickle cell, paid for by insurers and hospitals.
VRTX.moat: Its patented cystic fibrosis pills are the main treatment patients have, and years of science are hard to copy.
VRTX.grows: New medicines like Journavx for pain and Casgevy, plus drugs being tested for kidney disease and diabetes.
VRTX.risk: Patents running out, or new drugs failing in testing, could leave it leaning too hard on cystic fibrosis.

VSAT.sells: Satellite internet for airplanes, ships, homes and the military, plus secure radios and gear for the government.
VSAT.moat: Its satellites and military contracts are costly to copy, but cheaper rivals like Starlink are pulling customers.
VSAT.grows: More airlines adding Wi-Fi on planes and more defense spending on secure communications for the military.
VSAT.risk: SpaceX's Starlink offering faster, cheaper internet could keep winning the airlines and homes Viasat serves.

VST.sells: It makes electricity from gas, nuclear, coal and solar plants and sells it to homes, businesses and grids.
VST.moat: Big working nuclear plants take many years and huge sums to build, so a new rival cannot copy them quickly.
VST.grows: Data centers for AI need lots of steady power, so tech firms want long deals for electricity from its plants.
VST.risk: Electricity prices swing with gas prices and weather, and new power rules could cut what its plants earn.

VTR.sells: It owns senior living homes and medical office buildings and collects rent from residents, doctors and labs.
VTR.moat: It owns a huge number of senior homes, giving it data and buying power that small landlords do not have.
VTR.grows: More older people needing help with daily living fills its senior homes and lets it charge more for them.
VTR.risk: Too many new senior homes being built, high staff costs or high borrowing costs could squeeze its earnings.

VZ.sells: Phone plans, home internet like Fios and business networks, paid for by families, companies and the government.
VZ.moat: Building a nationwide phone network costs so much that only a few companies can do it, and people rarely switch.
VZ.grows: Home internet through phone towers and fiber, plus small price bumps and add-ons on its phone plans.
VZ.risk: Price fights with T-Mobile, AT&T and cable companies could force cheaper plans while its debt stays high.

WAB.sells: Wabtec builds locomotives, train brakes and safety gear, and fixes them, for freight railroads and city subways.
WAB.moat: Railroads run its locomotives and brakes for decades, so they keep buying its parts, repairs and upgrades.
WAB.grows: Old locomotives need overhauls and new ones, and cities keep adding and upgrading passenger trains.
WAB.risk: Railroads could cut orders when shipping slows, or rivals could win big locomotive and transit contracts.

WAL.sells: Western Alliance is a bank that lends to and holds deposits for businesses and home lenders in Arizona and California.
WAL.moat: Business customers like its special banking teams, but many banks offer loans and accounts that are very similar.
WAL.grows: More business clients, more mortgage lenders using its credit lines, and more deposits from those clients.
WAL.risk: Loans on offices and buildings could go bad, or big depositors could pull money out quickly in a scare.

WAT.sells: Waters makes lab machines that test what is in medicines, food and water, sold to drug makers and science labs.
WAT.moat: Labs build approved test methods on its machines and keep buying its columns, parts and service for years.
WAT.grows: New medicines need more testing, and every machine in use keeps needing fresh supplies and service.
WAT.risk: Drug companies and labs could cut spending, or rivals could build cheaper machines that labs trust as much.

WBD.sells: Warner Bros. Discovery makes movies and shows and runs HBO Max, CNN and TNT, paid for by viewers and advertisers.
WBD.moat: It owns famous stories like Batman, Harry Potter and HBO shows that nobody else is allowed to use.
WBD.grows: More people signing up for HBO Max around the world, plus hit movies, games and toys from its characters.
WBD.risk: People are dropping cable TV fast, and big streaming rivals like Netflix compete hard for viewers' time.

WCC.sells: Wesco delivers wires, cables, lights and network gear to builders, factories, power companies and data centers.
WCC.moat: Its huge network of warehouses and supplier deals lets it get the right parts to big jobs fast and cheaply.
WCC.grows: New data centers, power grid upgrades and factory automation all need lots of electrical and network parts.
WCC.risk: Construction and factory spending could slow, and makers could start selling straight to big customers.

WDC.sells: Western Digital makes hard drives that store data, sold mostly to cloud companies that run giant data centers.
WDC.moat: Building huge, reliable hard drives is very hard, and only a couple of companies in the world can do it well.
WDC.grows: Cloud companies and AI tools keep saving more photos, videos and data, so they need more and bigger drives.
WDC.risk: Drive orders swing up and down with cloud spending, and cheaper chip-based storage could replace some drives.

WEC.sells: WEC Energy delivers electricity and natural gas to homes and businesses in Wisconsin and nearby states.
WEC.moat: The government lets it be the only power and gas company in its areas, so rivals cannot string new lines.
WEC.grows: New data centers and factories need more power, and the state lets it earn a return on new plants and lines.
WEC.risk: Regulators could refuse price raises, or customers could switch to home solar and use less from the grid.

WELL.sells: Welltower owns senior living homes and rents apartments and care to older adults in the US, UK and Canada.
WELL.moat: It owns a giant set of homes in good neighborhoods and uses its data to pick and run them better than most.
WELL.grows: More people are getting older and need a place with care, while few new senior homes are being built.
WELL.risk: Rents could fall if too many new homes get built, or staff and care costs could rise faster than rents.

WEN.sells: Burgers, chicken sandwiches, fries and Frosty desserts, paid for by hungry diners and its franchise owners.
WEN.moat: People know and crave Wendy's square burgers and Frosty, and owners pay to use that famous name.
WEN.grows: Opening new restaurants abroad, selling more breakfast, and pushing app and delivery orders.
WEN.risk: Rivals like McDonald's and Burger King fight hard on price, and tight-budget diners may eat at home.

WFC.sells: Checking accounts, credit cards, home and car loans, and banking help for families and big companies.
WFC.moat: Its huge branch network and pile of customer deposits let it lend money cheaply across the country.
WFC.grows: Lending more to businesses, growing its investment bank, and helping wealthy clients manage money.
WFC.risk: Past scandals brought tough regulators, and a weak economy means more people fail to repay loans.

WGO.sells: Motorhomes, travel trailers and boats under Winnebago, Grand Design and Chris-Craft, sold through dealers.
WGO.moat: Campers trust well-known names like Winnebago and Grand Design, and dealers want those brands on their lots.
WGO.grows: New models, more families wanting road trips and lake days, and dealers restocking their lots.
WGO.risk: RVs and boats are big luxury purchases, so high loan rates or a slow economy can crush demand fast.

WING.sells: Cooked-to-order chicken wings, tenders and fries in many sauces, mostly ordered online by takeout fans.
WING.moat: Fans love its flavors, and its small takeout-focused shops make franchise owners eager to open more.
WING.grows: Opening many new shops in America and abroad, and growing digital and delivery orders.
WING.risk: Chicken wing costs can jump, and a pricey menu could push diners toward cheaper chicken chains.

WIT.sells: Tech help for big companies, like building software, running cloud systems and handling back-office work.
WIT.moat: Once Wipro runs a company's key systems, swapping it for another firm is slow, costly and risky.
WIT.grows: Companies moving to the cloud and adding AI tools that they need outside experts to set up.
WIT.risk: AI could do much of the coding work it bills for, and bigger rivals like Infosys and TCS win deals.

WKHS.sells: Electric delivery trucks and step vans for package and fleet companies, plus charging and data tools.
WKHS.moat: It is a small, early-stage maker with no clear edge over the bigger truck companies it competes with.
WKHS.grows: Winning more fleet orders as delivery companies switch from gas trucks to electric ones.
WKHS.risk: It has struggled to sell many trucks and may run short of cash before it can grow.

WLK.sells: Plastics and chemicals like PVC, plus siding, pipes and roof tiles bought by builders and factories.
WLK.moat: Its owns big chemical plants, but most of what it makes is a commodity that rivals sell too.
WLK.grows: More home building and pipe projects that use its PVC siding, pipes and other building products.
WLK.risk: Prices for plastics swing wildly, and a slowdown in home building cuts demand for its products.

WM.sells: Trash and recycling pickup for homes, businesses and cities, plus landfills that turn gas into energy.
WM.moat: It owns landfills and trash routes that are nearly impossible to copy because towns rarely allow new dumps.
WM.grows: Raising prices each year, adding medical waste services, and selling more landfill gas as energy.
WM.risk: Stricter rules on landfills or a drop in recycled material prices could squeeze its profits.

WMG.sells: Songs by stars on labels like Atlantic and Parlophone, paid for by Spotify, Apple Music, TikTok and stores.
WMG.moat: It owns a huge library of famous songs that nobody else can sell, and old hits keep earning money.
WMG.grows: More people paying for streaming apps, plus songs licensed to movies, games, ads and social videos.
WMG.risk: Artists releasing music on their own, AI-made songs, or streaming apps paying less per play.

WMT.sells: Groceries, household goods, medicine and electronics at Walmart, Sam's Club and walmart.com to families.
WMT.moat: It is so big that suppliers give it low prices, so its shelves stay cheaper than most rivals.
WMT.grows: Online orders with fast delivery, ads on its website, Sam's Club memberships and stores in India via Flipkart.
WMT.risk: Amazon and discount rivals winning shoppers online, or rising wages and costs squeezing its thin profits.

WOLF.sells: Silicon carbide wafers and power chips that carmakers, chargers and power-grid builders put in their machines.
WOLF.moat: Making silicon carbide is hard, but Chinese makers now sell similar wafers cheaply, so its lead has shrunk.
WOLF.grows: Electric cars, fast chargers, AI data centers and solar systems that need chips that handle high power well.
WOLF.risk: Heavy debt and losses after costly new factories, plus cheaper rivals and slower electric car sales.

WST.sells: Rubber stoppers, seals, syringe parts and injectors that drug companies use to hold and deliver their medicines.
WST.moat: Once a drug is approved with its stopper, changing parts needs fresh safety approval, so drugmakers stay.
WST.grows: More injectable medicines, like weight-loss and biologic drugs, each needing clean, safe packaging parts.
WST.risk: Drug companies cutting orders after stocking up, or a quality problem that hurts trust in its parts.

WTB.L.sells: Hotel rooms at Premier Inn and meals at Beefeater and Brewers Fayre for travelers and families in the UK.
WTB.L.moat: Premier Inn is the best-known budget hotel name in the UK, and it owns many of its buildings and beds.
WTB.L.grows: Opening more Premier Inn hotels, especially in Germany, and filling rooms with business and holiday guests.
WTB.L.risk: A weak UK economy, rising wages and energy bills, or struggling to win guests in Germany.

WULF.sells: Computer centers that mine bitcoin and rent power and space to AI companies that run big computer jobs.
WULF.moat: It has cheap, clean power sites, but many rivals can build similar mining and data centers.
WULF.grows: Signing more AI and cloud customers who rent its data center space for long periods.
WULF.risk: Bitcoin prices falling, power costs rising, or AI customers leaving or not paying as planned.

WY.sells: Trees and wood like lumber and plywood, sold to home builders, sawmills and lumber stores.
WY.moat: It owns giant forests that took generations to grow, and nobody can quickly plant a rival forest.
WY.grows: More new homes being built, plus selling land, carbon credits and space for solar and wind farms.
WY.risk: A slowdown in home building, wildfires, storms or pests damaging its forests and wood prices falling.

WYNN.sells: Luxury hotel rooms, casino games, shows and restaurants for wealthy guests in Las Vegas, Macau and Boston.
WYNN.moat: Governments hand out very few casino licenses, so new rivals can't simply open a casino next door.
WYNN.grows: More visitors to Macau and Las Vegas, plus a new resort it is building in the United Arab Emirates.
WYNN.risk: China tightening rules on Macau gambling, losing a license, or travel slowing during a recession.

XEL.sells: Electricity and natural gas delivered to homes and businesses in states like Minnesota, Colorado and Texas.
XEL.moat: Governments give it the only power lines in its towns, so customers can't pick a rival to deliver power.
XEL.grows: Building wind and solar farms and new power lines, plus data centers and homes that need more electricity.
XEL.risk: Regulators could refuse rate increases, or wildfires and storms could bring repair and lawsuit costs.

XOM.sells: Gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, Mobil motor oil and plastics sold to drivers, airlines and factories.
XOM.moat: Its giant oil fields, refineries and chemical plants let it make fuel cheaper than smaller rivals.
XOM.grows: Pumping more oil and gas from new fields and selling more chemicals and lower-carbon fuels.
XOM.risk: Oil and gas prices can crash, and a world switching to electric cars could need less of its fuel.

XPEV.sells: Smart electric cars sold mostly to Chinese drivers, plus robotaxis and humanoid robots still being built.
XPEV.moat: Its own AI chips and self-driving software help, but many Chinese carmakers sell similar smart EVs.
XPEV.grows: New car models, selling in other countries, and hoped-for robotaxi and robot businesses that are still early.
XPEV.risk: A brutal price war among Chinese EV makers could keep it from making steady profits.

XPO.sells: Trucking that moves smaller shipments for many shippers on one truck, paid by factories and stores.
XPO.moat: Its freight terminals near big cities are very hard and slow for rivals to build or get permits for.
XPO.grows: Charging better prices, adding terminals, and moving more freight when factories and stores ship more.
XPO.risk: A slowdown in factory and store shipping means fewer loads and lower prices across its network.

XPOF.sells: Franchises for studios like Club Pilates, Pure Barre, YogaSix and StretchLab, paid by owners and members.
XPOF.moat: Club Pilates is a well-known name, so new owners and members trust it over a no-name local studio.
XPOF.grows: Opening more studios with new franchise owners and signing up more members at each studio.
XPOF.risk: Fitness fads fade fast, and struggling franchise owners closing studios would shrink its fees.

XRAY.sells: Dental tools, implants, scanners, SureSmile aligners and supplies sold to dentists, plus medical catheters.
XRAY.moat: Dentists who pay for its scanners and CEREC systems learn them and keep using its matching supplies.
XRAY.grows: Selling more implants, aligners and digital tools as dental offices switch to digital work.
XRAY.risk: Rivals like Align and Straumann compete hard, and dentists can delay equipment upgrades in tough times.

XYL.sells: Pumps, water treatment gear and smart water meters sold to cities, factories and building owners.
XYL.moat: Cities install its pumps and meters for many years, then keep using its parts, software and service crews.
XYL.grows: Old pipes needing replacement, water shortages, and cities adding smart meters to stop leaks.
XYL.risk: City budgets can get cut or delayed, pushing back the big water projects it counts on.

XYZ.sells: Square card readers and software for shops, and Cash App for people to send money, pay and save.
XYZ.moat: Cash App gets more useful as more friends join, and shops on Square run their whole business on it.
XYZ.grows: More Cash App users using its card, direct deposit and pay-later loans, and more sellers joining Square.
XYZ.risk: Rivals like Apple, PayPal and Stripe compete hard, and loan losses could rise if customers can't repay.

YPF.sells: Gasoline, diesel, natural gas and fertilizer, paid for by Argentine drivers, farms, factories and power plants.
YPF.moat: It owns big oil fields and the most gas stations in Argentina, but oil and gas sell at world prices anyway.
YPF.grows: Pumping more oil and gas from the giant Vaca Muerta shale rocks and shipping some of it abroad as LNG.
YPF.risk: Argentina's government, price controls and money troubles can squeeze what it earns from every barrel.

YUM.sells: It lets franchise owners run KFC, Taco Bell and Pizza Hut shops and collects fees from their sales.
YUM.moat: People everywhere know and crave the Colonel's chicken and Taco Bell tacos, and a new chain can't copy that.
YUM.grows: Franchise owners opening new restaurants around the world, plus more orders through apps and delivery.
YUM.risk: Hungry customers drifting to cheaper meals, newer chains or cooking at home when money feels tight.

YUMC.sells: KFC and Pizza Hut meals in China, paid for by families, students and workers eating in or ordering delivery.
YUMC.moat: Its huge web of shops, kitchens and delivery trucks across China lets it serve food cheaper and faster.
YUMC.grows: Opening more KFC and Pizza Hut shops in smaller Chinese cities and selling more through its own apps.
YUMC.risk: A weak Chinese economy, price wars with local chains, or tension between China and America.

ZBH.sells: Artificial knees and hips, bone repair parts and the ROSA surgery robot, paid for by hospitals and surgeons.
ZBH.moat: Surgeons train for years on its implants and tools, so changing brands mid-career feels risky to them.
ZBH.grows: More older people needing new knees and hips, plus robots and data tools that help surgeons do it well.
ZBH.risk: Rivals like Stryker winning surgeons with better robots, or hospitals pushing hard for lower prices.

ZION.sells: Loans, checking accounts and cards for small businesses and families across Utah, Texas, California and the West.
ZION.moat: Local bankers know their business customers well, but many other banks offer the same loans and accounts.
ZION.grows: Western states adding people and businesses that need more loans and places to keep their money.
ZION.risk: Bad loans, especially on office buildings, or customers pulling deposits if trust in banks gets shaky.

ZS.sells: Cloud security that guards company workers, apps and AI tools from hackers, paid for by big businesses.
ZS.moat: Once all a company's internet traffic runs through Zscaler, ripping it out is hard, slow and scary.
ZS.grows: Companies moving to the cloud, using more AI and wanting safer ways for staff to work from anywhere.
ZS.risk: Rivals like Palo Alto Networks and Microsoft bundling similar security cheaper inside their own products.

ZTS.sells: Medicines, vaccines and tests for pets and farm animals, paid for by vets, pet owners and ranchers.
ZTS.moat: Vets trust its itch and flea medicines like Apoquel and Simparica, which took years of science to make.
ZTS.grows: Pet owners spending more on their dogs and cats, and new medicines for pain, skin and parasites.
ZTS.risk: Cheaper copycat medicines arriving when patents run out, or a new rival drug that works better.
